📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 Fresh York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Industry observers note that paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of latest love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

Recent findings suggest that the matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its Upcoming York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the New York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1386 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change.
  • It has been revealed that download your playlist as a .txt file.
  • It has been revealed that install Python on your system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

It has been revealed that download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

It has been revealed that install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

In a recent development, download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Industry observers note that run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Recent findings suggest that sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection.".

Sources indicate that on Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Owners can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Pick your speaker on your wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:.

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

In a recent development, exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

Set your levels with the mixer’s faders.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:.

It has been revealed that mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

It has been revealed that my cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:.

It has been revealed that your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:.

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

Industry observers note that you have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

In a recent development, this isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

If you are somebody who read these books and knows where this is going and knows where it ends, the show is not just tracking that, but it's adding really meaningful depth to what that moment will mean eventually, and to what they mean to each other in the moment now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The "Hunger Games" universe is full of wild, larger-than-life characters, especially when we're talking about denizens of the ultra-wealthy and super-powerful Capitol that controls Panem. Every year, during the annual Hunger Games that cull (or "reap") children from each of Panem's tightly controlled and impoverished 12 districts, Capitol citizens help beautify those kids before sending most of them to their deaths, and many Capitol higher-ups pursue plastic surgery and extreme fashion for high-concept looks.

One of those people in the latest "Hunger Games" book and movie, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is the erratic and unreliable District 12 stylist Magno Stift, who's legally married to the surgically-enhanced District 12 chaperone Drusilla Sickle (an unrecognizable Glenn Close in the film) and who's played on screen by Billy Porter. In the novel, our protagonist Haymitch Abernathy — a young version of the District 12 victor played by Woody Harrelson in the previous "Hunger Games" films and Joseph Zada in this fresh prequel — notes that nobody speaks highly of Magno, and "he's every bit as bad as they say." He continues, "While the other stylists do new costumes each year for the parade and interviews that happen before the Games, he seems to have a limitless supply of the same crappy coal miner overalls in an array of sizes.".

It has been revealed that when Magno finally demonstrates up, we see him through Haymitch's eyes: "Magno Stift's sun-leathered skin has been tattooed with a snakeskin pattern. He wears a long shirt made of metal diamonds and no visible pants. His sandals lace all the way up to his pelvis, and from each of his ears dangle tiny, living garter snakes that twist and turn in misery." Eventually, he stops showing up to work when one of his wearable reptiles poisons him. So, why does Magno look familiar in the movie?

According to recent reports, you've definitely seen Magno Stift actor Billy Porter in at least one of his recent high-profile projects, so let me walk you through some of them. After earning fame and acclaim for his role as Lola in the Broadway stage musical version of "Kinky Boots," which won him a Tony and a Grammy, Porter's big-screen career slowly began to take off. Though he did, to be totally fair, appear as a singer in the 1996 classic "The First Wives Club," Porter's newfound name recognition in the 2010s earned him roles in films like "The Humbling" alongside Greta Gerwig and Al Pacino, the 2020 comedy "Like a Boss" with Tiffany Haddish, and 2021's "Cinderella," which gave Porter one of his biggest roles yet as the fairy godparent Fab G.

According to recent reports, during a 2021 interview with People Magazine, Porter talked about gender-flipping the role played by none other than Whitney Houston in the much-loved 1997 TV film adaptation of the stage musical "Rodgers & Hammerstein's Cinderella" starring Brandy. "When I was 14, my dream was to be the male Whitney Houston," the actor quipped before adding, ""Magic has no gender. That is the most crucial for me.".

After starring in "Cinderella" with Camilla Cabello and James Corden, Porter directed the coming-of-age film "Anything's Possible," popped up in the senior comedy "80 for Brady," and got dramatic in "Our Son" with Luke Evans and Andrew Rannells. So, what about Porter's small-screen career? It's booming, too.

Sources indicate that billy Porter's early years on TV include credits on "So You Think You Can Dance" as a performer and stalwart procedurals like "Law & Order," as well as its massively successful spin-off "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" — but after winning that Tony and Emmy and hosting an eight-episode 2013 special called "Land of Lola: Backstage at Kinky Boots," Porter was finally on the map. Aside from "American Horror Story: Apocalypse" and other recurring and guest arcs on reveals like the 2021 "Gossip Girl" reboot, Porter's most recognizable role is as Prayerful "Pray" Tell, an emcee in the New York ballroom scene, on Ryan Murphy's series "Pose." Not only did Porter get the chance to play a character who shares his HIV diagnosis (something the actor revealed in his own life in 2021), he won an Emmy for playing Pray Tell and became the first-ever gay Black man to win in any lead Emmy category. As Porter told People Magazine in 2021, it was also an notable role for him for other reasons:.

Sources indicate that "'Pose' and Pray Tell have been a proxy for my healing. The trauma was so difficult. The grief was so heavy. The antiretroviral drugs [for HIV] came, and everybody moved on. There's a whole generation of us that really never got a chance to process having lived through the AIDS crisis [and] having lived through an epidemic.".

You can see Billy Porter (briefly) play Magno Stift in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which is right now playing in theaters.

According to recent reports, the best part about any Grand Theft Auto game is the cheats, and Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers on that front. Rockstar's latest includes a whole mess of password-protected secrets that will really let you have some fun in Vice City. You'll have to work for them, though. GTA 6's cheats are deeply hidden, and will require you to jump through a few hoops to start using them.

Here's everything you need to know about cheats in GTA 6, from how to unlock them, to the list itself.

[Ed. note: We're still working to hunt down every cheat code, but until we find them all, this will give you an idea of what you'll need to do to unlock them all.].

In a recent development, patch (Nov. 21): We've updated this guide with inputs for three cheat codes.

Industry observers note that if you're looking for a way to enter cheat codes the moment you start GTA 6, you're going to be disappointed. You won't be able to use them until you have fully cleared the story. Once you finish the game and return to your save file, you'll find a newly introduced Cheat tab. Open your Map, tab over to Progression, and scroll to the end to find the Cheats menu.

Industry observers note that you won't get the actual cheat codes immediately. Each one is locked behind a requirement. That can be as simple as finding a specific car to earn the ability to summon it, or as demanding as having Jason and Lucia hold hands for four hours. Once you clear a condition, a pop-up message will tell you that you've unlocked a latest Cheat code, and the unlock requirement in the Cheats menu will be replaced with the code.

Recent findings suggest that notably, your progress throughout the game, even before beating it, does contribute to these requirements. By the time you roll credits and unlock the Cheats menu, you'll likely already have a few of them unlocked.

To activate a cheat code, first pull out your phone by pressing Up on your D-Pad. Then hold down L1 and R1 on the home screen. (We have only been able to test the PS5 version of the game so far, but our assumption is that you'll need to hold LB and RB on Xbox Series X.) While holding those buttons, you'll have to enter the unlocked code with the D-Pad. Based on our testing, you won't be able to activate a code until you've actually beaten the game and unlocked the Cheats menu.

It has been revealed that note that activating a cheat code will disable saving for the rest of your play session. You also won't be able to earn achievements while cheats are on. Always remember to save before activating a cheat so you don't lose any progress.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So you’re trying to pick between the $99 Fitbit Air and the $179 Fitbit Edge. Both have a lot in common — they share the same heart rate sensor, charger, and Google Health app ecosystem. But there are also a lot of differences between the two latest trackers. I’ve been wearing the Fitbit Air since it launched in May 2026, and I’ve recently taken it off my wrist to test the new Fitbit Edge. Read on to find out what I liked and disliked.

If you’re looking to read reviews of both trackers before Black Friday, check out our Fitbit Air review as well as our Fitbit Edge review here on Tom’s Guide.

Recent findings suggest that with no screen, buttons, or alerts to distract you — plus nearly a week of battery — the Fitbit Air is as easy-going as it is affordable. It’s also one of the best fitness trackers of the year and our overall favorite tracker for most Fitbit fans.

The Fitbit Edge is the perfect successor to the Fitbit Charge 6. It sports a bigger/brighter display, easier-to-use controls, more accurate elevation tracking, access to Google's latest health and safety features, and better battery performance. In our Fitbit Edge review, we said it offers just the right amount of fitness tracker for most folks.

If you’re into running, walking, or cycling, the choice is an obvious one — for $80 more than the Fitbit Air, you’re definitely getting a better fitness tracker with the Fitbit Edge. It has built-in GPS, which means you can leave your phone at home, and a 1.34-inch AMOLED display, which allows you to see live feedback as you move.

The Fitbit Edge also has an altimeter, which tracks your elevation during workouts and how many stairs you’ve climbed during the day, and an ECG monitor.

Despite being bigger and heavier than the Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge still does a good job of disappearing on the wrist. It’s dainty, and Google has released a huge range of swappable straps to suit every style. If you want a fitness tracker that’ll disappear, this isn’t quite as tiny as the Fitbit Air, but it still ticks that box.

In a recent development, at 32g and 11.58mm thick, the Fitbit Edge is by no means bulky on the wrist, especially compared to the likes of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 I’m normally wearing. That remarked, compared to the Fitbit Air, it’s still not as comfortable to wear overnight. One of the main selling points of the Fitbit Air is its ultra-light design. It weighs in at 12g, and the textile band is fast-drying, so unlike others on the market (cough, Garmin Cirqa) you won’t be left with a soggy wrist after showering, swimming, or washing the dishes.

Industry observers note that there’s a reason why screenless trackers seem to be a growing trend: once you lose the non-stop buzzing on your wrist, it’s really hard to go back. Again, the Google ecosystem and the fact that these two Fitbits share a charger allows you to swap between the two, but if you’re looking for health, recovery, and sleep tracking and already own a regular watch, the Fitbit Air is the obvious choice.

It’s also worth noting here that, from a health perspective, you’re getting the same experience with the Fitbit Air, and it’s nearly half the price.

Fitbit promises seven days of battery life on both devices, and while I found that to be true with the Fitbit Air, no matter how many workouts I did, it was a different story with the Fitbit Edge.

Of course, this is largely down to the built-in GPS. Out of the box, the GPS on the device is automatically set to dynamic, which means it switches between using your phone’s GPS and the built-in GPS. When you switch the tracker to using the built-in GPS, I found it takes a hit on battery life, using around 11% for an hour-long run, and it didn’t last a full week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

Sources indicate that to aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole upcoming task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Recent findings suggest that “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a newly introduced idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

Recent findings suggest that hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

It has been revealed that “I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro stated. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Sources indicate that hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The crucial part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro noted, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I promptly made a newly introduced design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

In a recent development, in addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro stated. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

Industry observers note that during one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and remarked, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro noted. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I recently switched music streamers from Apple Music to Tidal. I like Tidal's strict anti-AI features, the fact that it pays higher royalties to artists than other major streamers, and its focus on high quality audio. I wrote a post featuring eight hacks for Tidal users, but I wanted to highlight one in particular: How to transfer playlists without paying anything.

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Sources indicate that run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

The Downfall Of The Terminator Franchise Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's a question which has plagued the "Terminator" franchise for decades: why hasn't anyone been able to top the first two films?
  • The ultimate problem with the "Terminator" franchise is twofold.
  • It has been revealed that it's true that the general tone of the first two "Terminator" films is a dark, brooding, horrific one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's a question which has plagued the "Terminator" franchise for decades: why hasn't anyone been able to top the first two films? Setting aside the usual caveat that no sequel can hope to match the dizzying heights of some of the most influential sci-fi/action/horror movies of all time, it's a decent question. After all, every "Terminator" movie save one has involved star Arnold Schwarzenegger in a key role, so it's not like his absence has hurt the series. And even though the return of another key actor in the series, Linda Hamilton, helped 2019's "Terminator: Dark Fate," that film still had its challenges. A conventional wisdom answer to the problem of rescuing the "Terminator" series is that the original creator/director James Cameron should fully come back and make another installment, yet his involvement with "Dark Fate" means success wouldn't necessarily be guaranteed.

The ultimate problem with the "Terminator" franchise is twofold. One glitch is the staggering example set by the first two films, which would be hard for any franchise to overcome. The other concerns the one moment that the downfall of the franchise can be traced back to, which is ironically one of the moments most cited by fans as a highlight of the series: the ending of 2003's "Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines." To be fair, most of "Terminator 3," despite its decent quality, is to blame for putting the franchise on a path it can't quite escape from. Yet it's the ending, as bold as it is, which struck a deterministic note that ended up being too harsh for the series to bear. "Terminator" has always been dark, yet its hopeful subtext is key to its recipe, and that's something which has been left out of every installment since "Terminator 2.".

It has been revealed that it's true that the general tone of the first two "Terminator" films is a dark, brooding, horrific one. After all, these are movies in which Linda Hamilton's Sarah Connor is on the run for her life from an unstoppable killing machine, where either she or her young son John suddenly find themselves having to survive the threats of a dark future while having little help from the modern day around them. Yet an important thing to remember about "The Terminator" is that Skynet's proposal to assassinate Sarah by sending a Terminator back in time was only implemented because John wins the war against the machines in the future. "The Terminator" is a time travel story, and is thus subject to the various paradoxes inherent to the genre. Yet its tale has a deterministic logic to it, one which is predicated on humans surviving despite their near-annihilation by the machines.

According to recent reports, "Terminator 3" effectively undoes the ambiguous hopeful ending of "Terminator 2," where Sarah and John had possibly prevented Judgment Day for good. While the third film's logic is sound from a time travel point of view (i.e. how could any "Terminator" movie have happened if Judgement Day never does), it does make "Terminator 2" feel too much like it was all for nought. Adding to that quiet despair is the bigger tragedy of actually seeing Judgment Day occur, meaning that the efforts of a now adult John (Nick Stahl) to try and stop it from happening again make not just "Terminator 2" but most of "Terminator 3" feel deflating. The ending of "Terminator 3" is a great example of how a cool twist can work logically, yet emotionally undermine a film (and, in this case, a franchise) too much.

Industry observers note that the first two "Terminator" films leaned into the time travel paradox by presenting a deterministic situation while supporting free will. "There's no fate but what we make for ourselves" is a key phrase which can be interpreted several ways, as either a bitter observation or a message of hope. While the deterministic path that "Terminator 3" and "Terminator Salvation" took was logically sound, they didn't provide enough of the aspirational side; the latter film was a time travel story in subtext only.

The next two movies in the franchise course-corrected in a bizarre way, embracing the wide-open possibilities of the series' time travel component with little to no regard for the characters or the audience. "Genisys" is too pleased with its twists to let any of them land emotionally. In comparison, "Dark Fate" has much richer characterizations, yet it alienates from the opening twist, and turns the series' lore on its head in a way that doesn't fully land. The franchise's one shining moment post-"Terminator 2," the TV series "Terminator: The Sarah Connor Chronicles," was sadly canceled just as the intricate narrative it weaved was bearing the type of lore-changing fruit that "Genisys" and "Dark Fate" tried too hard to grow.

In general, the "Terminator" sequels after "Judgment Day" have attempted to serve both the series' deterministic and free will concepts, which are inherently paradoxical. So, while every one of the "Terminator" sequels have introduced some fascinating (and occasionally excellent) ideas, they all revolve around an inescapable fate, whether it's one that already happened or one that will happen. While I believe the series' fate could still be changed, it's ironic that the thing we're hoping gets saved is now the "Terminator" films themselves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is in the wild, one thing has become clear: The open-world crime stuff is secondary. This thing's a life sim. GTA 6's life sim bona fides are so undeniable that, within the first two days of its release, a not-insignificant swath of players have eschewed the elaborate robberies and high-tension shootouts to instead embrace the ancient gaming tradition of "finding IRL locations and Leo memeing at them.".

Players of reality-inspired open-world games have always done this, whether it's finding the Bean in Watch Dogs' version of Chicago or visiting the John Wick hotel in DLC for The Division 2. But with GTA 6, which takes place in a satirized version of Florida called Leonida, players were always going to take it to another level. This game is from Rockstar Games, a studio so well-known for its attention to detail it once infamously implemented horse testicles that shrink in reaction to cold weather. GTA 6 has been in development for a decade. Its leads have conducted "research" trips to Miami-Dade County for just as long. A perfect storm for some ridiculously faithful world design that's resulted in brain-melting levels of realism.

What's most remarkable is that Rockstar's attention to detail isn't just limited to reimagining iconic Miami landmarks like the Adrienne Arsht Center or the E11EVEN nightclub, though the game does have those. It's also found in recreations of nondescript buildings you'd otherwise never think twice about. This design ethos is best illustrated in one viral clip in which an unidentified creator films Jason walking through an apartment complex before coming to a stop on a patio overlooking a South Beach meridian. The creator, continuing to film, stands up in real life, then walks out of their own front door and onto a patio of the same exact building. ("This is crazy [exploding head emoji]," they wrote. "My apartment is in a video game.").

Sources indicate that even in the realm of sports, Rockstar wasn't just drawn to the major leagues. Yes, GTA 6 includes a riff on Miami's Kaseya Cener (homebase of the Miami Heat), but it also includes a pixel-perfect facsimile of the Miami Marine Stadium. Built in the early '60s as a regatta venue, the stadium went on to host film shoots, presidential rallies, and concerts from the likes of Queen, The Who, Jimmy Buffet, and other megawatt stars, according to the nonprofit Restore Miami Marine Stadium. Then, in 1992, Hurricane Andrew took the venue out of commission. It's spent the past three decades collecting rust and graffiti. But in GTA 6, it's just...there. (In August of this year, Miami voters passed a referendum that paves the way for a potential restoration.).

Sources indicate that fans have been unpacking these references throughout the entirety of GTA 6's marketing cycle. Following Rockstar's release of the second GTA 6 trailer, back in May 2025, I could've sworn — based on a vanishingly brief 0.5-second glance — that the South Beach party spot The Clevelander would serve as a location in the game. The bar's marketing department never responded to my initial request for comment. Now that I've played, I can confirm that, yes, it's absolutely in the game, in all its flamingo-pink glory. The Clevelander is somewhat of an institution, having remained a South Beach party spot for decades on the back of some extremely lucky local ordinances, but at face value, it's not all that distinct from any other South Beach bar: neon lights, a questionable pool, overpriced drinks. And yet, it's in GTA 6 too.

It has been revealed that the locations GTA 6 players seem drawn to point out tend to be in the Miami metropolitan area, which makes sense: It's the population nexus of the state. But Vice City encompasses a small portion of Leonida's map, and Florida itself poses no shortage of things to reference beyond the Miami-Dade County limits. Who knows what players will find and Leo meme at? Though there's one thing not worth seeking out. In its quest to construct an alternate reality, Rockstar neglected to include arguably the most Florida landmark of them: Disney World.

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

In a recent development, chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

The original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

Scott Z Burns wrote a fantastic script. Unfortunately for me, as we speak, it's not happening.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What a difference seven-odd months make. Near the tail-end of September 2011, Fox Searchlight dumped Kenneth Lonergan's "Margaret" six years after it was filmed, only for its star, Mark Ruffalo, to Hulk-out in "The Avengers" the following May. But even so, Lonergan's movie — one of the best of the 21st Century — deserves so much better than to merely be remembered as a box office bomb.

You see, one of the joys of live theater is bearing witness to a performer who's captured the music of an uncommonly gifted playwright's dialogue. In my lifetime, I've seen Philip Seymour Hoffman and John C. Reilly make a meal out of Sam Shepard's "True West," Rosemary Harris and Elaine Stritch tear up Edward Albee's "A Delicate Balance," and Jeffrey Wright and Don Cheadle set the stage ablaze with Suzan-Lori Parks' "Topdog/Underdog." On that same level, a late-20-something Ruffalo caused an off-Broadway stir in the fall of 1996 with his portrayal of troubled teenager Walter Straub in Lonergan's finely wrought drama "This Is Our Youth." He exuded shaggily handsome charm as a purposeless kid with a short-term game plan that involves absconding with $15,000 of his wealthy dirtbag father's money.

Industry observers note that lonergan remembered this and cast Ruffalo in his 2000 film classic "You Can Count on Me." Then, when the actor started booking studio gigs, Lonergan cooked up "Margaret." It's a New York City epic about a teenager (Anna Paquin) who struggles to cope with a fatal city bus accident she inadvertently put in motion, with Ruffalo playing the bus driver whose ill-advised, but innocuous, flirtation leads to a horrible accident on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. This is as close to a clean logline as you can get with Lonergan's rich, sophisticated text, which baffled its dilettante, bigoted, multi-millionaire producer Gary Gilbert.

Recent findings suggest that "Margaret" was a talent magnet. Kenneth Lonergan's blisteringly brilliant screenplay drew in Mark Ruffalo, Paquin, Matt Damon, J. Smith Cameron, Allison Janney, Matthew Broderick, Jean Reno, and Rosemarie DeWitt. The great Jeannie Berlin, a Best Supporting Actress Oscar nominee for her knockout work in 1972's "The Heartbreak Kid," also appeared in the movie (her first since 1990's "In the Spirit"), and she was dubbed Best Supporting Actress by the Village Voice Film Poll for her turn as the sister of the victim killed in the aforementioned accident.

Industry observers note that "Margaret" is a drama without villains. Anna Paquin's Lisa is a misguided and impulsive teenager. She is in search of justice where nothing of the sort can be found and tracks down Ruffalo's bus driver. He's well aware of the threat she poses to his steady bus-driving job, though, and shoos her away. But she persists, and her version of the events of that deadly day aren't entirely wrong, yet she still shares some responsibility. Yet, she can't accept that, so her catharsis will not arrive via a conviction.

Structurally, "Margaret" splits its time between Lisa's errant pursuit of justice and her mother (Cameron) as she tries to connect with a suave suitor played by Reno. Everyone loses. But this loss forges a stronger bond between mother and daughter. It binds them anew during a Lincoln Center performance of "The Tales of Hoffman," where, wordlessly, they patch up their wounds. (Heal? No. Those scabs will always be pickable.).

It would be nice if a movie like that could go toe-to-toe with something on the level of "The Avengers," but there it is. Still, if you only really know Lonergan for his Oscar-winning "Manchester by the Sea," make it a priority to finally watch "Margaret.".

Eight Crucial Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet.
  • In a recent development, your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network.
  • Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

In a recent development, your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

Sources indicate that while some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

Recent findings suggest that the password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Recent findings suggest that two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets customers connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Sources indicate that any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Recent findings suggest that routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since the starship Enterprise first launched its mission to boldly go where no one has gone before in 1966, "Star Trek" has inspired countless things that we've seen in our modern world.
  • Sources indicate that there is, however, one thing inspired by "Star Trek" that seems very unlikely, both for its unusual real-world connection and the fact that it seems to run counter to the franchise's vision of a moneyless, post-scarcity utopia: the McDonald's Happy Meal marketing tie-in.
  • Long before it made it to outer space, the Happy Meal got its start in Guatemala, when a franchisee named Yolanda Fernández de Cofiño came up with the idea of offering kid-sized portions to customers in order to draw in families.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the starship Enterprise first launched its mission to boldly go where no one has gone before in 1966, "Star Trek" has inspired countless things that we've seen in our modern world. Astronaut Mae Jemison, for example, credited Nichelle Nichols' performance as Lt. Uhura with inspiring her to become the first African-American woman to make it into space. Even the flip phones of the '90s were at least partially inspired by the design of the communicators on the original "Trek.".

Sources indicate that there is, however, one thing inspired by "Star Trek" that seems very unlikely, both for its unusual real-world connection and the fact that it seems to run counter to the franchise's vision of a moneyless, post-scarcity utopia: the McDonald's Happy Meal marketing tie-in. That's right: "Star Trek: The Motion Picture" was the first movie to be featured in a Happy Meal.

Long before it made it to outer space, the Happy Meal got its start in Guatemala, when a franchisee named Yolanda Fernández de Cofiño came up with the idea of offering kid-sized portions to customers in order to draw in families. McDonald's executives liked the idea and hired advertiser Bob Bernstein, who decided to bundle those smaller portions into a box that would feature bright, kid-friendly colors and a small toy to keep the youngsters entertained while mom and dad threw down on their Massive Macs. Thus, the Happy Meal was born, and after being tested in 1977, it rolled out nationwide in 1979.

Sources indicate that needless to say, it was a hit with customers, but the last piece of this familiar fry-scented puzzle would come at the end of the year, when "Star Trek" was revived for the substantial screen with the entire main cast of the show returning to their roles. When the film ran over budget during production — not to mention injuries and other problems plaguing the set — Paramount's Vice President of Marketing and Licensing, Dawn Steel, was tasked with figuring out how to cover some of the rapidly expanding costs. She went looking for brand partners, and apparently someone at McDonald's was enough of a Trekkie to go for it. This approach was so successful that it would become almost mandatory for blockbuster movies to have some sort of fast-food tie-in as the years went on, a marketing tactic that would even change the direction of entire franchises, like it did with the infamous "Batman Returns" tie-in.

Sources indicate that looking back, doing a Happy Meal tie-in for "Star Trek: The Motion Picture" was, well, kind of a weird choice. As much as "Trek" had become a cultural touchstone due to the popularity of syndicated re-runs after its original three-season run, the film is a pretty slow, ponderous affair. It's largely about negotiating with a sentient space cloud, punctuated with bits of action like the scene where two members of the ship's crew die screaming for almost a full minute in a transporter accident. It's not a particularly gory or violent movie and there's nothing too objectionable, but it's not exactly "Bambi" — which would get its own Happy Meal tie-in in 1988 — either.

According to recent reports, it's especially funny to think about the movie's slow-paced meditations on the unknown and the toll of aging in the context of the Happy Meal itself. Considering that the ad for the Happy Meal involved a Klingon yelling things like "yum-yum" and laughing at the jokes printed on the boxes, they might have given kids a bit of an unrealistic idea of what they were going to get at the movie theater.

How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • It has been revealed that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

It has been revealed that “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

According to recent reports, “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

For Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

According to recent reports, “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

According to recent reports, “Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado stated. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford mentioned, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other massive studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agatha Christie is one of the most popular authors of all time. The English writer crafted many classic stories in the 20th century, and introduced a number of iconic heroes, many of whom are still being adapted to this day. One of these characters is Miss Marple, who made her debut in 1927, when she featured in a short story titled The Tuesday Night Club, which was published in The Royal Magazine.

Then there’s Hercule Poirot, arguably Christie’s most popular fictional character. Christie first introduced the Belgian detective in The Mysterious Affair at Styles, which was written in 1916 and published four years later in 1920. Poirot was a popular character upon release, but Christie’s hero became a sensation around six years later.

Sources indicate that it’s no surprise, then, that Hercule Poirot was brought to movie theaters soon after. The character made his massive screen debut in 1931s Alibi, with Austin Trevor playing the hero. However, Trevor’s iteration of Poirot deviated greatly from Christie’s books in many ways, including not sporting the detective’s classic mustache.

Industry observers note that since then, dozens of actors have gone on to play Poirot in both movies and television. Arguably the greatest Poirot adaptation of all is David Suchet’s series, which began in 1989, but the detective has still had plenty of excellent films, too. For example, both Peter Ustinov and, more recently, Kenneth Branagh helmed Poirot mystery movies that were received with great acclaim.

The most famous Poirot story, in both literature and film and television, is Murder on the Orient Express. Christie first crafted this story in the early 1930s, and it was initially published as a six-part series in the Saturday Evening Post under the name Murder on the Calais Coach. With Murder on the Orient Express, Christie created the perfect locked-in mystery, with all the characters stuck on a train for days, knowing that one (or more) of them is a murderer.

According to recent reports, kenneth Branagh took on the role of Poirot, and the responsibility of adapting Christie’s iconic work, in 2017s Murder on the Orient Express remake. Like many Poirot movies that were released in the 20th century, Branagh assembled an exciting group of actors to play the train occupants. The cast included Johnny Depp, Michelle Pfeiffer, Judi Dench, Penélope Cruz, Willem Dafoe, Daisy Ridley, Leslie Odom Jr., Josh Gad, Derek Jacobi, Olivia Colman, and Tom Bateman.

Industry observers note that branagh’s remake was successful in many ways. The cast was exceptional, especially Michelle Pfeiffer and Willem Dafoe. Additionally, the film looked spectacular, with a blue and white color palette radiating from the screen. Branagh is a critically acclaimed director, and he certainly brought his A-game to this movie.

Yet, Murder on the Orient Express (2017) struggled in some areas, too. For many, the film felt overly familiar, which may be a harsh criticism given that the story is nearly one hundred years old and has been told dozens of times (and in many different languages, too). Additionally, Branagh’s portrayal of Poirot was a bit of a mixed bag. He captured the essence of the character well, but was vastly different physically from how Poirot is described in the books.

Industry observers note that the best of Kenneth Branagh’s three Poirot films was his last, A Haunting in Venice. With this film, it felt as if Branagh had finally found his voice in telling a Hercule Poirot story, both as a director and as an actor. Branagh seems at his most comfortable on screen in this film, and works well within the darker tone that A Haunting in Venice provides.

At the same time, this film felt less predictable than the two that came before, in part because it wasn’t adapting one of Christie’s most famous novels (and because it took more liberties from its source material, too).

Peter Ustinov played Poirot in six films in total, three of which were released in theaters, with the others going straight to television. One of the theatrical releases was Death on the Nile (1978), a film that serves as a much better adaptation of the story than Branagh’s. Like most of the other Poirot films, this movie recruited several high-profile actors.

According to recent reports, there was Peter Ustinov as Hercule Poirot, and he was joined by David Niven, Lois Chiles, Simon MacCorkindale, Mia Farrow, Bette Davis, Maggie Smith, Angela Lansbury, Olivia Hussey, George Kennedy, and Jack Warden. Of these, Mia Farrow, Maggie Smith, and Angela Lansbury truly stood out, all giving exceptional performances. The surrounding film was excellent, too, with amazing visuals (having actually been filmed on location) and a captivating script adaptation of Christie’s original story.

According to recent reports, another Ustinov Poirot film is Evil Under the Sun, which was released in 1982. This is Ustinov’s best Poirot movie, in part because the English actor finds his groove to the fullest here. He’s charming, witty, and genuinely funny, too (such as in the scene where Poirot pretends to swim in a bathing suit).

Like Death on the Nile (1978), Evil Under the Sun also has jaw-dropping visuals, having once again been filmed on location. The film itself is more playful than its predecessors, too, which makes it more entertaining overall.

Recent findings suggest that four decades after the story was first released, Murder on the Orient Express made its way to the major screen with a film of the same name. This movie is a relatively faithful adaptation of the book, telling the story of the murder of American businessman Samuel Ratchett (aka Richard Widmark) aboard the famous Orient Express. From there, Poirot is forced to investigate the crime, and prevent the train journey from getting any more deadly.

Industry observers note that murder on the Orient Express (1974) had a star-studded cast. Albert Finney played Poirot, and did so with his usual charm and enthusiasm. Finney was joined by a number of A-list actors, too, including Lauren Bacall, Ingrid Bergman, Sean Connery, John Gielgud, Vanessa Redgrave, Michael York, Anthony Perkins, and Martin Balsam. Upon the release of the film, the ensemble cast was praised for their respective performances.

In a recent development, in fact, several of these performers received accolades for their work in the film. For example, Bergman won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her role as Greta Ohlsson. More broadly, the film itself was the recipient of six Oscar nominations in total, and that includes a Best Actor nomination for Finney and Best Adapted Screenplay for writer Paul Dehn.

Recent findings suggest that the praise that this adaptation received was well deserved, too. The film does a spectacular job of bringing Christie’s story to the big screen, making these characters (and Hercule Poirot in particular) truly come alive. This film may be a bit dated when watching it in the modern day, however, but Christie’s story still remains timeless in many ways.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it's almost time to close out 2026, so there are only a handful of new episodes of "Saturday Night Live" left this year. NBC's staple late night sketch comedy show is presently in the middle of Season 52, and they're coming off quite a celebrated episode after comedian John Mulaney returned to host for a seventh time. Mulaney has become one of the most reliable returning hosts, which is why he's also one of the best "SNL" hosts of all time.

But that's in the past, and "SNL" is always looking ahead to the next show. As we head into the busy holiday season, you're probably wondering when you can take a break and catch some laughs with a new episode of "SNL." Plus, you don't have time to wait and see whether there's a new episode when Saturday night rolls around. That's why we're here to let you know if there's a new "SNL" on November 21, 2026, as well as keep you posted on what's coming up next for "SNL.".

There is no upcoming episode of "SNL" on November 21, 2026.

John Mulaney's episode was the last of three consecutive episodes running from Halloween through mid-November, and it's rare that executive producer Lorne Michaels pushes the cast and crew to do more than that in a row, as the series is truly exhausting to produce each week. (You can learn more about how the show is produced through a series of "SNL" documentaries available on Peacock that chronicle exactly how the show's team makes it happen over and over again.).

You would do well to check out John Mulaney's episode, if you haven't already, because it delivered the best episode of the season, including this sketch that every family is probably fighting about:.

Plus, let's not forget that Mulaney delivered what has now become a traditional New York-based musical sketch, including a special guest appearance by former cast member Bowen Yang:.

Recent findings suggest that since Thanksgiving is coming up, "SNL" is taking a short break before returning for several more episodes in December. Speaking of which...

"SNL" will be back with a fresh episode on December 5. More than likely, we'll get another three episodes in a row before Lorne Michaels gives the cast and crew their traditional holiday break over Christmas and through New Year into mid-to-late January. There's a chance we might only get two, since the third Saturday would be December 19, and that's pretty close to Christmas, but we don't know for sure yet.

When "SNL" returns on December 5, the episode will be hosted be someone who has been drumming up a lot of buzz, thanks to their appearance in a highly discussed movie that's still in theaters now.

Industry observers note that amanda Seyfried will be making her hosting debut on the December 5 episode. Yes, this is the first time Seyfried has hosted the show. In fact, this is the first time she'll be making any appearance on "SNL," having never previously made a cameo in other episodes. But she's proven to be funny in comedies like "Mean Girls" and "Ted 2" (pictured above) over the years, so we're excited to see what she can do on "SNL.".

Seyfried is at the moment riding high after a (SPOILER ALERT) riveting appearance in "You Can See Everything," the documentary from directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder that follows convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes as she prepares to serve her federal prison sentence. Seyfried's role in the movie is so compelling and unique that some are wondering if there's potential for her to get a Best Supporting Actress nomination (she partakes in pivotal reenactments that help define the movie's fascinating framework and revelations).

In addition, Seyfried voices Cinderella in an animated Netflix movie called "Steps," hitting the streaming service starting on November 20, and she also stars in "The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd," a upcoming movie written and directed by actor Tim Blake Nelson. The latter has been playing film festivals across the country, but it's not clear if it will be given an awards qualifying release in theaters otherwise before the end of 2026.

Seyfried will be joined by musical guest Don Toliver, a rapper whose fifth studio release, "Octane," became his first number one album this year.

"SNL" typically starts at 11:30pm ET, though that can potentially get disrupted by live sporting events or breaking news, which can delay the show slightly. However, in those cases, the show still unfolds live, but it's tape-delayed for those who will be watching "live" on NBC and/or Peacock.

When "SNL" is airing live, you can watch either on NBC through your usual television provider or by streaming live through Peacock.

It has been revealed that don't worry if you're not at home when the show starts at 11:30pm ET. NBC uploads new sketches to YouTube not long after their air live. Plus, full new episodes are available to watch on Peacock the next day.

Sources indicate that in addition, Peacock holds a library of old "SNL" episodes from across the show's decades-spanning history. However, those episodes don't always have all the sketches or musical performances due to complicated licensing rights for music.

For those who might like a little comedic flavor from across the pond, there's also "Saturday Night Live UK." Though you can't easily watch live here in the United States, latest episodes of "SNL UK" hit Peacock on Sunday evenings the day after new episodes air.

After you watch the latest episode of "SNL," be sure to check out "The Ten to One Podcast," featuring me as one of the hosts recapping and reviewing upcoming episodes of "SNL.".

Stay tuned for the latest details on when "SNL" has a upcoming episode, right here at /Film.

I’ve watched every Hunger Games movie — and the best one isn't what you think
