How I made a custom game engine for Satelital

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spectralorbit

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch.
  • It has been revealed that as a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch.
  • Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch. And last week I released Satelital, a rule-discovery game about learning alien logic.

It has been revealed that as a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch. My motivation was to learn the actual fundamentals behind the technology of videogames. This meant I had to build most of the tools I would need myself, including the game engine, renderer, puzzles, editors, UX, design, art and music.

Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it.

Recent findings suggest that the main reason I got into programming was the idea of eventually working on games. I spent many years working on web and building mobile apps. It was fun, but I felt like I wasn't going in the direction I really wanted to.

So one day, after listening to every Jonathan Blow talk I could find and playing too much The Witness, I decided to finally give it a try.

It has been revealed that I spent many days and countless hours looking for the best tool I could use to make a game, but nothing left me satisfied. The closest I got to having fun with gamedev was with the LÖVE framework making a few jam games. But even with that, it felt quite limiting to not really know what was happening behind the graphics I somehow managed to animate on my screen.

I remember hearing about shaders and parallel programming. The concept always felt very arcane and mysterious to me, but now writing them is the thing I enjoy the most while coding.

I finally decided to jump into the swimming pool and actually learn C⁠+⁠+. I had to learn how to manage memory and how not to shoot myself in the foot with the wrong tools. I started using SDL2 while trying to use the C⁠+⁠+ standard library as little as possible.

Before getting too deep into the engine, I actually finished a prototype of the puzzles not long after learning how to draw some simple graphics with C⁠+⁠+. It had very early versions of four kinds of puzzles that mostly survived until the final game. It was made entirely with SDL2, but I soon realised that if I wanted more interesting graphics, I would need to use shaders and decided to switch to OpenGL.

Sources indicate that with the help of LearnOpenGL I quickly had a triangle on the screen. From there, learning things like lighting, tonemapping, normal maps, shader effects and everything else opened up a whole newly introduced way of looking at computers for me. Before, my idea of how a computer actually draws to the screen was quite naive. When I started learning graphics I just wanted to be able to manually change the color of each pixel individually, but in the end the idea of running a program in parallel for every pixel clicked for me.

One thing that made a huge difference while working on shaders was having code reloading. Before that, I had a complex system that stored constant values in config files, which would later get passed through uniforms into shaders. Then a custom development menu would provide some UI to tweak those values at runtime. With that I stopped having to reload and compile everything for every little change I wanted to make.

It worked, but having to maintain all this extra scaffolding was slowing me down. Another unexpected downside of this setup was that, in some cases, the shader compiler couldn't optimize the code as well as it otherwise could, since knowing constant values ahead of time helps it make better decisions.

It has been revealed that having shader reloading made a huge difference. Being able to change some code, save the file and immediately see the result on screen was very useful. Iterating on shaders became much faster and more fun. This was probably my biggest regret about not having it from day one.

Industry observers note that for a massive part of the development I was using SDL2, mainly to create a window, read input and get a surface to draw on. But it felt wrong to depend on a library that was several times bigger than my entire game just to handle a few seemingly simple tasks. I decided to drop that dependency and make my own platform layer that I could understand and maintain. I wouldn't have to wait for someone else to fix a bug anymore because now I could just change it myself. It wasn't that hard to end up with a single file with a few thousand lines of code that supported both macOS and Windows. I'm now looking forward to working on mobile and console ports, it feels like it might be a fun thing to work on.

Sources indicate that at some point during development, compile times were getting longer, so I decided to look into what was going on. I checked where all that time was going, and to my surprise a lot of it was spent compiling standard library things. Stuff like std::function was particularly slow for example.

Recent findings suggest that eventually I realised that I wasn't actually forced to use the standard library just because it was there, and the subset I needed wasn't that hard to implement myself. It took me a month to replace it with my own base library, but it was so worth it. Not only did compile times get faster, but I also learned how a lot of things I had always taken for granted in other languages actually worked.

At some point I started looking into Vulkan because I wanted HDR. I couldn't get it working on macOS through OpenGL and I was worried about OpenGL being deprecated in the future. Also I didn't really want to build the whole engine around an API that might become deprecated.

Moving to Vulkan was rough at the beginning. There was so much boilerplate to type and understand. Also, when I started working on the engine, there wasn't much documentation around how to implement a good backend with it. In hindsight, I feel that even though I got a lot of valuable things from tutorials and books, most of them were overcomplicating something that could be much more straightforward. I still have nightmares about trying to resize a window...

Getting Vulkan working on macOS was actually surprisingly easy thanks to MoltenVK. It was nice not having to learn Metal and being able to keep the same codebase on Windows. The engine started out only working on macOS, so I was afraid I'd run into a lot of challenges when porting it to Windows. But I was quite nice to see Vulkan just working the same day I tried it.

My philosophy from day one was to only grow the engine towards exactly what I needed. This was a long solo project, so trying to build a general purpose engine first, without knowing what I needed, would probably have meant never finishing the game. I did waste time on things I thought I would need, but I cut them when I knew I wouldn't be using them. Because I was also learning C/C⁠+⁠+ along the way, I made many coding mistakes but I wasn't afraid of major refactors. Cleaning the codebase helped me bring up my morale.

From the beginning I wanted to avoid making a 3D engine since I knew that might complicate things too much. But after I finished the prototype, I kept learning about shader techniques and effects. So in the end, my goal was to get as close as possible to a 3D look without actually having to load any 3D polygons.

To do this, I chose an orthographic top-down view so I could just prerender the assets in Blender and then load their albedo, normal and height maps as textures. Having a fixed camera meant I could render all the assets from exactly the same perspective, so they would always fit together properly in the game. Other things that needed to be animated were drawn in the pixel shader using SDFs. The terrain of the planets was too big to be stored entirely in textures, so in most cases I had to procedurally generate them in shaders too.

Since I wanted a 3D look with dynamic lighting, I also needed dynamic shadows. The final approach I settled on was ray marching. With the height map of each prop, I could make them look as if they were actually sitting in a 3D space, even though everything was still rendered in 2D. In the shader I basically march along the direction of the light and sample the height map to figure out where a shadow should be drawn.

Having the height map was also useful for other things. For example, I could use that information to make objects interact with the water in a convincing way. Objects can actually submerge in the ocean instead of looking like flat images drawn on top of it. This is also how the waves can interact with the shore around an island.

Industry observers note that the engine was only one part of making a complete game. I also had to build a custom level editor. I wanted to make it as easy as possible to design and iterate on puzzles, so I integrated an edit mode that allowed me to change puzzles and the enviroment at runtime and see the changes in real time.

In a recent development, it was quite fun to quickly draw and tweak puzzles directly in the game. It helped me discover so many ideas. After making thousands of puzzles, you start to develop a sense of beauty about how a puzzle should be. Having this editor allowed me to get into the zone. I could spend hours making puzzles without actually thinking about the tool I was using.

Industry observers note that alongside the in-game editor I made a custom Blender plugin that could load my level config files into Blender. The game had a file watcher that could detect changes in the baked textures of the 3D models rendered by Blender. But it could also load level data and provide another way to edit. The upside was being able to just use Blender tools like multi-select, but aside from that, it wasn't actually that useful. It was cool to make though, and it's an interesting demo. But just being able to edit things in-game was much better, since you can see how it will actually look in the end. Though having mentioned that, looking at the levels in an actual 3D environment feels quite nice.

Building the game with all these custom tools brought some concerns. They worked on my machine, but when I started playtesting I began to find lots of bugs that were tricky to reproduce. The hardest ones were related to graphics, due to differences in hardware and drivers on machines I didn't have access to. Tools like Vulkan validation layers were quite useful, though they didn't catch everything.

Sources indicate that another thing that was tricky to deal with was shader compatibility. When using GLSL, if you rely heavily on making visual effects with noise related functions, you will find issues with things like sin or pow because the specification doesn't guarantee their precision. So I had to be constantly checking that everything looked the same on as many different hardware configurations as I could find. For a while, I didn't notice that the distribution pattern of my stars looked different across vendors. It looked correct, but I wanted to have the same placement of stars wherever you played to make it feel more like an actual place.

Sources indicate that having good logs to see how the internals of the game were working ended up being very useful. It was essential for me to have them after I released the demo and started getting feedback from users who were seeing errors I couldn't reproduce. Many of them reported a black screen when trying to open the game for the first time, and these were caused by many different kinds of problems. Sometimes it would be a missing extension, sometimes a third party Vulkan layer injecting code that prevented the frame from being drawn, or some other particular driver matter. Without the logs showing the exact point when the error happened, it would have been almost impossible to fix these bugs without having the actual hardware.

The logs ended up being quite useful for performance. For example, when trying to do optimizations for Intel GPUs, I noticed that some of the biggest shaders were being compiled in a non-optimal way. I basically ran the whole game in just 2 big shaders, one to blend the scene with all the quads, and another pass where I do lighting, shadows and effects like water, where the final normal and height map of the scene are presented. Because these shaders were so big, they couldn't be compiled for SIMD16.

These integrated Intel GPUs are quite common on laptops, and they can shade 16 pixels at once, but only if everything in the shader fits in a small amount of very fast memory. Because my shaders grew so much and I wasn't even aware that this would be an actual issue, the driver was quietly falling back to shading 8 pixels at a time, making the game run noticeably slower. Once I had this information in the logs, I could see what I needed to trim down. I reduced the number of values I needed to keep around as much as possible, while also avoiding duplicated code caused by things like macros until everything fit again.

During development I was always careful about how demanding the game was, but after switching to a faster computer I started paying less attention to it. It's quite easy to just settle for something that looks good enough and move on to the next thing when you're busy. That's why I started targeting the Steam Deck and aiming for stable 90 FPS. It helped me keep performance in sight and avoid things that would make the game too slow on low-powered platforms.

Industry observers note that I feel like I threw away a lot of work during development because the art and design of the game changed several times. In hindsight, I think it was good to keep the mentality of avoiding things that would make the game slow and keeping an eye on the performance stats. But it was only towards the end of the game that I could simply focus on performance without worrying about optimizing things in a way that would make them hard to generalize or reuse in the future, since the game was finished.

In the end I actually added a performance mode that tones down a few special effects, but I think it was a good decision to do that when the game was finished. Otherwise, you suddenly need to be testing and tweaking more than one version of the game while making changes and adding newly introduced things.

A frame limiter was something else I added to help slower laptops maintain a stable framerate. This also brought the necessity of adding an option to draw the cursor in hardware. For the whole development I was drawing the cursor within the game in software, and that meant some lag was unavoidable. Many users complained about this when the demo was released.

Sources indicate that this happens when you use Vsync because the last frame you're seeing is actually buffered, so the frame is already behind the input. The OS has a special mode for drawing the cursor that prevents these concerns, but then you lose the ability to apply effects to it, like fluid animations or doing some lighting around it. Being aware of this also helped me focus on reducing the input lag of the game as much as possible. When running the game with the frame limiter, you notice immediately that the cursor becomes super laggy. For that case, having a hardware cursor was necessary.

Looking back on all these details, being able to change basic engine things like that is super hard, or almost impossible, with closed engines. I worked with Unity before, doing some ports, and the mentality there was that you had to follow a set of "good practices" and deal with whatever was decided for you, even though the hardware in most cases could do better. It was very rough and slow at the beginning when making a custom engine, but the freedom you get at the end of development is very satisfying.

It has been revealed that I feel lucky about how I got the chance to take this long journey and actually make it to the end. I feel like I stumbled into something really interesting that made me lose count of all the nice moments of realization I had while working on this project.

After all these years, I'm quite happy now to have found the perfect excuse to actually study the things I love the most to work on.

In a recent development, if you enjoyed this article, consider giving Satelital a try. The game is available on Steam, with a free demo available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looks like Hollywood could be heading into the newly introduced year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

It has been revealed that “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump stated. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’.

Trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Trump stated his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors confirmed more than 60 newly introduced House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he remarked, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

According to recent reports, “Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she noted in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

Recent findings suggest that A floor vote has yet to be announced, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s fresh Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

According to recent reports, this year is a significant year for anniversaries of some of our biggest franchises, and Pokémon is just one example. It has been three decades since the first video games, Pokémon Red and Pokémon Green, released in Japan on 27 February 1996, after Satoshi Tajiri came up with the idea and teamed up with Ken Sugimori to create the original designs of some of our favorite 'mons.

Now, 30 years on, and Pokémon is one of the biggest franchises in the world, and with its tenth generation expected to begin next year with the launch of Pokémon Winds and Waves for the Nintendo Switch 2, the Nintendo universe indicates no signs of slowing down.

With over 1,000 Pokémon making up the Pokédex, some faces are more familiar than others, and as the franchise's mascot, nobody is more recognizable than Pikachu. Designed by artist Atsuko Nishida with help from Ken Sugimori, Pikachu was released internationally in North America in 1998 and has become the face of the franchise ever since. As such, they have had many different designs, and its 30th anniversary redesign is no different.

To help celebrate 30 years of Pokémon, and of course, Pikachu, Pokémon Co. has declared a 6-centimeter solid gold Gholdengo. Not only that, but Pikachu will also be standing by their side. With the Gholdengo statue consisting of 730 sheets of gold leaf and standing at a life-size 3.9 feet, Pikachu will not be far behind with 200 sheets of gold leaf and measuring just about 20 inches tall. However, the slightly small catch here, is that the Gholdengo statue comes in at just under $10k.

Industry observers note that from September 30th to October 5th, 2026, the pair of statues were available to view on the eighth floor of Yokohama Takashimaya, Japan, but if you wish to see them in the flesh now, you will have to fork out on that eye-watering price tag. However, there is no denying that they will make for the ultimate collectible. What indicates 30 years of a franchise more than gold-clad figures that cost an arm and a leg to purchase?

Over on r/pokemon, fans discussed the brand-new collectibles, including the amount of gold used and what it means for that price tag, with one user sharing, "A fitting metaphor for how materialistic this franchise has become lately." Another agreed, adding, "TPC really is doing anything except working on refining their games, aren't they? At this point, Pokémon isn't a game license anymore, it's just a franchise of products. And yeah, no Pokémon player will be able to afford this." Another user had a handy tip, sharing, "If you buy $8,000 of gold and pay someone $1,000 to cast this, you can get two.".

It has been revealed that as we gear up for a brand-upcoming Pokémon era, we can only imagine what the next thirty years will have in store for us. Now, however, we can look forward to the launch of Pokémon Winds and Waves, which is just as exciting as a gold-clad Gholdengo and Pikachu, but a lot cheaper.

For example, not only do all three tell you how long you slept, but also how much of that sleep duration was spent in deep sleep, REM sleep, and core sleep (along with how long your night-time awakenings last). They also all provide sleep scores, which measure your overall sleep quality on a scale of 1 to 100.

According to recent reports, you can find the key sleep metrics in the Oura app, Garmin Connect app, and the Apple Health app respectively. For the screenless Oura and Garmin, this is the only way to view your sleep data. But you get immediate feedback from your Apple Watch via the Vitals app on the monitor.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide more sleep tracking accuracy than the Oura Ring 4, with a build that improves the sensors' contact with skin and 12% more accuracy in its overnight Heart Rate Variability (HRV) monitoring.

I've found the Oura Ring one of the most dependable consumer sleep trackers on the market. It's especially good at knowing when you're asleep vs awake; studies show up to 96% accuracy when compared to clinical polysomnography (PSG).

Sources indicate that I can see the Oura Ring 5's accuracy first hand. For instance, my Apple Watch sleep scores are always much higher than my Oura Ring — despite regularly getting under seven hours of sleep.

That stated, the Apple Watch does provide a sleep apnea detection tool (available on the Apple Watch Series 10 and up), which analyzes your breathing patterns to detect disturbances that might signal sleep apnea.

Meanwhile, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor provides a readiness score, which tells you how prepared your body is to handle daily activities (such as workouts) based on your sleep data.

According to recent reports, our lead tester for the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor, Eve Davies, remarked that the Garmin is "more focused on overnight breathing rates, oxygen levels and respiration rates — is essentially more ‘nerdy’ and geared towards athletic recovery". For data lovers, there's a lot to unpack.

Industry observers note that it's also worth mentioning that the Oura Ring 5's sleep latency metric is missing from the Apple Watch and Index Sleep Monitor. It has been revealed that however, the lifespan of an Oura Ring is that of a giant tortoise when compared with the Apple Watch. The Apple Watch requires daily charging, with the latest 12th Generation's battery life lasting no longer than 24 hours.

The Garmin has quite a lengthy battery life, lasting up to eight nights (however, this can depend on your sleep duration). However, you also wear it less than the Oura Ring 5 or Apple Watch — if you strapped it to yourself all day, expect that battery life to go right down.

✅ You value optimal sleep comfort: Thanks to a custom fit and a sleek, lightweight build, the Oura Ring 5 is perfect for a barely-there feel.

✅ You don't own an iPhone: You need an iPhone to set up your Apple Watch, so consider the Oura Ring 5 if you're an Android user.

✅ You don't want to pay monthly fees: The Apple Watch has no hidden subscription costs.

✅ You want immediate feedback: With a screen to view your metrics, the Apple Watch is the only option that doesn't require fiddling about with an app.

✅ You want more versatility: There's a lot more to the Apple Watch than sleep tracking, including highly-rated fitness tracking, and there are plenty of models to suit your requirements.

✅ You want the most budget-friendly tracker: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is never sold over $170, and you can reliably find it on sale during holiday seasons.

✅ You just want a sleep tracker: While the Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch put a lot of energy into fitness and health tracking, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is strictly for sleep tracking.

✅ You want a long battery life: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor can last up to eight nights on a single charge.

According to recent reports, yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the latest installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most notable part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:.

It has been revealed that in our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your people and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect[2]. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.

In a recent development, notes:[1] Ultimately, you have limited resources. Architecture is about trading off some requirements, so that your app can run with limited resources. Take CAP theorem as an example. You have to trade off consistency or availability or partition tolerance for your database. If you don't understand that tradeoff and ask AI to build a database that has all 3, it would reinvent Google Spanner++ and expect Google scale datacenter to run it.[2] This post is trending on HN. Some have correctly pointed out that good developers already do architecture and bad architects propose ivory tower architecture that falls apart during implementation. I have built ivory tower architecture whenever I am handsoff. This will become more common with AI, if we don't debug its code or don't hand code critical parts of the app from time to time. So, don't stop coding completely, but it's not a full time job anymore.

In a recent development, all-in-one soundbars are a dangerous game. How does one balance center channels for dialogue with a subwoofer for the best blockbuster movie action? In the case of the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus, with semi-difficulty.

Sources indicate that don’t get me wrong, the price is incredibly appealing — $249 for a 3.1-channel soundbar is super affordable — and the minimalist design won’t cause any controversy. But is this enough to make it one of the best soundbars?

Yes and no. Unfortunately, the bass tends to overpower dialogue in action-heavy scenes. But could this still be the soundbar for you if you only watch TV and YouTube? Find out in this Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus review.

If you’re looking for a reason to buy the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus, that sweet, sweet MSRP is the biggest one.

Industry observers note that at $249 at Amazon U.S. ($139 on sale) and £249 at Amazon U.K., the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is incredibly cheap for what you get. It’s an all-in-one “Dolby Atmos” soundbar — yes, that means with a built-in subwoofer. The basic model, Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, is $119, so you’re essentially paying $130 for a built-in subwoofer.

Recent findings suggest that at this price point, there’s very little competition. Of course, there’s the Samsung B750F ($297, 2025 model), which has a separate subwoofer and 5.1 channels (more upfiring speakers for better surround sound). Even so, this is $50 pricier, which can be a dealbreaker if you’re on a rigid budget.

It has been revealed that I’ve also tested the Samsung Q600F — MSRP of $499 but often on sale in the $300s — which is 2025’s model but has a 3.1.2 channel setup, which is the minimum you need for genuine Dolby Atmos. I’ll get into this more below, but that’s the long and short of it.

Industry observers note that the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349 with a 3.1 channel — so the same as the Amazon Plus and without the surround channels present on the Samsung Q600F — which I would recommend over the Plus if you have a little more to spare. Its separate subwoofer provides a stronger bass response without overpowering dialogue, unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus.

Like the $119 Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus model also has EQ modes. These are as follows: “Music”, “Movie”, “Sports”, and “Night”. There’s also individual bass level adjustment if you want to get really particular with your listening experience.

There's a dialogue mode, but this didn't isolate speech as well as I wanted it to, especially in louder, action-heavy scenes.

According to recent reports, music mode (connected via Bluetooth) is fine, although the bass was a little boomy and the vocals a little too sharp. I would recommend grabbing one of the best speakers, like the JBL Flip 7, to listen to music at home.

Sources indicate that so let’s get one thing straight: the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus does not have “true” Dolby Atmos. If a soundbar doesn’t have side-firing or up-firing channel speakers, it physically cannot project soundwaves in that way.

In Top Gun: Maverick's dogfighting scene, I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV.

According to recent reports, however, the Plus has “Dolby Atmos”, which means it can technically decode Atmos signals. While this obviously doesn’t produce a genuinely immersive experience, it does have its moments. In the dogfighting scene in "Top Gun: Maverick," I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV. As I’ll get into later, this pushed the dialogue to the back of the soundstage, resulting in me straining to hear speech.

It has been revealed that dolby Atmos was better in “K-Pop Demon Hunters, which is really surprising. Usually, “Top Gun: Maverick” blows other movies out of the water in terms of Atmos. Cheering crowds were louder and more immersive in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," and some dialogue was positioned well in the up-firing speakers. One character's voice was particularly crisp and immersive — the lowest female voice — which makes me think the soundbar is better at isolating lower mids than sub-bass.

Despite having a range of EQ modes and a palatable price, unfortunately, the Plus gets a 3.5-star rating from me for a reason. There's one majorly crucial thing holding it back.

According to recent reports, unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus really struggles to differentiate between dialogue and bass layers in action-heavy scenes. “Top Gun: Maverick” was particularly egregious here: Bass often overpowered dialogue, especially when the soundtrack was relatively heavy in flying scenes. I could barely hear Maverick's radioed dialogue to the characters in the control room over the string-heavy soundtrack and the flying airplane.

Recent findings suggest that this was incredibly surprising, as the cheaper non-Plus model excelled in the very same scene. Bass volume was set to the minimum, and I watched on “Movie” mode.

While not as egregious in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," I still struggled to hear some dialogue. Surprisingly, the music sounded excellent in this movie, but dialogue is arguably the most vital part. If you can’t hear the actors, what’s the point?

In a recent development, the consequences are really enormous: I struggled to make out dialogue in action-heavy scenes across the three movies I watched, which isn’t really what you want when using a soundbar. The whole purpose of a soundbar is to make dialogue more intelligible.

According to recent reports, however, I also watched "Gilmore Girls" on basic Netflix, which sounded great. If you predominantly watch TV or YouTube, I don't think you'll notice this concern. It's just a concern for action movie buffs. In that case, I'd recommend checking out the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375).

At $249, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is incredibly affordable. There are very few soundbars that can beat this in terms of penny-per-performance.

Industry observers note that the aforementioned Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349, so $100 more than the Amazon model, but has a dedicated subwoofer and a center channel for dialogue. I would personally save up more and buy the Sony model over the Amazon.

But if I were to save more money, I'd choose the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar (non-Plus) over the Plus version. Sure, there's no subwoofer, but it's just $119 and genuinely sounds fantastic. It's the best budget soundbar I've ever tested.

Hmm. This is a tricky one. I loved the basic Amazon Fire TV Soundbar — if you want seriously great sound at a low price, get that one. The extra $130 for the Plus model? Not worth it, if you ask me. I would either spend an extra $50 on the Samsung B750F or an extra $130 on the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, due to a lack of communication between the built-in subwoofer and the main channel speakers, dialogue can be overpowered during action-heavy scenes. Consequently, I can’t recommend this model over the Samung B750F. Personally, I would either get the cheaper Amazon Fire TV Soundbar or the aforementioned Samsung model. Or, you could save up a little extra for the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375) or the with Rears version ($489).

However, if you have an Amazon Fire TV and want something capable of integrating into the ecosystem seamlessly (even though you'll need a separate Fire stick or Fire TV), without having to spend an extra $50 on the B750F, the Plus is a great deal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon can’t seem to help itself from spinning off its biggest hit demonstrates into prequels, sequels, and offshoots. Bosch has been spun off into Bosch: Legacy; The Terminal List has been spun off into The Terminal List: Dark Wolf; Hazbin Hotel has been spun off into Helluva Boss. But it can be forgiven, because these spinoffs usually end up being worthwhile. The Boys’ animated spinoff Diabolical is one of the only anthology shows without a single weak episode, and its college-set spinoff Gen V showed us a whole upcoming side of that universe, with a cast of characters worth investing in.

Earlier this year, Reacher debuted its own spinoff, Neagley, and not only was it a satisfying expansion of the franchise; it may have even joined Frasier and Better Call Saul in the ranks of superior spinoffs that outshine their predecessor. After Prime Video released Reacher’s season 4 finale, it came with the entire first season of Frances Neagley’s spinoff.

Recent findings suggest that neagley is Jack Reacher’s closest confidant and ally, and she’d shown up to help him save the day in every previous season of Reacher, but she was absent from season 4, because she was being promoted to series lead. While Reacher was fighting political corruption and international assassins, Neagley was fighting a sinister cult in Chicago.

Neagley follows a pretty predictable plot, but it’s a worthwhile ride. It’s well-paced, agreeably action-packed, and stuffed with great actors, including Sten herself, who gets to bring more depth and dramatic weight to the character here than she ever did in her supporting roles on Reacher. The title character in Neagley is every bit the stone-cold badass she was in her previous appearances, but when she takes center stage in her own show, she gets to dig a little deeper into the vulnerability and insecurity and fear being masked by that badass facade.

The series opens with Neagley’s childhood friend stepping in front of a train. His death looks suspicious, as does his recent residency with a local cult, so Neagley jumps on the case, determined to get to the bottom of it. From there, you’re hooked. If you’ve seen the last four seasons of Reacher, you know Neagley and her friends will eventually have enough evidence to storm the cult’s compound and blast them to kingdom come, but there’s a lot of great character drama and riveting action set-pieces on the way to that inevitable climax.

It has been revealed that reacher is one of the most formulaic highlights on television, and that’s what we love about it. In an age of subversive, serialized TV dramas, Reacher is a refreshingly old-school procedural about a noble hero drifting from town to town, serving vigilante justice. Every season, you know what you’re getting — a newly introduced town, a new threat, a new supporting cast, etc. — and there hasn’t been a weak installment yet, but Neagley may have beaten Reacher at its own game.

Neagley follows the Reacher formula to the letter. A personal conflict draws the hero into a dark conspiracy, she amasses a merry band of misfit allies including a love interest and a plucky kid to mentor, and she follows a series of clues and shootouts to an explosive climactic showdown. It satisfies as a Reacher-style action-adventure, but it goes above and beyond the expectations of that formula.

Reacher famously never changes, but Neagley actually evolved as a character throughout the first season of her spinoff. She confronted her demons, overcame her haphephobia, and embraced all her new friends as a found family. Neagley was a much darker, weirder show than Reacher, but it also hit on a deeper emotional level.

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

According to recent reports, today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI indicates.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

Industry observers note that the $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI indicates it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole latest world of cinema.

Video game adaptations have become more or less accepted in the mainstream these days, but the landscape was quite different around a decade ago. Back then, nearly every attempt to adapt a major video game franchise ended unsuccessfully, although there were a handful of outliers. A major Assassin's Creed movie starring Michael Fassbender received poor reviews and underperformed at the box office, while an even more expensive Warcraft adaptation failed to spawn sequels as well. Now, another relic of that era — one that actually made money — is about to be removed from its free streaming home.

Video game adaptations have certainly come a long way in the last decade. They've earned critical acclaim thanks to HBO's The Last of Us and this year's Resident Evil reboot, and commercial success thanks to A Minecraft Movie and The Super Mario Bros. Movie. A sequel to the latter film, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, was released to massive success earlier this year.

The niche is set to expand in the coming years, thanks to high-profile adaptations such as Call of Duty, The Legend of Zelda, and Elden Ring. However, the movie we're talking about was released during a particularly difficult period for video game movies, when the market was dominated by the poorly received Resident Evil franchise headlined by Milla Jovovich. Released in 2014, the film featured a Breaking Bad alum in the lead role, along with an MCU cast member, and a future Oscar winner.

Industry observers note that we're talking, of course, about Need for Speed. An adaptation of the long-running racing series, the film was directed by Scott Waugh, who helmed the Alan Ritchson-led action film Runner this year. Unlike its fellow video game adaptations of the era, Need for Speed was a solid hit at the box office, grossing more than $200 million worldwide against a reported budget of $66 million.

It has been revealed that however, the reviews simply weren't positive enough, nor did the film attract the sort of fan support necessary for the studio to green-light a sequel. It now holds a 23% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "With stock characters and a preposterous plot, this noisily diverting video game adaptation fulfills a Need for Speed and little else." Starring Breaking Bad favorite Aaron Paul, Dominic Cooper, Imogen Poots, and Rami Malek, the film will be removed from Tubi in the United States on December 1. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#74278. Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (526 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mozilla ↗ Open Full Page

Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mozilla

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world.
  • But there remains an vital limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.
  • According to recent reports, this has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone customers because many of these are built within our browser engine, Gecko.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an vital limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

According to recent reports, this has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone customers because many of these are built within our browser engine, Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

It has been revealed that as a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we noted Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced newly introduced rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Recent findings suggest that nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

Sources indicate that since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply patch the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a substantial tech tech giant. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

12 Best Robert Downey Jr. Movies To Watch Before Avengers: Doomsday, Including Oppenheimer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are some essential Robert Downey Jr.
  • According to recent reports, RDJ’s career reached an entirely fresh level when he joined the MCU timeline, becoming the face of a franchise that would dominate blockbuster cinema.
  • It has been revealed that his Oscar-winning work in particular proved that he could command an entirely different kind of screen presence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are some essential Robert Downey Jr. performances everybody should enjoy before he returns to the Marvel Cinematic Universe in Avengers: Doomsday. Robert Downey Jr. has enjoyed one of the most remarkable career transformations in modern Hollywood. Yet his ability to reinvent himself, take creative risks, and deliver memorable, distinctive performances has made him one of the most celebrated actors of his generation.

According to recent reports, RDJ’s career reached an entirely fresh level when he joined the MCU timeline, becoming the face of a franchise that would dominate blockbuster cinema. However, reducing Downey's filmography to his superhero appearances would overlook some genuinely extraordinary performances, including roles that demonstrate just how versatile he can be.

It has been revealed that his Oscar-winning work in particular proved that he could command an entirely different kind of screen presence. Now, with Downey preparing to return to Marvel in Avengers: Doomsday, audiences have an excellent opportunity to revisit the performances that established his reputation.

Richard III is an inventive adaptation of Shakespeare's tragedy, relocating the story to an alternate 1930s England where fascism has taken hold. Downey plays Earl Rivers, Queen Elizabeth's brother, whose political position makes him a target of Richard's murderous ambitions.

It's a relatively small role, and Downey doesn't have nearly enough screen time to make the same impression as some of his fellow cast members. Nevertheless, the role flaunts his acting talent and ability to convey sophisticated material – even among such an all-star cast.

Industry observers note that the Judge reunites Downey with the kind of morally complicated protagonist he plays particularly well. He stars as Hank Palmer, a successful Chicago defence attorney who returns to his Indiana hometown following his mother's death. The film's strongest material comes from the uncomfortable relationship between Hank and his father, Josopeh.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, The Judge struggles to balance its courtroom drama with its family melodrama. Its legal proceedings become increasingly conventional, and the emotional revelations occasionally feel engineered to produce a reaction rather than emerge naturally from the characters. Still, Downey gives the material considerably more personality than it might otherwise have had.

Sources indicate that A Scanner Darkly is one of the strangest films in Downey's filmography, and that's precisely why it's worth revisiting. Adapted from Philip K. Dick's novel, the animated science-fiction thriller uses rotoscoping to create an unsettling visual experience in which live-action performances are transformed into constantly shifting illustrations. Downey plays James Barris, a paranoid drug user who lives alongside Keanu Reeves' undercover narcotics agent.

Barris is an unpredictable presence, constantly talking and inventing elaborate theories. It allows Downey to indulge his gift for eccentric dialogue without turning the character into a conventional comic-relief figure. Downey's expressive delivery fits the material beautifully, even if A Scanner Darkly’s deliberately disorienting approach won't appeal to everyone.

Natural Born Killers is one of the most confrontational films of the 1990s. Its deliberately chaotic editing, exaggerated performances, and constantly shifting visual styles create an abrasive satire of America's obsession with televised violence and celebrity criminals. Downey plays Wayne Gale, a television journalist whose program turns the murderous Mickey and Mallory Knox into media sensations.

It's an especially interesting performance because Downey makes Gale both charismatic and deeply unpleasant. Natural Born Killers can be excessive, and the satire sometimes gets lost in its own stylistic aggression. Nevertheless, Downey's performance is an important part of its success.

Sources indicate that guy Ritchie's Sherlock Holmes gave Downey another opportunity to demonstrate his ability to make eccentric, intellectually gifted characters thoroughly entertaining. Rather than reproducing the familiar image of Arthur Conan Doyle's detective, the films present Holmes as an impulsive, physically capable and frequently antisocial investigator.

Downey makes an excellent Sherlock Holmes. His physical comedy, rapid observations and mischievous delivery create a detective who feels distinctly different from previous screen interpretations. With a third installment having been discussed for years, these films remain among Downey's most enjoyable blockbusters outside Marvel.

Ben Stiller's Tropic Thunder features one of Downey's most outrageous performances. He plays Kirk Lazarus, an Australian method actor who undergoes an extreme "pigmentation alteration" surgery to darken his skin for his portrayal of the black character. Even when the production descends into genuine danger, Lazarus continues behaving as though he is starring in an elaborate film production.

The role is deliberately provocative, and its humor depends on Downey's commitment to an absurd character who takes his own acting process far too seriously. His interactions with Stiller's increasingly frustrated director and Brandon T. Jackson's aspiring rapper Alpa Chino produce some of the film's funniest exchanges.

Chaplin gave Downey one of the most demanding roles of his early career. Playing the legendary Charlie Chaplin required him to recreate not only the comedian's distinctive physical performance but also the complicated personality behind one of cinema's most renowned performers.

Downey's transformation is remarkable. He captures Chaplin's movements, facial expressions and carefully controlled physical comedy, demonstrating an understanding of silent-film performance that goes beyond simply imitating the famous Little Tramp. Chaplin isn't entirely successful as a biography, but Downey's performance is consistently compelling.

David Fincher's Zodiac is one of the finest crime thrillers of the 21st century, and Downey delivers one of its most memorable performances as San Francisco Chronicle journalist Paul Avery. Based on the real investigation into the Zodiac Killer, it depicts the journalists and detectives whose lives become consumed by the search for an unidentified murderer.

Industry observers note that zodiac does not (and could not) provide the comforting resolution expected from a murder mystery, instead examining the damage that an unsolved case can inflict on the people pursuing it. Downey's performance is a crucial part of that approach, giving the film an unpredictable human dimension.

Kiss Kiss Bang Bang is arguably the film that first demonstrated how entertaining Downey could be after his career-threatening personal difficulties. The brilliantly irreverent neo-noir comedy stars him as Harry Lockhart, a small-time criminal who accidentally auditions for a Hollywood production and finds himself caught up in a murder investigation. Harry is an unconventional protagonist, frequently breaking the fourth wall to explain the increasingly ridiculous events unfolding around him.

Downey's sarcastic delivery and impeccable comic timing make the character immediately likable, even when his decisions are spectacularly questionable. More importantly, Kiss Kiss Bang Bang gives Downey the freedom to play a charmingly unreliable character without sacrificing the emotional vulnerability beneath his humor. Its success highlighted that audiences were still interested in Downey as a leading man, making it an essential stop before his Hollywood comeback.

Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer provided Downey with arguably the most significant dramatic showcase of his later career. Playing Lewis Strauss, the former chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, he delivers a controlled and calculating performance that feels completely removed from his familiar screen persona.

It has been revealed that downey is particularly effective during the film's Senate confirmation hearings, where Strauss' carefully maintained public image begins to unravel. Rather than relying on his usual quick-witted delivery, he communicates Strauss' insecurities through small expressions, measured dialogue, and an increasingly apparent desperation to control his own narrative. Downey won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for the performance, alongside a BAFTA and Golden Globe.

Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • Industry observers note that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

Industry observers note that I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

Recent findings suggest that I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an matter with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

In a recent development, I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Recent findings suggest that multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Industry observers note that last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

According to recent reports, after a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

According to recent reports, I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

It has been revealed that I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Recent findings suggest that is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

According to recent reports, what has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

It has been revealed that A great mystery book essentially turns its readers into detectives. The author knows that the story is meant to feel like a subtle contest between the characters and the audience, with each clue raising the question of who will figure things out first. When the payoff is great, even losing the contest feels like a reward. However, if it’s bad or delivered at the wrong time, the entire buildup falls apart in a single second.

Now, the 2000s were a turning point for the mystery genre because it got darker and more literary. Some of the best writers of the decade stopped asking who did it and started exploring the consequences of crime and the ways it can change people’s lives forever. That shift gave the genre a newly introduced emotional depth and gave us some of the best mystery books of the 2000s. Here are the top six mystery books of the 2000s.

The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time is the rare mystery that’s narrated by someone who sees the world completely differently from everyone around him. Mark Haddon’s novel follows Christopher Boone, a brilliant 15-year-old boy who loves math and hates being touched. One night, he discovers his neighbor’s dog, Wellington, lying dead on the lawn with a garden fork through it. Inspired by his hero, Sherlock Holmes, Christopher decides to investigate the crime himself and writes it all down as his own mystery novel.

The joke hidden in the title is that the dog barely matters. Christopher’s detective work leads him straight to the truth about his own parents, and Haddon lets readers figure it out a few pages before Christopher does. Watching him process absolutely heartbreaking news with the innocence of a teenager is one of the most painful parts of the book, to the point where readers can practically feel his confusion and fear as his whole world falls apart. The Curious Incident is a mystery that’s really about love and honesty, and it remains one of the most original novels of the decade.

Recent findings suggest that dennis Lehane’s Shutter Island spawned one of Martin Scorsese’s biggest blockbusters, but the eerie, gothic novel deserves to be appreciated on its own. The story takes place in 1954, when U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels and his partner, Chuck Aule, take a ferry to Ashecliffe Hospital, an institution for the criminally insane on a remote island in Boston Harbor. They go there to look for Rachel Solando, a patient who vanished from a locked room as if she had walked straight through the walls. When a hurricane traps them on the island, Teddy grows convinced that the hospital’s doctors are conducting secret experiments and hiding some very dark secrets.

Recent findings suggest that from there, Shutter Island works like a classic pulp mystery with coded messages and a confined setting that keeps tightening the noose on its characters. Lehane’s old-fashioned style of storytelling is the book’s greatest strength. The readers get so caught up in the mystery of Rachel’s disappearance that they barely notice the inconsistencies in Teddy’s actions. By the time the book delivers its big twist, it’s clear that the clues hidden along the way were never really about the missing patient. Shutter Island is designed to be read twice, and is still a genre-defining book today.

Sources indicate that the Shadow of the Wind is a mystery for anyone who has ever fallen in love with a book. Carlos Ruiz Zafón’s novel is set in Barcelona in the years after the Spanish Civil War and begins when a young boy named Daniel Sempere is taken by his bookseller father to the Cemetery of Forgotten Books, a secret library hidden in the heart of the city. Daniel is allowed to choose one book, and he picks a novel by an obscure author named Julián Carax. He soon discovers that someone has spent years tracking down and burning every copy of Carax’s work — and that he may own one of the last ones left.

In a recent development, zafón’s novel feels like stepping right into an old film. Daniel’s hunt for a forgotten writer soon evolves into a story about doomed love and family secrets. However, the most interesting part is how Daniel’s life begins to mirror the author’s in unsettling ways, especially when a brutal police inspector named Fumero starts taking an interest in him. Zafón fills the city with unforgettable characters and romantic prose that is easy to get lost in for hours. The novel became a global bestseller for good reason, given that it feels like a love letter to reading itself.

In a recent development, mystic River is another Lehane murder mystery that actually feels haunted. The story picks up in 1975, when three boys from a working-class Boston neighborhood are playing on the street when two men posing as police officers drive off with one of them, Dave Boyle. Dave escapes days later, but he comes back a completely different person, and the friendship between the three boys quietly falls apart. Twenty-five years later, Jimmy Marcus, now an ex-con running a corner store, learns that his teenage daughter has been murdered. Their old friend Sean Devine is the detective on the case, and on the night she died, Dave came home covered in blood.

According to recent reports, dennis Lehane is at his very best here, and Mystic River is often called his masterpiece. The mystery of who killed Katie Marcus is gripping, but the book is really about how one terrible day can quietly shape the rest of three men’s lives. The author moves between all three men, so readers always know a little more than any one of them, and that is where the book’s primary sense of tension comes from. Lehane also captures the loyalty and suspicion of a tight-knit neighborhood, where everyone knows each other’s secrets but no one wants to say them out loud. The ending is one of the most gut-wrenching in modern crime fiction, and it lingers long after the last page. Clint Eastwood’s Oscar-winning film adaptation of the novel is excellent, but Mystic River hits even harder in its original form.

Very few narrators admit they’re liars in the first few pages, but Rob Ryan does in Tana French’s In the Woods. The story opens in 1984, when Rob was one of three children who wandered into the woods near their Dublin suburb. He was found clinging to a tree with blood in his shoes, with no memory of what happened, and his two best friends were never seen again. Twenty years later, he is serving as a detective on the Dublin Murder Squad when a 12-year-old girl is found dead at an archaeological dig in those same woods. Rob and his partner, Cassie Maddox, take the case, but the catch is that Rob keeps his connection to it a secret.

Sources indicate that french’s debut reads less like a police procedural and more like a confession from someone who still hasn’t made peace with his past. The present-day murder is gripping, but the real tension comes from watching Rob slowly unravel as the woods pull him back in. His friendship with Cassie is warm and funny, and it adds to the story’s emotional stakes. The fact that the readers know he is not always honest makes the whole thing feel slightly off-balance. It’s also why the ending of the novel and its refusal to give easy answers have divided readers ever since.

According to recent reports, in Sweden, The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo was published under a much harsher title, Men Who Hate Women. This is a big clue to what Stieg Larsson really wanted to say with this story. The novel follows disgraced journalist Mikael Blomkvist, who is hired by aging industrialist Henrik Vanger to solve a 40-year-old mystery. Henrik’s niece Harriet vanished from the family’s private island on a day when the only bridge was blocked by an accident, which means someone on the island must have been responsible. Mikael soon realizes that he needs help from the brilliant but extremely private hacker Lisbeth Salander, who trusts almost no one. The Vanger case is a classic locked-room puzzle, built on old photographs and family members who all have something to hide.

However, Lisbeth’s is the reason the book became a global phenomenon. She is a character who has been failed by every institution that was supposed to protect her, and her refusal to be anyone’s victim gives the novel a unique kind of fury. She and Mikael are total opposites, but their partnership is one of the genre’s greatest odd pairings. The book covers a solid amount of ground. Despite its size, the story never wastes a page, and every thread pays off by the end. Larsson spent years as a journalist exposing extremist groups, and that anger at powerful men who escape consequences is felt on every page. He died before the book was published, sadly never seeing it become a hit that sold millions of copies around the world. Two decades later, Lisbeth Salander is still the gold standard for the modern crime heroine, and The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo remains a cultural phenomenon that mystery fans still talk about.
