💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that context-Generic Programming (CGP) v0.8.0 is out!
  • It has been revealed that CGP is a language extension for Rust, with pluggable trait implementations at compile-time.
  • Industry observers note that I'll start with cargo-cgp and the new documentation, then work through namespaces using a social-media application.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that context-Generic Programming (CGP) v0.8.0 is out! This release is about making CGP easier to learn and maintain. It introduces cargo-cgp, a new tool for one of CGP's longest-standing problems: compile errors that describe the code the macros generated rather than the code you wrote. cargo-cgp explains those errors in your terms. When a provider needs a field your type lacks, for example, it can tell you which field to add, and the expanded documentation explains why the provider needs it. Later, as your application grows, the new namespaces let you choose the providers for a whole group of components in one wiring entry.

It has been revealed that CGP is a language extension for Rust, with pluggable trait implementations at compile-time. It is an ordinary library on stable Rust: applications select providers through wiring that resolves to static calls, and you can adopt it one component at a time. The Overview explains the model.

Industry observers note that I'll start with cargo-cgp and the new documentation, then work through namespaces using a social-media application. The namespace walkthrough is the longest part, so you can read the tooling and documentation news on their own if you prefer. Allow about 35 minutes for the full post, including the code, or jump to the section you need:.

Since CGP began, verbose and confusing compiler errors have been one of the largest obstacles to adopting it. Leave out a field or a component binding, and the error message can name a generated trait or show a field name encoded as a Rust type. The compiler checks the Rust produced by macro expansion, so its explanation can be far removed from the code where we made the mistake.

Recent findings suggest that for a newcomer, that can mean learning advanced Rust traits and generics, along with CGP's internals, just to diagnose a small mistake. You might understand the program you are trying to write and still have little idea why it does not compile. Because the difficulty lies in how the compiler reports the expanded code, better syntax alone cannot address it.

It has been revealed that so I built cargo-cgp v0.1.0, CGP's latest error toolchain, to report those errors in terms of the code you wrote. cargo cgp check checks CGP code and explains a missing dependency through the fields, components, and providers involved, leading with the root cause. It does not yet reshape every class of error, though, so some still reach you in the compiler's own words. When you want to look deeper, cargo cgp expand highlights the Rust that the macros generated.

Let's try it on a small mistake from the area-calculation tutorial. We have an area provider that multiplies width by height, and a Rectangle that supplies only width. Here, the rectangle itself is the context: it is the value the operation acts on, and its fields supply the provider's inputs.

Save this library example as src/lib.rs in a Cargo package using cgp = "0.8.0":.

Sources indicate that the table selects RectangleArea, whose #[implicit] arguments read the rectangle's fields. Because we used delegate_and_check_components!, the compiler checks those dependencies at the wiring entry. Run cargo cgp check, and it points to the field we forgot:.

It has been revealed that the help line gives us the edit, height: f64. To see why the provider needs it, the dependency tree takes us back through RectangleArea to the area operation. For comparison, plain cargo check describes the same mistake through generated traits and a nested Symbol type:.

Following that suggestion, we add the missing field:.

The wiring check now passes, and the provider can read both fields to calculate the area. Fixing the mistake did not require decoding the type-level spelling of height.

Sources indicate that to produce this explanation, cargo-cgp wraps a nightly compiler and uses the Rust compiler's API to inspect the failed dependencies. It can follow their chain using information that would be difficult to recover from the printed diagnostic alone. That access is why the tool has its own compiler-linked driver.

Sources indicate that with cargo and rustup available, you can install the tool and set up its compiler-linked driver, then check your own project. The install needs Rust 1.96 or newer, and the tool is tested on Linux only so far:.

Industry observers note that cargo cgp setup installs the tool's pinned nightly and builds the matching driver. That nightly runs only cargo-cgp's checks, so your application keeps its normal toolchain for ordinary cargo builds. CGP itself still compiles on stable Rust, and you can use it without installing cargo-cgp at all.

Sources indicate that use plain cargo to build, run, and test applications. cargo-cgp supplies check for diagnostics and expand for reading the Rust generated by macros, with CGP's type-level constructs restored to readable notation. The installation guide covers setup, updates, and the Nix alternative, and the cargo-cgp v0.1.0 release notes list what this first release supports.

A release post can show you an interesting feature and still leave you unsure how to use it in your own program. For too long, CGP left readers in that position. Most explanations lived in blog posts like this one, with each post introducing features as they arrived. There was little room to explain every construct or give readers a complete account of how the pieces fit together.

CGP is a side project, and finding the time to fill those gaps has been difficult. Writing a comparable body of documentation entirely by hand would likely take me months of full-time work. I do not expect to have that time in the near future, and waiting would leave readers facing the same gaps.

Advances in AI and agentic coding made it practical to take on that work. Agents, primarily Claude Code, wrote much of the latest documentation under my direction, over many iterations of planning and revision. If a blog post leaves you wanting more detail, you can now turn to:.

Across more than 360 pages, the website now contains roughly 365,000 words of documentation prose, excluding code blocks and the mirrored skill files. At 300 words per printed page, that would be about 1,200 pages before code listings.

It has been revealed that I understand why readers may be skeptical of AI-written explanations. A word count says little about their usefulness, and I would not expect a one-shot prompt to produce useful material at this scale. The planning, source checks, and repeated revisions are essential to the quality I am aiming for. I encourage you to read the pages and tell me where an explanation is vague, incorrect, or reads like generic AI output.

I direct the work, set the rules, and choose what gets documented. The process starts with the knowledge base, where agents record how CGP works and check claims about syntax and macro expansions against the implementation, tests, and expansion snapshots. That account becomes the basis for the website pages, which agents write and revise against the project's writing guides.

When a page needs an enhancement, the agent can pick up from the same record. That saves me time because each revision starts from what the record already holds about CGP. The knowledge-base overview explains how the record supports the project.

I review the pages myself, though not all in the same depth. I read in full every page that explains CGP's ideas or the decisions behind its design, which includes the Concepts pages and the blog posts. The reference pages for individual constructs follow their writing guides, and I spot-check them. But neither kind of review catches everything. Like the source checks, it can miss mistakes, so the knowledge base can still contain errors. I remain responsible for what the project publishes.

I would like to explore the methodology further in a dedicated follow-up post. For now, How CGP's Documentation Is Written explains the process and where its checks stop. The AI disclosure describes who writes and reviews the documentation, tooling, and core library.

Sources indicate that if you already work with an AI assistant, try exploring a small CGP example together. With the /cgp skill loaded, you can ask it to explain an unfamiliar wiring entry, trace which provider a method uses, or help investigate a compiler error. This gives you a way to explore the internal details as they become relevant, with explanations suited to your Rust experience.

It has been revealed that the skill gives the assistant a condensed guide to current CGP: the consumer/provider model, wiring, dependency declarations, and debugging with cargo-cgp. It can help the assistant investigate macro expansions and guide you through installing and using the checker. For deeper questions, it can consult the fuller knowledge-base record.

Recent findings suggest that before it works on your code, the skill checks which cgp release your project uses and tells you when that differs from the release it describes. You still need to review and verify the assistant's suggested code. The installation page explains how to install the skill in your agent, and Using the Knowledge Base with Your Agent covers deeper investigation. Neither is required to use CGP.

The release also introduces namespaces, for grouping components as an application grows.

When an application has only a few components, writing out its delegate_components! table is straightforward. Each time we split behavior into another component, though, we add a routing entry. Eventually, someone opening the application has to sort through a long list of bindings before they can see which ones belong together. The implementations have become more reusable, but the configuration has become harder to follow.

It has been revealed that I have tried a few ways to address this difficulty. Provider bundles collect implementations, but applications still have to list the components they forward to each bundle. The earlier preset system reduced some repetition too, with limitations I will return to below.

In a recent development, with namespaces, we can now give those groups names and select their implementations together. I'll work through a social-media application whose production and test configurations share a PostgreSQL-backed core but use different content filters. By the end, that difference will be visible in one wiring entry.

According to recent reports, if you have already maintained a large wiring table, you may prefer to jump to the namespace syntax or the migration guide. Otherwise, let's start with the small application and see how its wiring grows.

Suppose we are building a social-media service that manages customers and posts. We need a database handle and a place to choose the implementations the service uses, so our context will represent the application. This is a different role from the earlier Rectangle, where the context was the data being operated on.

The snippets illustrate wiring rather than a complete web service. They assume use cgp::prelude::*; and omit domain type declarations and database query bodies. The web-app walkthrough follows the same example, and its compiling source uses placeholder database operations.

Our service starts with one manager trait for users and another for posts.

It has been revealed that the methods describe what the service can do. Adding #[cgp_component] lets us write their implementations separately from the application that uses them: it generates a provider trait such as UserManager and a wiring key such as UserManagerComponent. The application will choose a provider through that key.

It has been revealed that choosing a manager provider chooses all its methods together. A component can hold several methods, associated types, and constants, just like an ordinary trait, and grouping the user operations keeps this first version simple. As the service grows, we will see where choosing those methods together becomes inconvenient.

According to recent reports, for the PostgreSQL implementations, each method declares the database handle it needs as an implicit argument. The providers can then work with any application supplying that dependency:.

In a recent development, any context with the required PostgreSQL database field can reuse these providers. If we wanted a SQLite-backed application, we could write SqliteUserManager and SqlitePostManager against the same interfaces and select those instead.

For our production application, we supply the database field and choose the PostgreSQL managers:.

According to recent reports, both managers share one dependency: the database field that #[derive(HasField)] makes available to their implicit arguments. The combined delegation-and-check macro verifies that ProductionApp can use the selected providers. For now, those two entries cover all the user and post operations.

In a recent development, now suppose the service needs to reject censored usernames and spam posts. Before inserting a user or a post, its manager must consult a filter. We can add a component for each check and declare the manager's dependency on its consumer trait with #[uses]:.

Sources indicate that each manager compares its filter's score with a rejection threshold before writing to the database. The #[uses] attribute declares the fresh trait dependency, while #[implicit] database still supplies the database handle. The remaining manager methods are omitted here.

In production, filtering might involve an AI model or a cloud service. We would rather not make those calls every time we test the rest of the application. A deterministic string-matching filter lets tests run more rapidly while keeping the same PostgreSQL managers:.

Both contexts supply the database field and select the same managers. Only the filter entries differ, so tests can exercise the database implementations with deterministic filtering.

According to recent reports, the wiring has grown along with the dependency tree. Each context now has four entries, so the two contexts together already have eight to keep in step, even in this small service.

In a recent development, adding CanCensorUsername to the user manager looked straightforward. But that bound belongs to the whole PostgresUserManager implementation, so even get_user now requires a context with a censor. Retrieving a user never runs the filter. The dependency arrives because retrieval and creation share a provider. The post manager has the same problem with spam detection, and every unrelated dependency we add makes the managers harder to maintain and test.

According to recent reports, as we add operations, the domain boundaries become less obvious too. get_user_profile_picture might fit in the user manager, but it could need an entirely different set of dependencies. get_user_posts concerns both owners and posts. Naming a manager after an entity does not settle which operations are useful to group together.

There is also a reason to keep the caller's interface narrow. Deleting a user is destructive, and we may not want every piece of code that works with users to be able to do it. Yet if we added delete_user to the manager, even generic code that only retrieves users would gain access to deletion. Giving retrieval its own trait lets that code ask for exactly the operation it needs, and nothing more.

That points to a simple but powerful pattern that CGP makes practical: splitting each manager into fine-grained traits, each holding one operation or a few closely related ones. Each provider can then declare only the dependencies it uses. For the user operations, that gives us:.

The user-creation provider needs the censor, while the getter needs only the database:.

GetUserWithPostgres can be used with a database alone, while CreateUserWithPostgres keeps its censor dependency. A caller bounded by CanGetUser can retrieve users without depending on creation or deletion. The same split gives us separate post-creation, retrieval, enhancement, and deletion components.

Splitting the components solved the getter's problem, but CreateUserWithPostgres still does two jobs: it checks the username, then inserts the user into PostgreSQL. Only the insert has anything to do with the database. If we added a provider for SQLite, it would have to repeat the same check. Because creation now has a component of its own, we can move the check into a wrapper instead, and apply it to whichever user-creation provider we choose:.

In a recent development, the wrapper rejects censored names, then hands an allowed request to InnerCreator::create_user. Its #[use_provider] attribute requires that inner provider to support user creation for the same context. Because it takes another provider as a parameter, we call FilterCensoredUsername a higher-order provider.

CreateUserWithPostgres can now focus on constructing the SQL insert query. When wiring the application, we can select it directly or add filtering with FilterCensoredUsername. A local-first application could instead select FilterCensoredUsername and reuse the same filter. Changing the database would not require copying the username check.

According to recent reports, filterSpamMessage applies the same separation to post creation. It uses CanDetectSpamMessage to reject spam, then forwards an allowed post to its inner PostCreator. The wiring can therefore choose FilterSpamMessage independently of the database provider's implementation.

In a recent development, with dependencies isolated and filters reusable, the individual providers are easier to work with. The production wiring, however, now has to select seven CRUD operations and two filters:.

According to recent reports, splitting the managers took our wiring table from four entries to nine, and a real application might have dozens or hundreds. Imagine opening that table for the first time. To learn how the application handles users, you have to pick the user bindings out of the list, and everything else reads as noise that hides what ProductionApp actually does. The application then looks far more complex than it is, which is one reason long wiring tables have made CGP harder to adopt.

According to recent reports, the table shows us too much at once. If we break it into smaller groups, a reader can take the wiring one piece at a time, so let's start by collecting the user bindings into a provider bundle of their own:.

Industry observers note that with new PostgresUserComponents, we declare an aggregate provider: its table delegates each operation to another provider. A reader can examine the user wiring on its own, without the post operations and filters alongside it. We can collect those into PostgresPostComponents and AiContentFilterComponents in the same way.

Back in the application, we forward the components to their bundles using array keys:.

The bundles make each group easier to read, but they do not shorten what the application has to list. Its table still names all nine components, now split across three lists, and each list repeats the keys its bundle already holds. So adding a user operation takes two edits: one to the user bundle, and another to every application that delegates to it. In a large codebase, that second edit could mean many places. We would rather tell the application to use PostgresUserComponents for “all user components,” but that group has no name we can wire.

Ideally, the configuration would say something like this, with a key for each group:.

The ??? keys are the hard part. Each entry in the table becomes a trait implementation for one key, so UserCreatorComponent: … gives the application one implementation that answers lookups for user creation. A key that stood for all user components would need to produce one implementation per component in the group, and Rust's trait system has no way to expand a single entry like that. So CGP needs another way to recognize a group: either its own lookup rules, or a macro that expands the group into its keys. Namespaces take the first route, but the macro route is worth a look first.

Sources indicate that one possibility would be a helper macro that supplied the list of keys for each group. That would let us write a hypothetical table like this:.

According to recent reports, here, all_user_components!() would expand to [UserCreatorComponent, UserGetterComponent, UserUpdaterComponent], with corresponding lists for posts and filters. Like the ??? keys above, these helpers are pseudocode rather than supported syntax.

Unfortunately, this runs into the order in which Rust expands macros. Rust expands them lazily, from the outside in, so delegate_components! runs first and receives all_user_components!() as literal tokens. At that point the helper has not expanded, and the component list does not exist yet. The table would need eager expansion, where a macro expands the macros inside its input before reading it, and stable Rust offers no way for a macro to do that. Even if it did, CGP would still have to generate helpers like all_user_components! and export them so that their names and imports keep working in other crates, and Rust's macro system has limited support for that.

My earlier preset system tried to solve the same problem, but it supported only a hierarchy like single inheritance. A context could inherit one preset, such as a user preset, and Rust's coherence restrictions then stopped it from also inheriting an independent post preset. I also experimented with combining several presets through macros, but the lack of eager macro expansion, together with the way imports and aliases resolve inside macro output, made that approach tedious to use.

Those attempts helped clarify what I wanted from the feature: an application should be able to name a group and choose its implementation bundle without enumerating every key. In v0.8.0, namespaces express that choice through trait resolution and paths. Existing preset users can find the conversion in the migration section.

We can now replace the ??? keys with paths that name the user, post, and content-filter groups. With the component prefixes registered, our application table becomes:.

The namespace DefaultNamespace; statement connects these paths to our components. Each component registers a route in the built-in DefaultNamespace, as we will do in a moment with #[prefix], and the statement tells the table to follow those routes. Namespaces are opt-in, so without this statement the table ignores the registered routes. A lookup for UserCreatorComponent, for example, follows a route that begins with @app.core.user, so it reaches the entry that selects PostgresUserComponents. Adding another user operation to the user group therefore leaves this table unchanged. The individual bindings still live in the bundles, while the application chooses only which groups it uses. Later, we will also define a namespace of our own.

To make this work, we give each component a prefix using #[prefix]. For CanCreateUser, we register @app.core.user in the built-in DefaultNamespace:.

CGP appends the component marker to this prefix. Once a context joins the namespace, a lookup for UserCreatorComponent follows the route to @app.core.user.UserCreatorComponent.

It has been revealed that the getter and updater belong to that group too, so we register them under the same prefix. For the getter, that means:.

Post operations get their own @app.core.post prefix:.

According to recent reports, finally, the filter components register under @app.extra.content_filter, also in DefaultNamespace. These registrations name the groups without choosing any providers for them. That choice stays with each application, so production, tests, and a SQLite variant can share the same routes and still select different bundles.

In a recent development, production and tests both use the PostgreSQL user and post operations. Rather than select those bundles separately in each application, we can collect them under their shared parent, @app.core. The paths are hierarchical: @app.core.user sits under @app.core, which sits under @app. An intermediate bundle can therefore gather the core operations, while another gathers the extras:.

Sources indicate that notice that these intermediate bundles also join DefaultNamespace. When a lookup reaches a bundle, it receives the bare component key, and the namespace statement redirects that key to the paths in the bundle's own table. Our earlier leaf bundles use bare component names already, so they do not need that statement.

The production configuration now selects two groups:.

A single entry for @app.core now covers both core groups. Because paths are hierarchical, it matches every route beneath that prefix, so user and post lookups both reach it, and so would a core group we add later. Take UserCreatorComponent again. Its route, @app.core.user.UserCreatorComponent, begins with @app.core, so ProductionApp forwards the lookup to PostgresCoreComponents. Inside that bundle, the namespace statement routes the component a second time, which brings it to the @app.core.user entry and on to PostgresUserComponents.

It has been revealed that for testing, the core stays the same. Only the extras entry changes, selecting DummyExtraComponents for deterministic filtering:.

For a local configuration, we could make the other choice: keep the production filters and select a SQLite-backed core:.

In each case, one entry tells us how the configuration differs from production. TestApp changes the extras, while LocalApp changes the core. With flat tables, we would have to compare the individual component entries, perhaps written in different orders, to reach the same conclusion. We can now read those decisions directly from the wiring.

Recent findings suggest that the selected providers still need their dependencies. Each context must supply the required fields and other traits, and the hypothetical SQLite core would need its corresponding database handle.

Recent findings suggest that will these providers work together? A delegate_components! block can compile before Rust has checked the providers' dependencies. We can ask Rust to check them now with check_components!, naming the components we need on the concrete application.

In a recent development, apply the same nine-component check to TestApp and any local variant. Earlier stages need checks matching their components: before splitting the managers, for example, check UserManagerComponent and PostManagerComponent.

Industry observers note that the check lists the individual operations, even though the wiring now routes them in groups. A group entry only says where a lookup goes, so the check confirms that every operation we rely on actually resolves. Run it on the real application context, which supplies the database field and the other dependencies. An aggregate provider is only a bundle of implementations, so checking a bundle as if it were the application would ask it for dependencies that only the context can supply.

The namespace documentation explains the lookup model, and the delegate_components! reference covers the path syntax.

So far, we have organized the wiring around choices we might want to change: PostgreSQL or SQLite, production or test filters. Bundles work well for that arrangement. We could add a PostgresWithLoggingCoreComponents variant, for example, and select the logging-backed core in the same place.

According to recent reports, but an application starting out with PostgreSQL may have little reason to define interchangeable database bundles yet. Early in a project, developers often prefer one implementation per feature, tied to its interface on purpose, because that keeps the application easy to reason about. If several contexts should always use the same user and post implementations, having each one select those bundles repeats a choice that never varies. We can instead record those choices once in a namespace and leave only the varying parts to each context. These are default implementations.

Recent findings suggest that I see defaults as a way to adopt CGP gradually. Ordinary traits may already be enough for a single-crate application with one implementation of each operation. If that application later needs more modularity, it can move code into CGP components and record its initial provider choices as defaults. Bundles can follow when there are useful groups to swap.

Let's keep the routes we already registered in DefaultNamespace and define a configuration namespace that inherits them using the new cgp_namespace! macro:.

Recent findings suggest that defaultAppComponents starts with the prefixes and any default bindings supplied by its parent. We can add our application-specific choices here without changing what other namespaces select. Every context that joins this configuration namespace will share those choices.

For a simple provider, we can place its binding beside its implementation. Add #[default_impl] to our earlier GetUserWithPostgres definition:.

Recent findings suggest that the implementation now declares that DefaultAppComponents uses it at @app.core.user.UserGetterComponent. If we prefer to collect the bindings in one place, we can write the same choice in the namespace body instead:.

It has been revealed that these are alternative ways to register the same binding, so writing both would create a conflict. The namespace body looks like a delegate_components! table, but its choices apply to every context that joins the namespace. We bind the provider at the full path because the bare key is already taken. The route inherited from DefaultNamespace uses UserGetterComponent to send lookups on to @app.core.user.UserGetterComponent, so a second entry for the bare key would conflict with it.

These defaults are fixed choices. Once the namespace binds a provider, a joining context or inheriting namespace cannot override it, even with a more specific entry. A context also cannot disable just one default while retaining the rest of that namespace. So a choice that should vary between contexts belongs on a path the namespace leaves open, as we will do with the filters below.

In a recent development, there is also a constraint on where we write the registration. With a prefixed path, the binding must live in the crate that owns the namespace, here DefaultAppComponents. The path expands to CGP's PathCons type, and owning a component marker nested inside that type does not satisfy Rust's orphan rules. An unprefixed local component marker has different ownership rules, covered by the #[default_impl] reference.

Industry observers note that filterCensoredUsername is generic over its inner provider. For this configuration, we want to choose both the wrapper and its PostgreSQL implementation. We can assemble that complete provider choice directly in the namespace body:.

After we bind the remaining user and post providers in the same way, the application only needs to choose its filters. For this example, our production wiring then becomes:.

Industry observers note that every context that joins DefaultAppComponents gets its user and post providers from it. We left the filter path open so a test context can select DummyContentFilterComponents there instead.

It has been revealed that we kept the prefixes in DefaultNamespace and the provider choices in DefaultAppComponents for a reason. Another configuration, such as a SQLite one, can then inherit the same routes without also inheriting PostgreSQL choices it could not override. So the routes belong in a base namespace, and the fixed choices in a configuration namespace that inherits it.

If we later need to replace one of these fixed defaults, we choose a namespace that leaves its destination open. We could return to the base DefaultNamespace and supply the required bindings explicitly, as in the earlier bundle examples.

It has been revealed that while the application lives in one crate, #[default_impl] conveniently keeps each binding beside its implementation. Once providers move into crates of their own, that attribute would sit in a crate that does not own the namespace, which the ownership rule above forbids. So we move the bindings into the configuration namespace's body instead, and the namespace's crate assembles the providers from there.

There is room to start with direct wiring, share fixed choices through defaults, and introduce interchangeable bundles as the application needs them. I would choose whichever arrangement makes the current decisions easiest to see, rather than build the full hierarchy in anticipation of future growth.

Sources indicate that namespaces are the largest change, but several smaller additions also make CGP easier to write, read, and use in more kinds of crates. You can use these without following the full application refactoring above:.

For the smaller changes, such as clearer errors from the handler macros and the restrictions this release lifts, see the v0.8.0 release notes.

Upgrading from v0.7.0 needs source changes. The largest is the removal of presets, which namespaces replace in this release, and most applications will also need explicit imports for items that used to come from the prelude. The v0.8.0 release notes list every change, with the upgrade steps in order.

Industry observers note that two projects built with CGP move to v0.8.0 at the same time. cgp-serde 0.3.0 can now serialize and deserialize enums, and Hypershell 0.2.0 assembles its language from a namespace instead of presets. If your code builds on either, the cgp-serde v0.3.0 and Hypershell v0.2.0 release notes give the upgrade steps.

The preset system described earlier is removed in v0.8.0. Its shared provider choices can become namespace bindings, while groups that need to remain interchangeable can become aggregate providers selected through paths.

Recent findings suggest that the following v0.7.0 example defines a preset and inherits it into a context. This is old syntax and does not compile with v0.8.0:.

A configuration namespace can preserve the preset's fixed user-provider choices. Register the user components under @app.core.user in DefaultNamespace, using the #[prefix(... in DefaultNamespace)] attributes shown earlier. Then replace the preset with this namespace:.

Recent findings suggest that the migrated context must also supply the censor required by its creation wrapper. Register UsernameCensor under @app.extra.content_filter in DefaultNamespace. With the user components and filter registered, replace the inheritance attribute with explicit delegation on the context:.

The example above deliberately checks only the migrated user group and its filter. Add the post operations and any other dependencies your application uses.

An aggregate provider keeps the user-provider group interchangeable. If configurations need that variation, retain PostgresUserComponents using delegate_components! { new PostgresUserComponents { ... } } and select it with @app.core.user: PostgresUserComponents, as in the main walkthrough. Choose between this configurable bundle arrangement and the fixed namespace bindings above according to what should vary.

The removed preset constructs and their replacements are:.

cgp::prelude now exports only the names CGP code usually writes: the macros, the derives, PhantomData, and a few traits and providers such as HasErrorType, CanRaiseError, UseType, and DefaultNamespace. The code the macros generate reaches CGP's items through a separate cgp::macro_prelude, so the prelude no longer has to carry those items. If your code names one of the dropped items through the glob import, the compiler reports that it cannot find it, and you import it from its module:.

The dropped names come from these modules:.

In a recent development, A derive does not need its trait imported, so #[derive(HasField)] still works through the prelude, while a HasField bound or a .get_field() call needs the import. A provider for a handler trait such as Computer imports its key, ComputerComponent, beside the trait, because the provider's header names the key, as Other improvements describes.

It has been revealed that raw compiler output changes slightly as a result. Where v0.7.0 printed a type such as cgp::prelude::Chars, the compiler can now print cgp::macro_prelude::Chars, as in the cargo check comparison above.

According to recent reports, the type-level types also lose their Greek-letter names. v0.7.0 declared them as π, ε, σ, θ, ζ, ψ, δ, and ω, with Cons, Nil, Either, Void, Chars, Symbol, Index, and Field as aliases, and the prelude exported both spellings. Only the English names remain, so code that wrote a Greek name switches to the English one, imported from cgp::core::field::types. Raw compiler output changes with them, printing Cons<…> and Chars<…> where v0.7.0 printed π<…> and ζ<…>.

Recent findings suggest that the default features of cgp are now empty, so the library builds without std or an allocator. In v0.7.0, the defaults turned on DebugError and DisplayError, the error providers that format an error into a String. If your wiring uses either, turn on the alloc feature:.

The associated-type separator in #[use_type] changes from :: to .:.

It has been revealed that equality imports use the new separator too. Write #[use_type(HasErrorType.{Error = AppError})]. An import from another context changes shape as well, with the context named after in: #[use_type(@Types::HasScalarType::Scalar)] becomes #[use_type(HasScalarType.Scalar in Types)]. The #[use_type] reference covers each form.

A component that generates a UseDelegate dispatcher moves the derive_delegate key of #[cgp_component] into an attribute of its own, one per dispatcher:.

A new component does not need either form, because the open statement from Other improvements dispatches it per type.

It has been revealed that the extra-feature macro crates are renamed from cgp-extra-macro and cgp-extra-macro-lib to cgp-macro-extra and cgp-macro-extra-lib. Update direct dependencies on those crates. Imports through cgp::prelude keep their names.

Self-contained handler-macro expansions may leave imports unused. Remove imports the compiler reports when they existed only for the old expansion.

According to recent reports, #[cgp_auto_dispatch] rejects attribute arguments and typed receivers such as self: Box. It previously ignored the arguments or miscompiled those receivers.

Industry observers note that the new Struct! and Enum! prelude exports can make a macro name ambiguous. Qualify the call if another glob import provides the same name.

DelegateComponent, IsProviderFor, HasField, and HasFieldMut no longer carry custom #[diagnostic::on_unimplemented] messages. Plain cargo check now reports an unmet bound on them in the compiler's own wording, and cargo cgp check rewrites those errors into its own summary. If a test compares compiler output, as a UI test does, update the messages it expects.

cgp-error-eyre enables eyre's automatic default-handler installation and tracks the caller of raise_error and wrap_error.

In a recent development, cgp-error-std changes how wrapped errors are displayed. Ordinary Display prints only the outer detail, while alternate Display and Debug include the chain. This avoids duplicated sources when a reporter walks source() itself. Update output assertions that depend on the old formatting.

Recent findings suggest that the minimum anyhow and eyre dependencies rise to 1.0.104 and 0.6.14 respectively. The backend READMEs in the CGP repository describe their use.

We started with two manager choices and ended with applications that could share a core, change their filters, or use a different database. Namespaces let the top-level wiring express those choices even as we split the implementations into smaller pieces. I hope that makes similar refactorings easier to follow in your own projects, with cargo-cgp and the latest documentation there to help when something is unclear.

CGP still takes time to learn. Its ecosystem is small, and I still have work to do on the tooling and documentation. My suggestion is to try it on one problem you already have. If you already use CGP, try grouping one area of your wiring while keeping its component checks in place. If you are upcoming to CGP, the Quickstart provides a smaller starting point.

I would appreciate hearing where you still struggle to trace an implementation, understand a diagnostic, or follow an explanation. Those examples will help me decide what to improve next. You can share them in GitHub Discussions. Thank you for reading and trying CGP.

In a recent development, I wrote the draft of this post, and an AI agent revised its prose and checked its code and claims against the CGP knowledge base. See How AI is used in this project.

Dani Kessel Odom (they/them) is an autistic lead writer and TV critic who covers sci-fi highlights like Doctor Who and Pluribus, fantasy shows like The Magicians and Percy Jackson, and horror of all kinds. They also cover Marvel and DC TV shows and movies, with a robust knowledge of comic books. Their TV reviews can be found on Rotten Tomatoes.

Dani is also part of ScreenRant's books team, using their fiction writing and literature studies as the backbone for their book analyses.

Industry observers note that they have covered events, such as the Denver Fan Expo. Professionals in the field, such as Damien Leone and Lucy Hale, have shared their articles. Their review of Ponies was quoted in the show's TV trailer.

Recent findings suggest that in university, they majored in English Writing with a minor in psychology. They have always had a passion for analyzing TV and movies, even taking filmography and scriptwriting classes in university. They also studied and participated in onstage and onscreen acting extensively from the ages of 7 to 18.

Aside from working at Screen Rant, Dani has worked as a freelance editor and writer over the past decade, often in a ghostwriting capacity.

Warning: This article includes SPOILERS for Percy Jackson & The Olympians season 3 and Rick Riordan's The Titan's Curse!

Disney+’s Percy Jackson season 3 jumps straight into the story, subtly setting up the most painful death in The Titan’s Curse from the start. The adaptation of Rick Riordan’s iconic book series is back, and it’s the best season yet. As critic El Kuiper mentioned in her review of Percy Jackson season 3 for ScreenRant, “Everything about Percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3 is more ambitious…” One of the biggest ways this indicates up is that this season is more gripping and wastes no time setting up the main story.

In a recent development, past seasons have been criticized for taking the tension out of the story, and the writers seemed to have taken note. Like in the book, Annabeth is kidnapped almost immediately. However, the show introduces Atlas early instead of waiting, letting the characters and audience know the danger the Campers face. They cut the capture the flag game, which made sense in the Percy Jackson book but would’ve felt awkward in the TV show. Percy and Thalia get to use their water and lightning powers instead of having the moment cut off before anything happens.

On top of that, The Titan’s Curse includes a few major deaths. They don’t spoil this, unlike past seasons, which put substantial book twists into the dialogue. There’s no telegraphing. That being stated, Percy Jackson & the Olympians season 3 wastes no time foreshadowing Bianca di Angelo's death, the most tragic of all.

In chapter 13 of The Titan’s Curse, Bianca dies after she triggers Talos, the bronze automaton, in The Junkyard of the Gods by taking a Mythomagic figurine for Nico. She sacrifices herself so the rest of the quester group can continue. While the first two episodes only cover chapters 1 through 6, the Disney+ adaptation already set up Bianca’s death with three key hints, the most notable of which happens at the end of Percy Jackson season 3, episode 2.

Firstly, the Oracle chooses the questers instead of them deciding who’s going themselves, which is one of the least notable changes Percy Jackson season 3 makes to the book. The green mist spreads as the prophecy is read to pick out the 5 campers and Hunters who will go. To the unknowing eye, the order may seem completely random. After all, they pick people on lines like “The Bane of Olympus demonstrates the trail” and “Campers & Hunters combined prevail,” which aren’t focused on a single individual. However, the oracle picks Bianca di Angelo on the prophecy line about a quester being lost in the land without rain.

Read Along With Percy Jackson Season 3.

"My Rescue Operation Goes Very Wrong".

"And Old Dead Friend Comes To Visit".

Percy Jackson season 3’s credits once again hint at what’s to come in the rest of the season. About halfway through them, Talos, the giant bronze automaton, stomps his foot down on a Hunter. Because Bianca isn’t a Hunter yet, those who haven’t read the book won’t be able to put two and two together, though. The third hint is in the season trailer. When they say, “Victory will require sacrifice,” they cut together shots of the characters. They transition from Bianca in a Hunter’s jacket in the arid environment to Nico running through the forest crying.

Bianca di Angelo’s death is already very impactful in the book because she dies right as she’s figuring out who she is as a Hunter and who she is outside her caretaker role. She’s a prime example of an older sister who’s forced to be a parent instead of a child, and that finally starts to change right before she dies. However, the Percy Jackson & The Olympians TV show already sets it up as a more tragic death.

It has been revealed that the show spent more time establishing the relationship between Bianca and Nico. They are much closer, which will make her sacrifice to get him a trinket more impactful. It will feel devastating that she will never get to see him again, and he will have to continue living without her. On top of that, Bianca didn’t choose to leave Nico in the TV show; the Oracle chose her.

Sources indicate that plus, Bianca has more of a personality onscreen. She has animated facial reactions, a wider emotional range, and strong opinions. She has connections to the other characters before she joins the Hunters, if she joins the Hunters. Obviously, we won’t know until more Percy Jackson episodes drop if that will happen. In the book, her existence and death felt to some like a plot device for Nico’s story. However, it’s already easier to get invested in her in the TV show, which will make her death feel more like a loss.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Messages sorted by: [ date ] [ thread ] [ subject ] [ author ] More information about the Gnupg-announce mailing list.

Industry observers note that messages sorted by: [ date ] [ thread ] [ subject ] [ author ] Hello! We are pleased to announce the availability of a new GPGME release: version 2.3.1. This version fixes a *critical security bug* found in all prior versions. We also release a new Gpg4win versions and and GnuPG Desktop and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions which all make use of GPGME. Description =========== By using an OpenPGP key containing a crafted very long user id it is possible to trigger a double free. This double free can be used exfiltrate data from applications by sending for example signed data. Exploiting this bug to mount an Remote Code Execution attack (RCE) can't be ruled out. Thus an immediate patch is highly suggested. Our internal ID is T8557 (https://static.dev.gnupg.org/T8557) The CVE-id is CVE-2026-129975. This vulnerability was discovered by Johan Carlsson and we were informed by GitLab on 2026-11-12. Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated disclosure; due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier and thus we also disclosed the GPGME bug on 2026-11-20. The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the status lines and key listings from gpg. Initially a buffer of 1024 bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required. When reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the function. Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to the freed memory. Eventually the context is released and the memory freed a second time. Due to other allocations in between the common double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered. Impact ====== All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected. Examples of software using GPGME are - Gpg4win - GnuPG Desktop - GnuPG VS-Desktop - Most mail clients - Many XMPP clients - Samba - Flatpack Solution ======== Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1. If you need a DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version. For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME 2.3.1. If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to very old versions. There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT. Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19) ================================================ [compared to version 2.2.0] * New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM. Add mappings for algos used bei backends. [rMa85fa49236] * Fix a double free in the status line read code. [T8557,CVE-2026-129975] * Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release: ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ GPGME_PK_DLTHM NEW. GPGME_PK_MLKEM NEW. GPGME_PK_MLDSA NEW. Release-info: https://dev.gnupg.org/T8427 Getting the Software ==================== Please follow the instructions found at or read on: The GPGME source code compressed using BZIP2 and its OpenPGP signature are available here: https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 (1393k) https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2.sig A sufficient patch to solve the security bug for older versions is attached. Note that version 2.3.0 was never publicly available. Debian Packages =============== We also provide Debian style packages for a couple of Debian variants. See https://repos.gnupg.org/deb/gnupg/trixie/ or use the menu to switch to other distros/releases. Windows Installer ================= A new version of Gpg4win (5.1.2), our full featured Windows installer, including the fixed version of GPGME, the Kleopatra GUI, and a PDF reader has also been released. Head over to https://gpg4win.org/ Checking the Integrity ====================== See https://gnupg.org/download/integrity_check.html The checksum for gpgme is: 1134a407b50204ee6fb9efaa6e1451c2460e543e gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 *Thank you all* Your GnuPG hackers p.s. This is an announcement only mailing list. Please send replies only to the gnupg-customers at gnupg.org mailing list. * List of Release Signing Keys: To guarantee that a downloaded version has not been tampered by malicious entities we provide signature files for all tarballs and binary versions. The keys are also signed by the long term keys of their respective owners. Current releases are signed by one or more of these five keys: ed25519 2020-08-24 [SC] [expires: 2030-06-30] 6DAA 6E64 A76D 2840 571B 4902 5288 97B8 2640 3ADA Werner Koch (dist signing 2020) ed25519 2021-05-19 [SC] [expires: 2027-04-04] AC8E 115B F73E 2D8D 47FA 9908 E98E 9B2D 19C6 C8BD Niibe Yutaka (GnuPG Release Key) rsa3072 2025-05-09 [SC] [expires: 2033-03-03] 3B76 1AE4 E63B F351 9CE7 D63B ECB6 64CB E133 2EEF Alexander Kulbartsch (GnuPG Release Key) ed25519 2026-07-20 [SC] [expires: 2036-06-30] D02A E491 73BD AD56 E4F8 8223 707E 56D3 DEF4 115C Ingo Klöcker (Release Signing Key 2026) brainpoolP256r1 2021-10-15 [SC] [expires: 2029-12-31] 02F3 8DFF 731F F97C B039 A1DA 549E 695E 905B A208 GnuPG.com (Release Signing Key 2021) brainpoolP384r1 2026-02-23 [SC] [expires: 2034-02-23] 1493 269D E61F 124A A69A 316E 3ADF 34EB DBB2 00A4 GnuPG.com (Release Signing Key 2026) The keys are available at https://gnupg.org/signature_key.html and in any recently released GnuPG tarball in the file g10/distsigkey.gpg . According to recent reports, in a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the firm complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

According to recent reports, apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

It has been revealed that at the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a upcoming filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic states Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Industry observers note that apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple indicates decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”.

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

It has been revealed that under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”.

Sources indicate that according to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a fresh order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a certified personal trainer, I work with a wide range of clients who have lots of different fitness goals. But for my clients in their 60s and beyond, there’s usually one objective that drives their training: improving balance and stability.

Sources indicate that I recently started working with a 60-year-old client who wanted to focus on just that. She noticed that she was a little more unsteady on her feet than she used to be, and had a few close calls with falling. After a thorough check-up with her doctor, we began our work together with the following routine.

These exercises aren’t just for seniors. It’s never too early to start thinking about your balance, so give them a try during your next workout. They’re appropriate for any fitness level and you won’t need any equipment to do them (but adding a dumbbell or two will always make things more challenging).

Check in with your doctor before trying any new workout, especially if you have balance concerns.

Recent findings suggest that these exercises aren’t hard, but doing them correctly is important. Beginners should consider meeting with a personal trainer or physical therapist for feedback and guidance on form, and to get modifications if needed.

Industry observers note that you’ll just need some room and an elevated platform, like a stair step, for this workout. Hang onto a chair or another stable surface for additional support if you need it.

Recent findings suggest that start by doing each exercise for one set of 10 reps. As your balance improves, you can add an additional set and increase your reps to 12. You can also use small dumbbells for the step-up to balance to ramp up the difficulty.

These exercises can be done on their own or as a warm-up for other activities.

You may feel muscle fatigue when doing this workout, but you should never feel sharp pain. Stop the workout immediately and consult your physician if you feel sharp pain at any point.

Here’s how to do the exercises:.

The exercises in this workout force you to find equilibrium when your center of gravity is maintained over a smaller surface area – either one foot for the standing marches, step up to balance, and side step to balance, or a narrow placement of two feet for the heel-to-toe walks.

In a recent development, during these exercises, your deep core muscles like the rectus abdominis and internal obliques engage to stabilize and support your entire body. Your glutes and hip stabilizing muscles also work to keep the hips in a level position. The stronger these muscles are, the more conditioned they’ll be to keep you upright and sturdy during everyday movement.

Additionally, exercises like the step-up to balance strengthen key muscle groups in your lower body, like the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes.

66 Years Later, Charles M. Sculz's Favorite Peanuts Strip Is Undefeated

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that first seen in 1960, and then three years later as featured in the first animated Peanuts feature film, a now-iconic scene of Charlie Brown, Linus, and Lucy van Pelt lying on the grass and staring at the clouds won audiences over worldwide.
  • Sources indicate that it's hard to argue the effectiveness of the scene, too, given the lovable loser Charlie Brown's practically embarrassed, sheepish reaction to Linus' superior commentary.
  • Famously used as the intro scene for A Boy Named Charlie Brown, this iconic cloud watching Peanuts strip is quoted practically verbatim as this primary trio of kids unleashes their takes on the clouds flying overhead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that first seen in 1960, and then three years later as featured in the first animated Peanuts feature film, a now-iconic scene of Charlie Brown, Linus, and Lucy van Pelt lying on the grass and staring at the clouds won audiences over worldwide. In its essence, it's a great dichotomy of imaginative childhood wonder at shapes in the clouds, with Linus' comparisons being notably more highbrow and specific, while Charlie Brown's were, naturally, utterly humbled by this due to their sheer simplicity. Yet, creator Charles M. Schulz created this strip that's now commonly reported among his favorites such as in The Complete Peanuts volume 5: 1959 to 1960 via Win Wiacek.

Sources indicate that it's hard to argue the effectiveness of the scene, too, given the lovable loser Charlie Brown's practically embarrassed, sheepish reaction to Linus' superior commentary. But between the commentary of the three, all of their comments are fairly valid, with the August 14, 1960 comic strip quickly immortalized in both animated format and shortlisted by fans as a personal favorite of Schulz's. It says a pretty good basic summary of how each character views the world, while serving as an excellent scene to set the tone for A Boy Named Charlie Brown.

Famously used as the intro scene for A Boy Named Charlie Brown, this iconic cloud watching Peanuts strip is quoted practically verbatim as this primary trio of kids unleashes their takes on the clouds flying overhead. The outspoken Lucy gives a perfectly rational, simplistic approach, seeing them as major balls of cotton, while even prompting the other two to use their imagination to convey what they see. Linus gives an intensely specific set of descriptions like topographical maps, an American realist artist, and an oddly specific description of the Stoning of Stephen.

It's especially funny to watch the animated version as Charlie Brown repeatedly cranes his neck, clearly trying to spot what Linus sees in the clouds above, growing more distressed that he's just not seeing it.

Then comes Charlie Brown's turn, as he's called on to say what he sees. He gives throwaway animal shapes like a ducky or a horsey, perfectly legitimate options for a child to give, but retracts them, perhaps believing he could have used his imagination more effectively. None of the kids laugh or are even phased beyond Charlie Brown himself, as the film moves to the opening credits sequence from then on.

Sources indicate that it sets the tone well for what viewers can expect from the characters, and the comic strip clearly inspired other moments like 1975's Snoopy! The Musical, in which Charlie Brown is joined by an even larger group of friends who consistently talk over him with what they see in the clouds. It even has an identical ending, with everyone turning to a blushing Charlie Brown, who once again gives his throwaway animal shapes even after a song's worth of colorful descriptions. Perhaps more than anything else, this comic strip has continued to strengthen the perception of Charlie Brown as a character, and his particular struggles.

Recent findings suggest that the humility of Charlie Brown is a recurring element of Peanuts, both cementing his own vulnerability while keeping him grounded, affable, and unpretentious. His descriptions are those of the average kid, while people like Linus seem to offer up elevated perceptions of mundane reality. But it's also that same openness and self-awareness that show Charlie Brown's honesty as a character, willing to offer up what he sees while also being open to thinking a little further, or even just withdraw, in any of the adaptations of this particular Peanuts strip. It's awkward, and seeing him cut off every time in the musical number is rough, but it's completely relatable.

Part of being a kid is indulging one's imagination on all ends of the spectrum, as it helps their cognitive and social development. Charlie Brown might pull away, but at least he still described what he saw in the clouds, and it's clear that Schulz put a little bit of himself into that scene, namely, the shy, withdrawn side of the boy as he struggles to engage like the other kids. But it's also important that this side of childhood, vulnerability, enables anyone to be open to greater growth opportunities, whether cloud watching in Peanuts, or any number of other perfectly relatable, real-world scenarios.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates new maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Organization all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. In a recent development, the great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. Sources indicate that adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a latest adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a latest report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report indicates Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

In a recent development, back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That stated, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was declared, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less vital in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

  • At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid intends for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid intends for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp customers running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Consumers can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for consumers running the public version without requiring another app revision.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

According to recent reports, iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also indicated that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Sources indicate that percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%.

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

Roman isn't left looking for a job long, though. Pierce offers Roman a job at Pierce's firm, seeing Roman's clear talent as a legal mind. However, Roman swiftly clashes with the culture at his new firm, and it's obvious why.

This forces Denzel to give a fairly uncharacteristic and complex performance. While Roman shares Denzel's proclivity for effortlessly spewing compelling dialogue, there's none of the gravitas that comes with Washington's more verbose, award-nominated performances. Roman has a well-educated, well-spoken tongue, but he doesn't have the smooth, silver tongue of someone like Alonzo in "Training Day," or even historical figures Malcolm X and Rubin "The Hurricane" Carter.

There's also a physical element to the performance. It's unclear whether he's wearing a relatively subtle fat suit, bulkier clothing, gained actual weight for the performance or some combination of the three, but Denzel as Roman is a noticeably larger figure than I typically associate with the actor. Not that he's ever diminutive on screen; he's as often an action star as he is a dramatic force of nature and typically he's in excellent shape. But the physique of Roman is one I'd associate more with Forest Whitaker than Denzel. In fact, I couldn't help but think about what the movie would be like with Whitaker, an incredible actor in his own right, as Roman instead of Washington.
