📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that bolt has demonstrated that a shared scooter can be more than a vehicle. It can also be a mobile geospatial sensor.

During its Wheels4Wheels pilot in Tallinn, Estonia, the company used sensors already installed in its scooters to assess pavement conditions, curb transitions and other features affecting wheelchair owners and people with reduced mobility.

According to recent reports, bolt says the project covered approximately 550 kilometres across all eight Tallinn districts, producing 40.5 million accelerometer readings and more than 66,000 surface-quality assessments. The resulting information was contributed to OpenStreetMap, according to Bolt’s accessibility programme page.

Industry observers note that publishing the results as open data makes the project more significant than a conventional corporate mapping exercise. Municipalities, routing applications and accessibility services could all potentially use the observations.

According to recent reports, the larger opportunity is the conversion of commercial vehicle fleets into continuously operating urban-observation networks. Thousands of scooters already traverse city streets during everyday operations, potentially detecting damaged surfaces and deteriorating infrastructure without requiring a dedicated municipal survey.

Recent findings suggest that according to Geo Week News, Bolt combined GPS with accelerometers, gyroscopes and cameras. The manufacturer reports that the pilot increased available surface-quality data in Tallinn by 26%. These figures have not been independently audited.

Recent findings suggest that the difficult step is converting motion signals into reliable accessibility information. A vibration could represent broken pavement, cobblestones, a drainage channel or an abrupt rider manoeuvre. Results may also vary with speed, tyre pressure, weather and scooter model.

Coverage presents another limitation. Scooters primarily travel where their use is permitted and commercially viable. They may miss residential streets, pedestrian paths and disconnected sections that create the greatest problems for wheelchair consumers.

Recent findings suggest that each observation therefore needs provenance, a confidence level and an effective validation method. The most key validators should include wheelchair and mobility-aid owners, who can determine whether a detected anomaly represents a genuine barrier.

Recent findings suggest that wheels4Wheels complements rather than replaces existing accessibility platforms. Wheelmap maps the accessibility of public places, while Project Sidewalk combines crowdsourcing, machine learning and street imagery to identify curb ramps and obstacles. Bolt adds passive, recurring fleet sensing.

A future workflow could use scooter telemetry to flag anomalies, imagery to classify them and local contributors to confirm their significance before the information enters OpenStreetMap.

According to recent reports, public discussion of the project has also highlighted a contradiction: poorly parked scooters can themselves block sidewalks and curb ramps. Bolt’s accessibility strategy must therefore address parking and obstruction management alongside data collection.

According to recent reports, if the company can demonstrate reliable classification, transparent data handling and meaningful participation by accessibility users, Wheels4Wheels could evolve into more than a mapping experiment. The sensing capacity already exists. The next challenge is turning it into trustworthy, routable and genuinely inclusive geospatial infrastructure.

For decades, “more bands” in Earth observation meant one of two things: you either work with multispectral sensors; four to ten broad bands, cheap, fast and familiar or else transition to the hyperspectral domain, which has hundreds of narrow, contiguous bands, costly and enormous data volumes. However, this gap is closing not by making hyperspectral high-resolution accessible, but by rethinking what “enough bands” actually means. A category is quietly establishing itself between the two: Superspectral, a curated set of roughly a dozen to a few dozen discrete bands, placed purposely at specific wavelengths that correspond to something physically meaningful, rather than being sampled continuously across the electromagnetic spectrum.

Recent findings suggest that multispectral sensors were built around a simple idea: a handful of broad bands such as blue, green, red, red-edge, near-infrared are enough to compute NDVI & NDRE, delineate landcover, and monitor vegetation vigour at scale. Many of these systems also carry a panchromatic band: a single high-resolution spectral channel spanning across the visible spectrum (400-800 nm), used purely to sharpen spatial detail rather than to add spectral information. That’s the multispectral-era trade-off at minimal where spatial resolution and spectral resolution were treated as two separate problems, solved by two different types of bands. It works and it still works, for a huge share of remote sensing applications.

According to recent reports, however, broad bands average out the very features that distinguish stressed vegetation from healthy vegetation, one water body from another, or one mineral from the next. A 100-120 nm wide band cannot resolve a narrow absorption or reflectance feature within it. Indices tied to specific physiological or physical processes such as pigment ratios, early-stage stress signatures and water turbidity, often require reflectance captured at precise, narrow wavelengths which a standard four or five-band setup was never designed to capture.

Why Hyperspectral isn’t the Universal Answer.

Industry observers note that hyperspectral imaging solves the problem by capturing contiguous and narrow bands. A 20-band sensor covering 500-700 nm at 10 nm interval is hyperspectral by this definition, while a sensor with 20 discrete, non-adjacent bands spanning the visible through infrared is still, technically a multispectral. That distinction matters because hyperspectral sensors carry real expense; complex optics, strict calibration requirements, and data volumes that stretch onboard storage, downlink bandwidth, and downstream ML pipelines. For most applied problems, that’s more data than the underlying problem statement actually needs.

The Middle Category: Superspectral.

It has been revealed that superspectral fits between the two. Rather than sampling the electromagnetic spectrum continuously, it samples it selectively – a dozen-plus discrete, narrow bands chosen because they align with known absorption or reflectance features, not because they happen to be adjacent on a continuum. It’s a knowledge-first approach to sensor design: instead of asking “how much of the spectrum can we cover continuously,” it asks “which specific wavelengths actually carry the signal we care about.”.

This only works if the band selection is grounded in the underlying physics or biology of the target. Which is exactly where the reasoning gets interesting — because the “right” dozen bands look completely different depending on what you’re trying to measure.

Building the Case: Three Domains, Three Different Superspectral Stacks.

It has been revealed that water promptly absorbs longer wavelengths, which is exactly why coastal and bathymetric applications require the shorter wavelength of the visible spectrum. In clear, deep water 400-450 nm wavelength penetrates furthest, making it the band of choice for shallow-water bathymetry and seafloor mapping. In turbid or CDOM-rich coastal water the picture inverts: suspended sediment and dissolved organic matter absorb and scatter strongly in the blue, and the transmission peak migrates toward green. On sediment loaded reef sites it has been observed shifting by around 100 nm into the green-yellow, peaking near 575 nm. A standard multispectral blue band, which is broadly tuned for atmospheric correction and land applications, is not optimized for this; a narrow, purpose-placed coastal-blue bands are. This is a case where one extra, carefully positioned band is more beneficial for the application than several additional generic ones.

Extending the vegetation logic straight into urban environments using Red-edge and NIR bands, but the physics doesn’t transfer as cleanly. Red-edge and NIR bands are diagnostic of chlorophyll and canopy structure, which makes them excellent for mapping urban vegetation fraction: street trees, park canopy, green-roof coverage, and green-space stress, all of which are legitimate and useful urban indicators, especially as proxies for urban surface extent and heat island risk. But Red-edge and NIR bands are not, a strong basis for classifying built materials themselves — asphalt, concrete, and rooftops don’t have a red-edge-style feature the way vegetation does. The spectral region that most cleanly separates impervious surfaces from vegetation and bare soil sits further out, in the shortwave infrared, where built materials and natural surfaces diverge most sharply. A Red-edge/NIR-only superspectral stack can tell you a great deal about a city’s green infrastructure; it can’t, tell you what the non-green parts of the city are made of. Getting that requires extending the band selection into SWIR — which is a fair, extension of the same superspectral principle: add exactly the band the physics calls for, nothing more.

Superspectral Sensors Exists: Drones to Satellites.

It has been revealed that micasense Drone payload: RedEdge-P Triple. A stacked triple narrowband camera bodies on one drone platform, each contributing a handful of 15 discrete, narrow, non-contiguous bands, pan-sharpened to 4 centimetres per pixel, enough to compute pigment and stress-sensitive indices that a standard five-band multispectral sensor can’t generate. This is the smallest-scale, most accessible end of the superspectral sensor; no continuous spectral coverage, just a deliberately chosen set of narrow bands.

Commercial VHR satellite: WorldView-3. Launched in 2014, WorldView-3 is explicitly described in the remote sensing literature and by its operators as a “Superspectral” sensor, a term used specifically to distinguish it from hyperspectral. Its imager collects 8 discrete VNIR bands (coastal, blue, green, yellow, red, red-edge, and two NIR bands), 8 discrete SWIR bands, and a separate 12-band CAVIS instrument for atmospheric correction (clouds, aerosols, water vapor, ice, and snow) 29 bands in total, but none of them contiguous in the way a hyperspectral band are. That distinction matters: WorldView-3 has been used for tasks like hydrocarbon and mineral detection that’s the domain of hyperspectral, precisely because its SWIR bands were placed at known diagnostic absorption features rather than spread evenly across the spectrum.

Research microsatellite: VENμS. A joint French–Israeli mission (CNES and the Israel Space Agency, launched 2017), was purpose-built VENμS Super-Spectral Camera (VSSC) with exactly 12 narrow bands between 415–910 nm, at 5.3 m resolution with a 2-day revisit. The band placement was designed specifically around vegetation status and the chlorophyll red-edge, plus atmospheric correction. It’s one of the cleanest real-world matches to the “12-18 narrow, targeted bands” definition of superspectral, since it was purpose-built as a science mission rather than adapted from a broader commercial sensor.

Next-generation Landsat constellation: Landsat Next. Planned for launch in late 2030/early 2031, the USGS and NASA’s Landsat Next mission is explicitly presented as “26-band Superspectral”, more than double the 11 bands on Landsat 8 and 9. It combines refined versions of Landsat’s legacy bands, ten newly introduced bands targeting applications like harmful algal blooms and snow hydrology, and five thermal infrared bands. When, a government agency formally classifies its flagship imaging mission as “superspectral” rather than multispectral or hyperspectral, that’s a strong indication the category has moved from marketing language to an accepted technical classification.

Why This Matters for GeoAI Pipelines.

The pattern across all three domains is the same, and it’s the real reason for superspectral as a category:.

It has been revealed that the multispectral or hyperspectral is a simple binary choice. Superspectral won’t replace either, broadband multispectral remains the workhorse for large-scale, low-cost monitoring, and hyperspectral remains necessary where continuous spectral coverage matters, like detailed mineral mapping or ore detection. But for the growing set of problems that need specific physical or biological signals – water quality, vegetation stress, urban green infrastructure and many more; without the overhead of a full hyperspectral sensor system, superspectral is becoming the realistic answer. It’s less “how much of the spectrum can we see” and more “how much do we actually need to see, and where.”.

It has been revealed that superspectral systems, by design, only see what they were told to look for. That’s a real trade-off, not a compromise to gloss over, it’s the whole point of this technology.

Apple today unveiled that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a latest post published on its developer portal, Apple today declared a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the company, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:.

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”.

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and revision their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:.

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”.

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud intends.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it introduces Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:.

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:.

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

In a recent development, it may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that time is one of the greatest tools when it comes to a film's classic status, as while there will always be those films that are massive success stories right out of the gate, it states so much more about a film if it continues to be talked about and celebrated decades after its release. Through constant rewatches, reexaminations, and word-of-mouth over the years, classic status can become that much larger, and even latest films can grow to be considered classics of their respective eras.

The 90s is one such era that is overflowing with films that are now being considered all-time classics, with each year of the 90s having its own selection of great classic films. 1996 specifically proves to be a year full of exciting and incredibly memorable cinematic experiences ranging in all different varieties of genre and style. With these legendary films having turned 30 years old in 2026, there is no better time than the present to revisit these films that are now undeniable classics.

Recent findings suggest that while the film originally had a mixed critical reception due to its overwhelming commercialism and a middling performance by Michael Jordan, time has been incredibly kind to the legacy of the original Space Jam, with it now being an unmistakable classic of the family movie genre. A part of it comes from the fact that this style of comedy, blending together 2D animation and live-action, is so severely underutilized in the modern day, with Coyote vs. Acme being the only major recent example of such a film.

Recent findings suggest that the film also acts as this glorious transport back to the culture and style of the 90s, working as this nostalgic look back at 90s basketball stars and 90s humor as a whole. Even with its flaws, the film proves to be incredibly rewatchable and a bundle of fun to witness, full of wild cartoony antics and even some inherent so-bad-it's-good elements that have helped maintain its icon status as a 90s classic.

According to recent reports, A wildly chaotic fight to survive the night and one of the most explosively entertaining vampire movies of all time, From Dusk Till Dawn blends together an array of different genres to find its distinct flavor of success. While horror is the primary and immediately recognizable genre, it also dabbles in aspects of crime and action in its execution, not even delving into its horror elements until its second half. The Robert Rodriguez film also finds great strength from the screen presence of its on-screen talent, with the likes of George Clooney, Quentin Tarantino, and Salma Hayek all leaving a large impact on the audience.

In a recent development, its one-of-a-kind execution and individuality as a horror film has made it that much more of an iconic and memorable experience over the years. The film is rife with personality and charm that makes it a blast from start to finish, unlike any other horror film of the era and continuing to find a niche 30 years after its release.

In a recent development, the works of David Cronenberg have grown increasingly appreciated in the years since their release, as general audiences and art house fans have grown more desensitized to his harsh, incredibly violent concepts, and are able to more deeply appreciate them in all their shocking nature. While Crash may not be filled to the brim with gore and body horror like his other films, the psychosexual strengths of the film have made it a fan-favorite of many modern film fans.

In a recent development, it's wild premise of people finding the eroticism in car crashes makes it one of the all-time most insane films ever made, yet the film never falters in the human elements of its pure insanity, making it all the more powerful and striking in its execution. Further amplified by a great performance by James Spader and exceptional directing by Cronenberg, Crash has become an undeniable classic of 1996, even if its NC-17 content made it so that many regions couldn't see the film until 1997.

The 90s are widely considered to be the Renaissance era of Walt Disney Animation Studios, when they were at the absolute top of their game and evolving the medium of 2D-feature length animation with a new string of talent and brilliance. While films like Aladdin and The Lion King always come to mind when considering the defining works of this era, one film that has grown more and more appreciation as one of the best Disney Renaissance films is The Hunchback of Notre Dame.

Sources indicate that this emotional musical retelling of the classic literary novel accomplishes so much in its navigation of the material, proving to be one of Disney's darkest and most mature films to date. This sense of edge and insightful layered themes have made it a critical darling since its release, having some of the highest highs of any Disney film ever made. While it may not have the raw commercial and brand appeal of other Renaissance films that became major franchises, The Hunchback of Notre Dame is still a masterpiece of animation that continues to be celebrated decades later.

While many of Adam Sandler's comedy films continue to be appreciated and have their distinct followings, there is something inherent to the comedy of his earlier films in the 90s that still make them icons of comedy in the era. Among these films, Happy Gilmore continues to be celebrated and appreciated as one of Sandler's best films, perfectly tapping into his distinct comedic strengths with a classic story of underdog sports. The film proved to be so beloved as a comedy classic that it even received a legacy sequel in 2025.

Sources indicate that the film inherits all of the greatest strengths that fans love about Sandler's comedies, seeing him as an idiotic yet lovable goofball who wears his heart on his sleeve. It certainly adds its own flair to the classic formula, making the character of Happy Gilmore more aggressive in nature, but the film at its heart is about as classic as a Sandler comedy can get.

In a recent development, one of many massively celebrated masterpieces from director Danny Boyle, Trainspotting is this dark and deeply emotional black comedy delving into drug abuse, proverty, and crime from a group of eclectic heroin addicts. As they soon prove to garner psychopathic tendencies, their lives manage to get much more chaotic and dangerous when the scale of their crimes proves to grow alongside their crippling addictions.

Industry observers note that while the film undeniably deals with some incredibly dark material, the approach and upbeat filmmaking of Boyle makes it incredibly entertaining from start to finish, able to find comedy from the darkest of concepts and feeling brilliantly bleak in its execution. The indie film had a lot of critical acclaim when it first released, but it wouldn't truly become a classic of the era until its home video release, where word of mouth made the film as much of a hit with general audiences as it was with the critics who first witnessed its greatness.

According to recent reports, one specific strength inherent to 90s filmmaking is that, as society at large was beginning to grow more accepting and appreciative of queer people and their struggles, film was able to more outwardly explore queer stories that weren't able to be told in previous eras. This directly led the way to films like The Birdcage, which paved the way for many exceptional queer comedies while also being one of the funniest comedies that the 90s has to offer. The film sees Nathan Lane and Robin Williams as a gay couple who must pretend to be straight so that they can be introduced to their son's fiancée's conservative parents.

Sources indicate that williams and Lane are two of the strongest comedic voices of the 90s, with them seamlessly working off of each other and bringing out the best ine one another in this comedic tour de force, making the film a delight from start to finish. It also helps that, unlike several other queer-centric comedies of the era that have aged poorly in the eyes of modern queer audiences, The Birdcage is still massively celebrated as an ahead-of-its-time masterclass of satirical comedy.

Tom Cruise was undeniably a Hollywood star in the 80s, but it wasn't until the 90s that he became such a massive household name and one of the biggest stars in Hollywood history. It's films like Jerry Maguire that most distinctly utilized his range and possibilities as an actor, showing his outstanding comedic strengths as opposed to the usual action blockbuster he would star in. The film sees Cruise as the titular Jerry Maguire, a sports agent whose livelihood is in jeopardy when he attempts to go about his job with honesty instead of constant deception.

It has been revealed that this iconic romantic comedy still stands as one of the most memorable and defining films in Cruise's entire career, as it perfectly plays to his strengths outside of the action genre as an electrifying force of charisma and charm. The continued appreciation and celebration of the film can also be attributed to just how much of a cultural phenomenon and 90s icon that the film ended up being, as its sharp comedy and genuine emotion left a massive impact on audiences of the 90s and beyond.

The brilliantly dry and dark comedy of the Coen Brothers have made many of their films perfectly suited for classic status, whether it be immediate critical hits or films that grow into cult classics after years of appreciation. Fargo is arguably a film that took both approaches to classic status, being overwhelmingly critically acclaimed when it first released while also having its classic status majorly amplified by home video word of mouth.

Sources indicate that it certainly doesn't hurt that the film also directly inspired one of the greatest TV show masterpieces of all time, but the brilliance and classic status of Fargo was already in place long before the TV show completely redefined what Fargo could be. With an array of goofy and distinct characters and a central crime that continues to spiral into madness as it goes on, Fargo is one of the most brilliant yet endearingly hilarious crime movies ever made. It's one of few films whose classic status and overwhelming love continues to grow more and more with each passing year, feeling absolutely timeless in its execution.

Still widely considered by many to be the greatest slasher film ever made, Scream completely revitalized the genre and ushered in a newly introduced era of 90s slashers after a string of middling sequels threatened the longevity of the horror subgenre. This brilliant satire and parody of classic horror clichés flipped the genre on its head for many audiences, simultaneously acting as a love letter to the horror genre while also feeling much more approachable in its execution.

It's this perfect mixture of Wes Craven's genuinely impactful horror directing and a great comedic screenplay from Kevin Williamson that made the film not just one of 1996's biggest classics, but arguably the defining horror film of the entire decade. It's simultaneously rooted in 90s culture while also able to be enjoyed and appreciated at any time, being just as striking and impactful nowadays as it was when it first released. The film's influence on horror as a whole is also unmistakable, continuing to directly influence a wide array of horror comedies 30 years after its original release.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

In a recent development, you're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that organization or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

In a recent development, unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

In a recent development, next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

In a recent development, once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, revision the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck.
  • Xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen.
  • But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have many gripes with modern smartphones, but one of the things that really grinds my gears is the trend of Godzilla-sized camera bumps on the backs of phones, Apple's doing it, Samsung' seems to be planning on it, and a lot of Chinese brands look like they've been hit by a rogue hockey puck. I've been testing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which also has a large, iPhone-looking camera bump, but this time things are different.

Xiaomi has taken on the task of making the most out of that normally-wasted space on the camera bump by turning it into a screen. This is not the first phone to feature a rear-mounted screen, or even the first Xiaomi flagship to do so, but in a world of phones that all seem to feel and look the same, it's quite exciting to see a phone organization offer something that helps its phones stand out.

But the question is not whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's Back Display is interesting, it's whether it's able to justify its own existence.

It has been revealed that looking at the 18 Pro Max, my mind immediately jumped to the cover displays on compact foldables. The way the display wraps around the two main cameras is reminiscent of the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Motorola Razr. It's a little smaller than those screens, measuring 2.9-inches compared to those 4+-inch screens, but all three share a common purpose.

This is a way to use your phone without actually using your phone, using the smaller screen to look at basic information like the time or notifications on a smaller and more power-efficient display. At the same time, and as Xiaomi is keen to emphasize, it's a way to customize the look and feel of your phone in a way that cases and other accessories just can't manage.

According to recent reports, my initial thoughts upon looking at the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max and playing around with the screen weren't totally positive. I couldn't stop comparing it to the cover screens on foldable phones, and the fact that those screens are front-and-center when you take out your device. Xiaomi's screen is on the back, which is not part of my phone I tend to pay very much attention to.

But the more I used it, and the more I figured out that it wasn't just a glorified clock and notification alert, the more I realized that my initial reaction was the wrong way of looking at things.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sources indicate that the idea that this is potentially a very valuable feature clicked when I opened up the camera on the Back Display. This allows you to take selfies using the main cameras, in a similar fashion to foldable phones, using the rear-mounted screen as a viewfinder. This means you're taking selfies with the 200MP main camera, rather than the lower resolution hole-punch camera on the front.

Sources indicate that I'm not going to lie, though. This isn't a fully-fledged phone screen capable of running all the apps and services that you've got installed. It is significantly more limited than that, and the difference is like describing the difference between a smart home hub and a tablet.

The home hub may be useful for its own specific use case, but it doesn't have the same versatility or usefulness as a tablet running Android or iPadOS.

According to recent reports, the Back Display is great for glancing at notifications and the time, especially if you tend to leave your phone lying face down. It even supports Live Activities on a handful of apps, including letting you control music playback on Spotify. Plus, it's possible to customize your screen with different backgrounds and clockfaces, depending on what your own personal tastes and style might be.

So far so good, though I can't say that I've ever felt using my main screen for those tasks has ever been a particular burden — especially since I'm just not used to looking at the back of my phone.

Then again, if you already have a smartwatch, that's not going to mean much, since you already have the bulk of this information available on your wrist.

Xiaomi does seem to be hinging on Generative AI to turn this screen from a gimmick into something you'll want to use throughout the day, thanks to a built-in system that lets you vibe code your own apps.

Sources indicate that anyone that remembers the flop that was Windows Phone will know that success of a mobile platform hinges on app support. Your apps give the system value, and without developers actively contributing to an app store, there's little reason for people to actually invest in one of your devices.

So how do you get app developers on board to add utility to a niche display on the back of a handful of phones? You don't. You hand that job to the users, and let generative AI do all the hard work. So Xiaomi added a prompt-based system for creating Back Display apps from scratch, as well as an App Store of sorts that lets you see a curated selection of what other people have created.

Industry observers note that options I can see include workout schedules, mini games, educational tools, timers, and all kinds of different options, though I have no idea how effective or accurate they actually are compared to full-coded apps. Still, it's nice to see that there's a way to improve the usefulness of the Back Display — even if it would be nice to have proper Android apps on offer.

Industry observers note that I found that basic prompts did work, but the more detail you could offer the better the outcome. Xiaomi can "polish" your prompt to better your chances of generating a usable app.

However, this does not guarantee that the app would successfully generate — or that it would work. It took me multiple attempts to create a Doom clone, and even when it did, I kept getting killed off by a monster hiding out of my line of sight.

Sources indicate that so it's not quite as painless as having a developer-made app, and playing games on a small screen isn't ideal. But in the absence of additional features, this system is fairly good at filling that niche.

Industry observers note that I've spent my entire life looking at the front of my phone, and never really concerning myself with what's on the back. Even in the pre-smartphone era the screen was everything, whereas the back was just... not vital. If rear screens start to take off, that could change the way people interact with their phones in a big way. And that's obviously going to take a lot of getting used to.

Industry observers note that that's probably the biggest hurdle these rear screens will face. There's certainly no shortage of utility, especially with the generative AI apps. It's just reprogramming user habits to glance at the back of the phone rather than looking at their main display. It's going to be an uphill battle to convince people that these screens are worth it, especially when they have to compete with wearables.

If it weren't for the AI apps I'd say these screens don't have much of a chance. I'm not convinced that they will take off, aside from a few niche gimmicks, but at least they have some sort of unique selling point to work with.

Breaking: I'm quite pleased by the tech architecture of my art website

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Klauria

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the new static site generator they wrote to make it.
  • Earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online.
  • When it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the new static site generator they wrote to make it. This post isnât exactly that, but maybe only on a technicality, in that itâs not about this websiteâ¦.

Earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online. I donât much use social media besides Hacker News, but I wanted to share my work with friends and family. So Iâd been sending scans of my work in group chats. That was fine for a bit but so messy and disorganized. Sometimes someone asked, âWhere did you paint this?â Sometimes a friend wanted to see what it looked like in real life. My little brother suggested a map with a marker for each piece. That was a good idea! For that Iâd need a website and some code. Here, take a look at the map, its done now! You can zoom and click on markers to see the painting!

When it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me. One is the Wolf of Pragmatism, which wants to smash every problem with whatever hammer is nearest at hand: âIsnât this just some trivial React? Dump the images in S3 and call it a day. This website is for friends and family; you have no traffic to speak of. Put a CDN in front so your parents in India get reasonable performance.â.

The other is the Aesthetic Wolf: âThis should be a static website. The content almost never changes.â.

Recent findings suggest that yes. This is a static website. I do at most four, and on average less than 0.3, paintings a day. The content almost never changes. Why should javascript render the page on the userâs browser? Why should any code even run on the server? I should have the bytes for every page just sitting there, ready to be shipped. The correct server implementation for this problem is open followed by sendfile inside the event loop (Iâm joking but only kind of?). The Aesthetic Wolf won.

It has been revealed that but the problem with a static website is that for every new post, I need to add a file, and run a build, and deploy it to production. I made a hundred paintings this year! Even if I automate a lot of it, I wanted a better UI for stuff like adding tags and setting location. And the best UI for whatâs essentially a CRUD app is â¦ probably a web UI. But if I have a web UI that changes the content of the website, thatâs not a static website any more.

Now look at this colorful house!

Sources indicate that so what I really want is a website thatâs static for everyone else, but dynamic for me. I want a build system but I want it triggered by actions in a nice CRUD UI that I make, not GitHub actions or a terminal.

According to recent reports, hereâs my silly little solution to this silly conundrum. Iâm sure the design Iâm about to describe isnât novel, but I did come up with it. Iâm just pleased by it because itâs an efficient solution to the exact problem I happened to have. Itâs dollar-efficient for me, i.e., itâs free*. Itâs resource-efficient for Cloudflare, because the static assets are rarely rebuilt and mostly sit there cached. And itâs fast, because the bytes are mostly sitting there in a CDN waiting to be sent.

In a recent development, (Asterisk: the compute and bandwidth are free. The storage is at the moment free, but if I paint enough then Iâll go past the 10 GB free tier and pay a couple cents per month.).

According to recent reports, the main idea is that every html page is rendered on the server, but with a cache header telling Cloudflareâs infrastructure to cache the response forever (well, for 30 days). Then, whenever I upload a upcoming art piece or change the set of tags or anything like that, the request handler for this write operation invalidates all cached pages. Thatâs it.

Industry observers note that thereâs one detail that makes this work well for an image-heavy website: we generate several smaller sizes of each image at upload time, and I actually do it on the clientâs browser. Since Iâm the only uploader, that would be my browser. We need the smaller sizes for thumbnails and cards, where sending the full archival images would be way too slow. Those downsampled images are uploaded along with originals to Cloudflareâs R2, their S3-equivalent.

Sources indicate that why downsample at upload time? Cloudflare does offer an image service thatâll do the resizing the first time you make a request for that image at that size, and itâll cache that resized copy. But in my case I already know the three sizes I want, so itâs faster to just precompute and store them. The additional storage doesnât add up to much, because the archival images are enormous compared to downsampled copies.

All the metadata for all pieces goes in a single json file that also lives in R2. When someone requests a dynamic html page, like the one for pieces tagged #summer, a piece of code runs in a Cloudflare worker. It reads the json and generates the html, which is then cached until the next invalidation. Cloudflareâs CDN handles the rest: if someone in India later requests the same page, the cached artifact is sent to an edge machine in India and cached there for a while. I suppose Cloudflare can choose to rerun the worker instead of copying the artifact, which is fine by me. Based on my testing thatâs not what happens: the generator writes a timestamp on each page so I can see when it was generated.

In a recent development, the website has some interactive stuff like maps and timelines. Those are just embedded javascript that run on the clientâs browser and read that single metadata json file to initialize. They donât write anything back to the server, so thereâs no database or anything. Theyâre just displaying the information in different ways. For example, hereâs an interactive timeline of my pieces over the years. I havenât uploaded everything Iâve ever made, so this is biased toward recent stuff.

(To be very technically correct, this timeline component doesnât read the json directly. Its bars are drawn on the server, and it gets a per-month list derived from the metadata to handle clicking and paging.).

Hereâs what the page for a piece looks like. The metadata json has the information to figure out what pieces were done nearby and around the same time, so I show all that. This is an embedded iframe so you can scroll and click:.

In a recent development, this is where Pragmatic Wolf won. Hereâs the possible optimization: whenever I make an edit, we should invalidate only those pages that are potentially affected by that edit. A good build system certainly works this way: when you change one file, it recompiles only those artifacts that (transitively) depend on it.

Sources indicate that in my case, however, dependencies arenât explicitly written down anywhere. The code to generate a page just runs, and potentially any change in the metadata json could cause its output to be different. I could try to encode the dependencies for each page and component, but itâs so easy to get this wrong and introduce bugs in the future. The result is a half-updated website, i.e., a correctness bug.

In a recent development, so while itâs true that adding a latest piece only changes the #evening page if the new piece actually has that tag, I considered it too tricky to get this cache invalidation right, and decided to just invalidate everything. If I were using a normal static site generator then the CDN could potentially do this optimization by noticing that the hash of an artifact hasnât changed, so it doesnât need to be updated on every edge machine.

Anyway here is a waterfall in Washington, the one in Twin Peaks apparently:.

And hereâs the view from right outside my house in Brooklyn:.

According to recent reports, by the way, the specific javascript framework I ended up using is called Astro. Cloudflare bought them so theyâre pretty nicely integrated. But you donât really need it for this, you could write your own code to run in the Worker to generate the page. The whole trick is in some careful management of cache.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its fresh app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its fresh app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.

In a recent development, in practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. People can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that indicates where apps are sending data and lets people block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the firm says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”.

Recent findings suggest that unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users rapidly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”.

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:.

It has been revealed that “When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”.

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:.

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It has been revealed that it's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

Industry observers note that this big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and firm also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

According to recent reports, horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

In a recent development, I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

According to recent reports, alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

According to recent reports, I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

In a recent development, there's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

Industry observers note that I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

According to recent reports, I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

In a recent development, the current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.
