Inkling 2 Mini

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thinkingmachines

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.
  • Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token.
  • According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

SWE-bench Pro v2 Hard (51 tasks).

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

According to recent reports, most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

Industry observers note that while looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model, we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and WorldVQA.

In a recent development, inkling 2 Mini overcomes the knowledge gap by efficiently using search and tools. It leads open-weights models of similar size on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, and MCP Atlas. It is also strong on knowledge work benchmarks that incorporate search and tool use.

Researchers at Stanford measure intelligence per joule: how much energy an LLM needs per query to reach a given level of performance.Researchers at Stanford’s Hazy Research Lab and Scaling Intelligence Lab got early testing access to Inkling 2 Mini. Inkling 2 Mini scored 0.703 running on NVIDIA DGX Spark, significantly higher than other models: 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 0.159 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B and 0.036 for Qwen3.5-27B.Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI, Saad-Falcon and Narayan et al., 2025Inkling 2 Mini ran on NVIDIA DGX Spark (128GB) at MXFP8 precision with low reasoning effort in this experiment. The other models ran at NVFP4 (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) and INT4 (Qwen3.5-27B).

Efficiency combined with performance makes Inkling 2 Mini a strong choice for running multiple persistent agents on local hardware. All 20 residents of the energy-conscious village of Thinkyville are managed by Inkling 2 Mini running on a single offline MacBook.

Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or for instructions with many constraints: it scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both. It also trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini is a 24-layer model derived from our mainline predictive scaling ladder. The main changes from the mainline recipe were pruning two-thirds of the experts to reduce the model’s size and the introduction of looping to improve reasoning. The rest of training, including quantization and the data mix, followed our mainline recipe.

Inkling 2 Mini has 24 layers, divided into four blocks of six layers each. The two middle blocks run three times, while the first and last blocks each run once. This design builds on prior work on looped transformers and is motivated by the intuition that the middle layers of the model carry more abstract reasoning, while the first and last few layers devote more space to translating between embeddings and internal representations.Universal Transformers, Dehghani et al., 2018 In our experiments, looping the middle 12 layers resulted in larger gains in accuracy than looping the last 12 on 27 out of 28 different evaluations.

Compute-equivalent gain by loop position.

Industry observers note that our model uses attention residuals.Attention Residuals, Kimi Team: Guangyu Chen et al., 2026 Instead of adding every layer’s output into one running sum, each layer reads the outputs of the earlier blocks and learns its own mix of them. This allows richer information to pass between loops. Every pass starts with the output of the prelude (the first block). The second and third passes through the middle blocks also read the middle blocks’ outputs from the previous pass, which we call the message.

The previous loop’s message is merged with the prelude’s output via a gate that scales these along with the output of the previous layers in the block. This gate is learned during training: it initially blocks the entire message—which makes each loop start the same as in a non-looping model—and increases the gain on the message over time. This allows us to introduce looping during training in a stable manner.

It has been revealed that to evaluate the impact of looping, we compared an unpruned looping version to the unpruned non-looping model on our scaling ladder. The non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train, but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini was trained with 4-bit precision, which we describe in a recent article on Connectionism. We use 4-bit NVFP4 precision in the expert layers on all forward passes from pretraining through RL, bolstered by a dedicated kernel and hardware-accelerated on NVIDIA’s GB300 platform. The final 4 layers’ forward passes ran in 8-bit (MXFP8).

Inkling 2 Mini’s weights are deployed in the same numeric precision they were trained on—20 layers in NVFP4 and 4 in MXFP8—so there is no conversion loss from quantization.

Inkling 2 Mini started training with a sparsity of 48, with 8 experts being chosen out of 384. At a single point during midtraining, we pruned two-thirds of the experts, leaving the 128 experts that were most used in each layer. This was done to cut the total parameter count of the model, allowing it to run faster and on local hardware.

Recent findings suggest that after pruning, the model trained on 1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model. This step recovered the performance the model had before pruning by training the remaining experts to take over the work of the ones that were deleted.

In a recent development, following pruning and healing, Inkling 2 Mini underwent SFT with a similar data mix to Inkling 2 Small. This was followed by an RL that totaled 2.2T tokens over 2,000 steps. The post-training phase included on-policy distillation for training alignment, same as Inkling 2 Small.

A key tool for understanding and overseeing an AI system is monitoring its chain of thought (CoT), the reasoning a model writes out as it works through a problem. The usefulness of CoT monitoring stems in part from the standard non-looped transformer architecture, in which each token passes through a fixed stack of layers once. This limits the number of sequential steps of computation the model can perform before it must output a token, so reasoning that needs more steps has to be carried out in generated text, where it can be read.

Looping a transformer’s layers raises this limit. By running the same layers multiple times, looped models increase their serial depth without adding more parameters, meaning that they do more computation per token internally before verbalizing their thought processes via CoT. Reasoning that never appears in the CoT can’t be caught by a CoT monitor, which has led to concerns that looped transformers could be harder to oversee.

One reason we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini is to enable the community to conduct research on looped transformers. We are particularly excited for researchers to investigate questions of monitorability, and to develop interpretability techniques for understanding the computation within loops.

To explore how different amounts of looping affect model properties like monitorability, we also trained a variable-looped model, TML-d24-varloop-research, because Inkling 2 Mini only supports a fixed number of looping passes. To enable variable looping, TML-d24-varloop-research was trained with between one and five looping passes.TML-d24-varloop-research was primarily trained for 3 passes of looping, with lower exposure to 1, 2, 4, and 5 passes. Performance at these latter pass counts may understate what training specifically for them could achieve. See the model card for details. We have also made this model publicly available on Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that below we describe our preliminary analysis of how looping affects monitorability. Overall, we find that looping increases what these models can do without a verbalized chain of thought, but at this scale we do not see a meaningful reduction in the monitorability of their reasoning.

According to recent reports, as a first step, we measured how much additional reasoning looping enables by comparing looped and non-looped models of the same size on tasks answered with no CoT at all. We used Think Fast, a benchmark that estimates a model’s no-CoT time horizon: the length of task, measured in human completion time, that a model can complete at 50% reliability without using CoT.These models were not trained to answer questions without a CoT. To elicit no-CoT answers, we prefilled the start of the response so that the model must answer directly, skipping reasoning. Other elicitation techniques, such as fine-tuning, might yield higher no-CoT performance and are worth exploring.

As expected, looping increases no-CoT capability, though these gains eventually level off. The no-CoT time horizon of TML-d24-varloop-research rises from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three. Some of this is presumably due to the additional serial computation that looping provides. Beyond three passes, the time horizon is roughly flat. Interestingly, the model was never trained with more than five passes, and yet running it with ten does not significantly degrade its performance.

No-CoT 50% time horizon (human seconds).

As the number of looped passes increases past three, the gains are smaller, and on most tasks we observe similar performance. One exception is the N-Hop Lookup task, which cleanly evaluates serial reasoning: the model is given several lookup tables with fictional entries, and must follow a chain of lookups without writing anything down. We find that the model follows longer chains with more passes, improving out to ten loops.

In standard evaluations with CoT, we observe that more loop passes primarily benefit multi-hop reasoning rather than recall. Gains are largest on long-context retrieval (MRCR), followed by math and science reasoning (HMMT, GPQA Diamond, HLE) and long-horizon agentic tasks (SWE-bench Pro, BrowseComp). Closed-book factual QA is nearly invariant to loop passes (SimpleQA Verified, WorldVQA). See model card for full evaluations.

In a recent development, we next measured whether a model’s CoT reveals less about its reasoning as looping increases via two evaluations. First, we assessed how looping impacts the compression and legibility of a model’s CoT. Second, we measured how controllable a model’s CoT is, i.e., whether it can deliberately reshape its CoT to satisfy constraints. For each, we run TML-d24-varloop-research with one to five looped passes to study the effect of looping.

According to recent reports, note that TML-d24-varloop-research was only trained on variable pass counts from 1 to 5 during midtraining, and its RL was done with 3 passes. These experiments therefore do not tell us what a model trained with RL at a higher pass count would learn, and such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively. A cleaner comparison would include every pass count in RL, which we leave to future work.

In a recent development, compression and legibility. Since looping allows a model to spend more compute per token, we expect that it should need fewer CoT tokens to reach the same performance. We ran the variable-looped model at 1 to 5 passes, and found that as looping increases, the model generally achieves higher accuracy at each reasoning token budget, with diminishing returns after 3 passes. Notably, token efficiency on GPQA Diamond improves slightly from 3 to 5 passes, even though the model was trained with RL only at 3 passes, suggesting that some compression comes from additional computation itself, without RL at that depth.

Accuracy versus reasoning tokens.

DeepSWE v1.1 Accuracy (% of tasks resolved).

The observed CoT compression raises a question for monitorability: is shorter reasoning still readable, or does it omit key details about the model’s thinking? We compared traces from the variable-looped model on the GPQA Diamond questions that it answered correctly at all five pass counts. Reasoning at 5 passes was less than half as long as at 1 pass (1,661 vs. 3,703 tokens on average), but no less legible: sentence length and the fraction of words in an English dictionary were unchanged. On initial analysis, the difference is that the model is more direct and backtracks less on the way to the answer. The example below illustrates this difference on a simple question.

March 1 falls on a Tuesday in a year that is not a leap year. What day of the week is May 20 of the same year? Give the final answer on its own last line as ANSWER: .

Controllability. One way that a model could evade monitoring is by steering its CoT away from anything a monitor would flag. The CoT-Control-QA evaluationReasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought, Yueh-Han et al., 2026 measures this capability by asking questions from GPQA, HLE and MMLU-Pro paired with an instruction about the CoT itself, such as avoiding a keyword from the question. Longer CoTs are generally harder to control, so we pool responses from five reasoning efforts (0.1, 0.2, 0.7, 0.9 and 0.99) and show controllability at matched CoT length.

Both Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research have poor control over their CoT. Among CoTs of 750–1,250 tokens, Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research (at 3 passes) follow the instruction at most 0.1% of the time, compared with 0.3% for Inkling 2 Small, 0.4% for Inkling-Small, and 1.3% for Qwen3.8-27B. Because the controllability rate is so low, this evaluation is unable to distinguish controllability between different amounts of looping.

Chain-of-thought controllability.

CoT controllability (log scale).

To measure monitorability in agentic settings, we used LinuxArena, a control evaluation that measures whether an attacker model can perform malicious side tasks without detection when asked to perform a realistic software engineering task. We evaluated a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini, since the released model refuses many of the side tasks. In absolute terms, both this model and TML-d24-varloop-research can be easily monitored by models like Qwen3.8-27B, which detected almost all side task attempts in our evaluation. To obtain relative rankings in monitorability, we tested a weaker model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, as the monitor.

With the monitor able to access only tool calls and outputs, it misses a significant number of the attacks. However, we see no clear trend with the number of looped passes.

Agentic monitorability will be key to track in larger-scale models, especially with architectures that allow for greater unverbalized thinking, and we encourage continued study of the impact of looping in this setting.

The goal of monitorability is to understand what a model is doing, and our main approach is to read its verbalized reasoning. Studying its internal computation directly, the aim of mechanistic interpretability, is another. Because looped transformers do more of their computation internally, we think they are a particularly interesting and vital setting for interpretability research, and we hope our looped models will be useful artifacts for the community.

In a recent development, we are working with the National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF) to make these models more easily accessible to interpretability researchers. We also provided Goodfire, an interpretability research lab, early access to our looped models. They are working toward a mechanistic understanding of looped models, and have written up their early findings here.

Efficient intelligence makes Inkling 2 Mini a great choice for inference where speed is paramount, or for running on local hardware. At launch we support Inkling 2 Mini running on any Mac system (MacBook, Mac Mini) with at least 32GB RAM via Ollama. With native NVFP4 training and inference precision, Inkling 2 Mini runs efficiently on NVIDIA’s DGX Spark desktop AI computer. Quantized GGUF versions are available via Unsloth and llama.cpp for local inference.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is available for inference and fine-tuning on Tinker, and for chat on the Tinker Playground. Open source inference is available on SGLang, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, NVIDIA Dynamo, TokenSpeed, and Llama App, with RL fine-tuning support on SkyRL, Miles, and NVIDIA AutoModel. The full weights of Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-looped variant are available on Hugging Face.

Recent findings suggest that we work to empower people with strong models, tools to make them your own, and research that advances public understanding of AI. Inkling 2 Mini lets researchers study looped transformers, and it lets anyone run a capable model on their own laptop at the precision in which it was trained.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

In a recent development, VWFNDR + MBL launched on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

Recent findings suggest that on Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Recent findings suggest that colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Revealed at alpo.ge/remark.pdf on 20 November 2026.
  • Andrew Sutherland (MIT), checks run with Claude Code.
  • Industry observers note that the published Lean source compiles without errors, the five headline theorems depend only on the three standard axioms, every module has been replayed through the Lean kernel, two independently written kernels, nanoda and con-leche, accept the full exported proof, and lean4lean accepts every compiled module.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revealed at alpo.ge/remark.pdf on 20 November 2026.

Andrew Sutherland (MIT), checks run with Claude Code. Page last updated 2026-11-21 12:55 UTC. Results below are as of that time and this page will be updated as the remaining checks finish.

Industry observers note that the published Lean source compiles without errors, the five headline theorems depend only on the three standard axioms, every module has been replayed through the Lean kernel, two independently written kernels, nanoda and con-leche, accept the full exported proof, and lean4lean accepts every compiled module. con-leche's --compare mode, an independent implementation of Comparator's statement matching, confirms all five theorems against the challenge. The lake comparator run and the Lean-kernel replay of the export are still in progress.

According to recent reports, five theorems, proved in the submission's Main.lean. Their statements are below exactly as they appear in the challenge file, which imports only Mathlib. All the mathematical notions in them (riemannZeta, DirichletCharacter, DirichletCharacter.LFunction, IsPrimitive) are Mathlib's.

1. The Riemann Hypothesis, using Mathlib's own definition (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean): every zero of ζ other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … has real part 1/2. The condition s ≠ 1 is there because Mathlib assigns ζ a conventional value at its pole.

2. The same statement written out in the submission's own words. Lean accepts the two as equal by definition.

In a recent development, 3. No zeros to the right of the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function. For every modulus N ≥ 1 and every Dirichlet character χ modulo N, primitive or not, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 whenever Re s > 1/2. The one excluded case is the trivial character at s = 1, where the L-function has its pole.

In a recent development, 4. Zeros in the critical strip lie on the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.

5. The same for primitive characters, the form in which the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions is usually stated.

Recent findings suggest that scope. "GRH" here means Dirichlet L-functions: all moduli and all characters. Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions and automorphic L-functions in general are not among the statements that were checked.

Sources indicate that as a check that does not depend on Mathlib's definition of the zeta function, the proof was combined with kimihiro64/Robin1984 (commit acab1a3), an independent formalization of Robin's and Lagarias's criteria on the same Lean and Mathlib versions. Importing both gives two theorems about the divisor sum, with no hypotheses and no mention of zeta (ArithSolution.lean; statements alone in ArithChallenge.lean, which imports only Mathlib):.

According to recent reports, the combined export is 61,752,134,938 bytes, sha256 44651dcc482a6e06e8d626994221aff638e422fded189bf856e0c31176926f0d; its challenge export has sha256 088a57c9e7454fa5279a86a825e551828ac8431694855aadd1f6e6a6eb37bb1d. These statements still rely on Mathlib's definitions of the divisor sum, Euler's constant, harmonic numbers, exp and log, and on the Robin1984 proof, which is why that proof was put through the same checks.

The exported proof: output of lean4export on module Main. Unpacks to 61,570,595,788 bytes.

The exported challenge: the five statements with sorry proofs, importing only Mathlib. Unpacks to 350,862,970 bytes.

With Lean v4.36.0 installed, nothing needs to be built. You need roughly 100 GB of RAM and 70 GB of disk.

According to recent reports, nanoda alone took about 28 minutes on 80 threads. The Lean kernels are single-threaded and take much longer.

The fastest independent check is con-leche built from source (Lean v4.36.0, about two minutes to build). It needs about 50 GB of RAM and took under four minutes on 64 threads:.

Exponential Behavior in Magic: The Gathering

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Levineuwirth

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In perhaps the first instance where Magic: The Gathering caused a legitimate supercomputer to time out, exponential behavior strikes again as the bane of every computer scientistâs existence, prompting reflection: What is it about Magic: The Gathering that is so unique?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In perhaps the first instance where Magic: The Gathering caused a legitimate supercomputer to time out, exponential behavior strikes again as the bane of every computer scientistâs existence, prompting reflection: What is it about Magic: The Gathering that is so unique? Why has it been so hard to achieve a true software implementation of the game?

Industry observers note that I have been fascinated with Magic: The Gathering for years, not only as a remarkably fun and strategically deep game, but also as a mathematical and computational space. The game is remarkably complex, even Turing complete, with intricate keywords and a daunting amount of mechanicsa, presenting an immense computational challenge for making the game run on a computer, let alone machine-playable. There are multiple existing software implementations of Magic; Arena is the most prevalent, developed by Wizards themselves, but there are numerous challenges: the card catalog is notoriously incomplete, missing cards from the majority of the gameâs history; the matchmaking methodology, particularly for ranked play, is absolutely horrificb, and the performance of the game is quite poor, particularly when there is a lot on the stack. MTGO resolves the card catalog issue, but introduces issues of its own, including lack of adoption, a rather outdated and difficult to use interface, and so on. Meanwhile, Forge, an independent implementation, is promising at first glance â but the AI play is quite poorc, multiplayer is quite buggy and not truly supported, the interface is unintuitive, and the performance is still not ideal, even if improved over Arena.

In a recent development, I began theorizing methods to improve AI play of Magic as early as 2024 but did not begin any implementation work on this until mid 2026; I first evaluated Forge and then decided that it was not feasible to get Forge up to a level of performance such that it could serve as an experimentation environment for RL on Magic itself, and thus decided to implement my own rules engine, Arcana. I figured that I could also design with multiplayer in mind from day one as a nice bonus and motivator.

One of the sources of my fascination with Magic, and, indeed, one of the reasons that a truly performant and complete software implementation of the game has yet to be achieved, is the nature of abilities in the game. Abilities in Magic can compound exponentially, and the amount of different possible interactions that can occur when any ability is triggered leads to a situation where although there may not be an unfeasible amount of state in principle, the amount of checks that are required to ensure that no further side effects must be put on the stack also grows exponentially, and as we all know, exponential behavior is an enemy of us mere mortal computer scientists. My fascination with the exponential behavior of Magic came back to bite me in an unexpected way.

One of my favorite decks I ever devised was very simple in mechanicism and brutal in computational complexity. It revolves around a notorious card: Scute Swarm. To explain how this deck worked, we need a bit of background on the internals of Magic.

The core quantity of Magic: The Gathering is life; it can be thought of as the playerâs score, or an encapsulation of how well the player is doing. Each player begins with 20 life, and the primary way to win the game is to reduce the opponentâs life score to 0 (or below) before your own life score is reduced as such. There are different types of cards that can be used, and on any given turn, a player may use the resources granted to them by lands, the type of card that forms a basic currency in the game, to deploy whatever they wish within the gameâs limitations and rules.

Sources indicate that perhaps the most important type of card is a creature. These are equivalent to the prototypical card in most trading card games, like Pokemon; they can attack the opponent and defend from the opponentâs attacks. Scute Swarm is one example of a creature.

There are also tokens, which are special cards that are the result of an ability of a different card rather than a card that you play. One might use a card to earn a token, but one would not have a token in the deck that they build, and they would not ever have a token in their hand so to speak. The actual mechanics here are a bit complicated, but the big picture is that tokens come into existence as a result of some ability and not from being in the playerâs hand or deck outright.

It has been revealed that scute Swarm is perhaps the most notorious example of a Magic card that exhibits exponential behavior. It has the ability, when a upcoming land is deployed, to double the amount of copies of itself that exist. In practice, this is usually countered early, as Magic allows for many different waysd to avoid the exponential being realized (which, if substantially realized, will lead to victory for the person who played Scute Swarm practically invariably). If you combined this, I realized, with cards that produce life-gain whenever a new creature enters the battlefield, then one would have exponentially growing life. To make this even worse, one could play an artifact that doubles the amount of tokens that are created whenever any token is created, and throw in something to persistently double the amount of life gained. Seems like quite the loophole, eh?

In a recent development, for the arithmetic, the sixth land matters. Below six lands a Scute makes an ordinary 1/1 Insect. With six or more when the ability resolves, it makes a copy with the same landfall ability. Give each landâs triggers time to resolve before the next land comes down and every newly introduced copy gets to help with the next batch.e.

Suppose Soul Warden and Essence Warden are both in play. Each gives you one life for each newly introduced Scute. With a life-gain doubler thatâs four life per arrival, and with a token doubler each existing Scute makes two new ones. Hereâs what eight land drops would buy you under those assumptions.

This is totally egregious! Considering that a player begins with 20 life in Magic, and life gains are usually modest if present at all, a change of 3 orders of magnitude warrants that notoriety that Scute Swarm has. For comparison, I think (playing decks outside of this one) that, on paper cards, the highest life total I have achieved in a game is around 150.

The Scute curve is something we can work out on paper, but Arcana doesnât yet support scute swarm (deliberately, I might add). It was the purple curve that got me into trouble.

Now, who is this Liliana in the above plot?

Planeswalkers are, in a way, the heroes of Magic. They usually have multiple abilities, the most expensive of which (usually positioned at the bottom as the last one) we tend to call the âultimateâ â simply put, if you are playing against an opponent with a Planeswalker, youâd best ensure they donât trigger that ability. In some cases, the ultimate can create a special type of cardf called an emblem. Emblems are particularly concerning for you if your opponent has the opportunity to procure one, and particularly advantageous if you have the ability to use one, chiefly because they persist even if the Planeswalker is removed from play. An ability that an emblem provides will be in effect for the remainder of the game, typically leading to devastating and, importantly, compounding consequences for the opponent.

It has been revealed that liliana, the Last Hope is one such planeswalker. Her ultimate happens to create quite the dire situation not only for the opponent, but also for those who are interested in implementing Magic in software. When her ultimate ability resolves, the resulting emblem ensures that more and more zombie tokens are deployed onto the battlefield in a matter not too unlike that of Scute Swarm. Unfortunately for us as implementers, and for those who play against Liliana as losers, the amount of zombies that are deployed grows exponentially. What is unlike Scute Swarm is that clearing away the Zombies leaves the emblem intact and able to rebuild the army, whereas removing every Scute Swarm removes the source of its growth.

Industry observers note that letâs formalize what happens. At the beginning of each of your end steps (the last part of a playerâs turn), the emblem triggers. When that ability resolves, it counts the Zombies you control and creates that many more, plus two. With six Zombies already on the battlefield, you get eight newly introduced ones, leaving fourteen.

Industry observers note that let ZnZ_n be the number of Zombies after nn resolutions of the emblemâs ability. Start with no Zombies (Z0=0Z_0=0) and one emblem, and suppose nothing else adds or removes Zombies or changes how many tokens are created. Each resolution then gives us:.

Recent findings suggest that zn+1=Znâalready there+(Zn+2)âfresh arrivals=2Zn+2. Z_{n+1} =\underbrace{Z_n}_{\text{already there}} +\underbrace{(Z_n+2)}_{\text{new arrivals}} =2Z_n+2.

In a recent development, the first few populations are 0,2,6,14,30,62,â¦0,2,6,14,30,62,\ldots. After nn resolutions, that gives Zn=2n+1â2Z_n=2^{n+1}-2. Crucially, the army will always restart: even if every Zombie is destroyedg, the next resolution produces two more.

Industry observers note that this forms Lilianaâs purple curve in the comparison above: 510 Zombies after eight resolutions. That plot counts growth events along the horizontal axis: one emblem resolution for Liliana, or one land entry for Scute Swarm.

Arcana implements that counting rule directly:.

Sources indicate that here, x counts the new arrivals, and the loop produces a separate CreateToken effect for every one of them. The engine then has to process all those arrivals, including the rules checks and any abilities they set off. As the army grows, so does the work required to resolve the emblemâs ability.

According to recent reports, letâs step back for a second. I was trying to decide which gaps in Arcanaâs rules to fix next. I had 64 Pioneer decksh and a list of 37 cards with known issues. There were 2,016 distinct pairs of decks. I played each pair twice, once with each deck going first, giving me 4,032 games in which to count how often those situations came up.

According to recent reports, in an effort somewhat analogous to fuzzing, I scheduled that entire 4,032-game lineup another 100 times. Each run used a different random seedi, and both players chose their actions at random. That meant 100Ã4,032=403,200100 \times 4{,}032 = 403{,}200 additional games to see whether I could trigger a panic, crash, or stall in the engine.

In a recent development, all ~400,000 games are independent, with no intertwined dependencies between them. Thus, the work parallelizes nicely to HPC, and I typically run these games on a cluster rather than my own hardware. (This is especially notable when I run larger trials and RL experiments using the engine, but still nice-to-have for purposes like this!) Unfortunately, when I did this on this occasion, nine jobs hit their two-hour limit. The random seed and the two decklists let me replay a single stalled game on my laptop and time its individual steps.

In that game, one player activated Lilianaâs ultimate on turn 34. Once the army had grown into the thousands, one resolution of the emblem took 35 seconds on my laptop. That was a single engine step. Both players had let the ability resolve. Before either could make another decision, Arcana had to put every new Zombie onto the battlefield and check what its arrival triggered.

Recent findings suggest that letâs take the first of those Zombies. A creature you control might have evolve, an ability that can give it a +1/+1 counter when a creature with greater power or greater toughness enters under your control. The engine has to find every creature that qualifies as followsj.

This code is a walk of the battlefield. For each other permanent you control when one of your Zombies enters, effective_keywords computes its current characteristics to find out whether it has evolve. In this game, nothing had evolve, so the list came back empty. Then the next Zombie entered, and, most lamentably, the engine asked the same question all over again. Double the army and about twice as many Zombies enter, each scanning about twice as many objects. You can see where this is going: about four times as many checks are required to produce the same empty list.

Sources indicate that on turns 52, 54, and 56, I counted the Zombies at the start of the turn and timed the emblem when it resolved at the end. In one laptop replay those steps took 1.72, 7.78, and 35.15 seconds.

By turn 58, the opponent was at 31 life, facing 7,256 Zombies. At two damage apiece, sixteen unblocked Zombies would have been enough. The largest attack Arcana offered that turn used one creature.

Recent findings suggest that hereâs the view from the replay visualizer of the defending seat, just before the other player chose attackers. Donât miss the little badge in the corner of each Zombie pile! (The visualizer groups creatures with the same name, tapped state, power, and toughness onto one tile.).

In a recent development, at a table, I can say âall the Zombies attack youâ and turn them sideways. In fact, with paper cards, thereâs essentially no chance that I, nor any reasonable human, own 7,000 printed copies of a 2/2 zombie token â so weâre probably using some other methodology, whether pencil and paper or an app on someoneâs phone that acts as a counter. In Arcana, unfortunately for us, we have to be quite precise about the state and transformations applied to it: the random player picks from a list, and each entry specifies the entire attack. On turn 44, each eligible Zombie could do nothing, could attack the player, or could attack one of the three opposing planeswalkers. Thus, we have a total of five choices per Zombie. Even with only five Zombies, there would be 55=3,1255^5 = 3{,}125 ways to declare attackers, and as you might guess, when there are thousands of zombiesâ¦ yeah, not good!

Sources indicate that arcana had a budget of 1,024 declarations. When the combinations exceeded that budget, the idea was to keep a few useful possibilities, encapsulating the decisions a reasonable player might make rather than providing all options. My justification for this was that if playing on paper, because as Iâve stated no one has 7,000 printed zombies, it would be incredibly pedantic to say â3,759 of my zombies are attacking you, and 3,497 are attacking planeswalker Xâ â no onekwould ever do this. Arcana reduces the options such that one could pass, send a single creature at any defender, or send everyone who could attack a particular defender at once. The pass was already in the list when this code ran. Look at the order of the two loops.

On turn 44, the arithmetic worked out pretty nicely. Of the 58 creatures on the board for the attacker, 56 could attack. Four defenders gave those creatures 56Ã4=22456 \times 4 = 224 ways to attack alone. Add the pass and the four ways to send every attacker at a singular target, and you get the 229 entries in the replay. Only one of those sent the whole army at the player, so odds are that the random player would miss it.

Now, give that first loop 256 eligible attackers and the same four defenders. The single-creature attacks alone would take 1,024 slots, and passing has already taken one. That little return out exits the function, so crucially, the second loop never gets a turn.

Sources indicate that by turn 50, even a perfect player choosing from this list could send at most one creature. And what did our player actually do on turn 58? It sent one 2/2 Zombie after Oko, Thief of Crowns. The defending player stayed at 31 life. Then came the end step, and Lilianaâs emblem triggered again.

In a recent development, arcana already knew how to call a draw when it saw the same settled position often enough; we had a system analogous to threefold repetition in chess, though ours was more for the convenience of the hardware Arcana runs on rather than any player computational or human. The random-play test itself also had a limit of 20,000 actions per game. Each time Lilianaâs army doubled, that check saw a position it had never previously seen. On turn 58 the replay got as far as action 2,325, passing priority to let the emblem resolve. Sixty seconds later, my poor laptop probe was still waiting for that one call to return, with plenty of actions left in the budget.

According to recent reports, recall that we had 64 decks; only four of them actually contained Liliana, the Last Hope. (Doesnât her name take a special irony at this point? I find it wonderful.) Indeed, as one might expect, all nine jobs that timed out had one of those four decks in the game they left unfinished. For the next run, then, I made the test harness count every permanent on both sides of the battlefield. With the limit set to 500, the check in the random-play test looks like the following.

It has been revealed that that explains the slightly odd-looking result from replaying another stalled game with the limit on. It stopped on turn 48 at 576 permanents, 0.16 seconds into the game! Why was this, you ask? An entire batch of tokens can arrive during one step. The harness sees the latest board as soon as that step finishes, records the turn and size under its own outcome, board_cap, and moves on to the next game. When I count wins, losses, and draws, I can still see exactly which games the experiment cut short.

Sources indicate that this got the experiment moving again, but there are two engine changes Iâd still like to measure on this replay. One is to work out which permanents have evolve once and reuse that answer for as long as the relevant characteristics stay the same. The other is to reserve room for the all-in attacks before filling the menu with singles. I think both are necessary potential directions; the first might buy Liliana a cheaper end step, while the second would give the attacking player a chance to end the game before she gets one.

In a way, this was inevitable, wasnât it? I had it coming. Saying I knew the trouble I was creating when I envisioned the Scute Swarm deck with its exponential synergies would be an understatement; in a way, I recall having this subtle feeling of foreboding when I had the idea and first put a concept together in Arena. I knew both in principle what would happen (âwhat number comes next in the sequence 2, 4, 8, __?â) and what I wanted to see happen in effect (âjust how much life can I gain?â). Years later, it seems the true meaning of this foreboding sensation has been revealed to me. Liliana has obliged me, at a somewhat greater expense.

According to recent reports, perhaps what I find most remarkable about Liliana, though, is how legible the instruction is on her emblem, regardless of where within that exponential growth you are. One of the chief criticisms of Magic as a game is that the instructions are often jargon heavy and difficult to interpret; indeed, one seldom sees a card (other than something like a basic land, of course) on Scryfall which hasnât accumulated multiple official rulings on interpretation over the years. Yet I think that with Liliana (who herself has accumulated such interpretations, indeed, so perhaps Iâm wrong) this is a nonissue. If you have 0 zombies you make 2, and if you have 7,256, you make 7,258 all the same. The amount of ink that the instructions need to describe the latter is exactly the same as how much describes the first, yet the latter can evidently be the cause of much more tumult. Thatâs some of the magic of Magic for me, in a way. I can hold a deck of 60 cards just like my Scute Swarm creation in my hand in an afternoon and years later, Iâm still discovering exactly what it is that Iâm holding.

These are split between âevergreens,â which are the ones more familiar players like myself will know, and the rest; Magic introduces at least one new keyword for every new set introduced, which can often be the source of great confusion. Luckily, the new ones are usually explained, and Scryfall is only a quick search away.â©ï¸.

It has never been proven (Arena is closed-source) but has been widely documented that, particularly at the highest levels of play, Arena almost uniformly ranks decks against other decks of similar archetypes. This infuriating situation defeats the variety in deckbuilding and strategization that makes the game fun. I quit playing Arena when I was ranked Mythic, and I lament the fact that I was not 18 yet and thus couldnât participate in the Pro Tour qualifier that I wouldâve otherwise been eligible for, as for this reason, I will never return to serious Arena play.â©ï¸.

Even worse, in fact, than that of Arena, which seems to be deterministically coded based on a few âstarter decksâ that do not rotate; at least Forgeâs can be played with any arbitrary deck!â©ï¸.

Instant removal is the obvious one, but if such is not available, countering the spell while it is on the stack is another option, as is exiling the card before the sixth land comes down.â©ï¸.

See the Scute Swarm entry in the Zendikar Rising release notes.â©ï¸.

Itâs actually a marker, not a card, but for our conversational purposes, itâs effectively a âcardâ as we would define it in colloquial English speech. Sorry, not sorry.â©ï¸.

So, no, sorry, as much as I admire it as a card, Extinction will not save you. Exponentials always win.â©ï¸.

#74216. Industry News: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

Industry News: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that you know “the look” by now.
  • According to recent reports, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • Sources indicate that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

According to recent reports, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

Sources indicate that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

According to recent reports, the problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT highlighted me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

In a recent development, while most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

According to recent reports, the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

In a recent development, this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

Sources indicate that if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

Sources indicate that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

Sources indicate that I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

It has been revealed that to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

Sources indicate that that means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple only rolled out high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a newly introduced report offers an revision on release timing.

A latest report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh patch on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the fresh models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production aims signal a March release for the products.

Kim Yeong-ho, writing at ETNews:.

Samsung Display plans to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside fresh Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

In a recent development, with Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the newly introduced models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

Sources indicate that are you holding out for an iPhone 18 or iPhone Air 2? Let us know in the comments.

The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this week's column is bleak.
  • Sources indicate that you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers.
  • Industry observers note that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

Sources indicate that you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Industry observers note that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

In a recent development, here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart swiftly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

According to recent reports, as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber demonstrates up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

According to recent reports, nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#74212. Tech Report: 10 Artists Who Should Perform The Next James Bond

Tech Report: 10 Artists Who Should Perform The Next James Bond

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Robert Pattinson set to play James Bond, the next big question, outside who will play the female lead, is what artist will sing the theme for his 007 debut.
  • It has been revealed that three 007 debuts came with a jolt of rock energy; Roger Moore's made his entrance to Paul McCartney & Wings' explosive "Live and Let Die," Timothy Dalton arrived to Aha's synth-driven "The Living Daylights," and Daniel Craig's Casino Royale opened with Chris Cornell's hard-rocker "You Know My Name." The history give producers plenty of reason to consider another rock theme for Pattinson's debut.
  • Oasis returned with authority in 2025 with a sold-out stadium tour that drew crowds of beer-drinking, Adidas-clad fans around the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Robert Pattinson set to play James Bond, the next big question, outside who will play the female lead, is what artist will sing the theme for his 007 debut. The franchise has drawn some of music's biggest names, from Shirley Bassey and Tom Jones to Madonna, Adele, Sam Smith, and Billie Eilish. The theme songs range from brassy orchestral showpieces and jazz-inflected sweeping pop ballads and full-throttle rock anthems, leaving plenty of room for the next artist to put their stamp on a Bond theme.

It has been revealed that three 007 debuts came with a jolt of rock energy; Roger Moore's made his entrance to Paul McCartney & Wings' explosive "Live and Let Die," Timothy Dalton arrived to Aha's synth-driven "The Living Daylights," and Daniel Craig's Casino Royale opened with Chris Cornell's hard-rocker "You Know My Name." The history give producers plenty of reason to consider another rock theme for Pattinson's debut. Here are 10 artists who should record the next Bond theme, ranked from the least obvious to the strongest fit.

Oasis returned with authority in 2025 with a sold-out stadium tour that drew crowds of beer-drinking, Adidas-clad fans around the world. The Manchester band's loud guitars and defiant attitude are made for stadium sing-a-longs, from "Champagne Supernova," and "Don't Look Back in Anger," to "Wonderwall." Two deeper cuts make a strong case for Bond. "Let's All Make Believe" and "Falling Down" are two cinematic songs that show how Oasis could bring both muscle and menace to a rock-driven theme.

Sources indicate that the group sounds like a great fit on paper, but persuading the Gallagher brothers to write and record an original theme may be a tough sell. The success of their reunion indicated the world still has an appetite for Oasis, whose last studio album, Dig Out Your Soul, came out in 2008. Asking the famously cantankerous brother to make their studio comeback on the movie's production schedule would be a huge gamble for Amazon MGM, who seem to be playing it safe. That makes Oasis one of the least likely entries on this list.

Industry observers note that fred Again.., born Frederick John Phillip Gibson, is one of electronic dance music's most unique producers. The English DJ and producer started out playing classical piano and percussion, and his connection to Bond goes back to the very first 007 novel. His great-grandmother, Ann Charteris, married Bond creator Ian Fleming in March 1952, a year before Casino Royale introduced James Bond to readers. That makes Fleming Gibson's step-great-grandfather.

Gibson broke through during the COVID-19 pandemic, turning voice notes, phone videos and social media clips into the emotional center of his tracks. On his 2021 hit "Marea (we've lost dancing)," he set a lockdown conversation with Marea Stamper, better known as The Blessed Madonna, to a dance beat. The track captured how much people missed the simple act of congregating together on dance floors, while giving them something to groove to in the meantime. He indicated his harder edge on "Rumble," a grimy dubstep collaboration with Skrillex and UK rapper Flowdan that won the Grammy for Best Dance/Electronic Recording. "Jungle" is another banger loaded with menacing sounds like a Tiger growl and the metallic click of a gun being cocked cutting through the pulsating bass. "Enough," from his 2023 collaboration with Brian Eno, reveals how much tension Gibson can create with little more than a voice and hazy ambient sounds. Fred Again.. would also be a natural choice to give an electronic twist to the original "James Bond Theme," composed by Monty Norman and arranged by John Barry.

According to recent reports, dua Lipa has a string of dance-pop radio hits, including "Training Season," "Latest Rules," "One Kiss," "Levitating," and "Dance the Night." The London-born singer scored two chart-topping albums in the UK with 2020's Future Nostalgia and 2024's Radical Optimism, and her three Grammy wins include Best New Artist and Best Pop Vocal Album for Future Nostalgia. The string sample on "Love Again" gives its disco groove a touch of old-school glamour, while the pulsating synths on "Houdini," co-written and co-produced by Tame Impala's Kevin Parker, suggest a more urgent, dance-driven Bond theme. "Homesick," the piano ballad she co-wrote with Coldplay's Chris Martin, makes the case for a slower approach that will allow her understated delivery to give the song the emotional weight to carry a sweeping 007 ballad.

Dua Lipa already has a close connection to the Bond casting race. Her husband, Callum Turner, was in the running to play Bond before Robert Pattinson landed the role. It's fun to imagine Turner making his Bond debut with Lipa singing over the opening credits. She'd be a strong choice for Pattinson's debut, too. With her grand pop hooks, dance grooves and enormous confidence, Dua Lipa would give the newly introduced Bond an electrifying opening theme.

Sources indicate that arctic Monkeys formed in Sheffield, England in 2002 and made their name with quirky guitar riffs, a powerful rhythm section with frontman Alex Turner's sharp observations and quick, conversational vocal delivery. Their 2006 debut, Whatever You Say I Am, That's What I'm Not, became the fastest-selling debut album in UK chart history at the time, and began a run of six straight UK number one studio LPs. The quartet's sound evolved from the frantic indie rock of "I Bet You Look Good on the Dancefloor," to the slinky, blues-driven riffs of "Do I Wanna Know?" and "R U Mine?," and the late-night ballad "No. 1 Party Anthem.".

Recent findings suggest that alex Turner's deep, soulful croon, drenched in his Sheffield accent, has a warmth and quiet confidence suited to a throwback Bond theme. The soaring strings of "There'd Better Be a Mirrorball" and the slow build of "Body Paint" show how naturally Arctic Monkeys could handle an orchestral ballad, while the ominous synth beneath "Sculptures of Anything Goes" gives shades of a dark underbelly that is equally intriguing. The band famously covered Shirley Bassey's "Diamonds are Forever" during their 2007 Glastonbury headlining set, and Turner told NME in 2011 that he would "love to do a tune for Bond." An Arctic Monkey theme would give Pattinson's 007 an opening with elegance, mystery and just the right amount swagger.

According to recent reports, muse formed in Devon, England, in 1994 and built their sound around distorted bass, heavy guitar riffs, classical piano and Matt Bellamy's soaring vocals. The trio's flair for drama runs through songs like "Uprising," "Resistance," "Madness, "Dead Inside," and "Thought Contagion." Muse have scored eight consecutive UK number one studio albums, from 2003's Absolution to 2026's The Wow! Signal. They won the Grammy for Best Rock Album in 2011 for The Resistance and again in 2016 for Drones.

It has been revealed that the group's 2012 track "Supremacy" is a cinematic song that pairs a heavy guitar riff with Matt Bellamy's hushed verses and dramatic orchestration that eerily resembles a Bond theme, complete with an arpeggiated guitar chord at the end. Muse already has a connection with Robert Pattinson through the first three Twilight films, from "Supermassive Black Hole" in the original soundtrack and "Neutron Star Collision (Love Is Forever)" for Eclipse. Bellamy also co-wrote the end-title music for the 2009 thriller The International. The band's theatrical, arena rock sound and classical influences would bring a bombastic energy to the Bond theme.

Sources indicate that lana Del Rey already has a lot of history with 007. She wrote "24" for Spectre, but producers chose Sam Smith's sweeping ballad "Writings on the Wall" for the 2015 film. She included the track featuring her soft and smoky vocals on her 2015 album Honeymoon. The vocalist also co-wrote and recorded "First Light" with longtime Bond composer David Arnold for the 2026 video game 007 First Light. She's already written two songs for Bond. The next step would be finally hearing one over the opening credits.

It has been revealed that del Rey's catalog makes a strong case for a Bond title sequence. "Shades of Cool," and "Honeymoon" have the slow-burning tension of classic 007 themes, while "Young and Beautiful" and "Born to Die" show how naturally her intimate voice carries over an orchestra. Her ability to blend romance and danger makes her a great fit for a Bond theme.

According to recent reports, radiohead have their own lengthy history with 007. Like Lana Del Rey, the British rockers recorded a song for Spectre, but producers went with Sam Smith's "Writings on the Wall." Radiohead released their rejected theme, "Spectre," on Christmas Day 2015. The brooding ballad opens with a sparse piano and Thom Yorke's fragile vocals before rising strings and the band joins in to bring the song to an orchestral climax.

It has been revealed that long before "Spectre," Radiohead covered Carly Simon's "Nobody Does It Better" the theme from 1977's The Spy Who Loved Me. Around the same time, they also wrote and recorded "Man of War" as a nod to Bond music. The band submitted it for Spectre, but producers passed again, and the band finally released it on OKNOTOK, the 20th anniversary edition of OK Computer. Both "Spectre" and "Man of War" are clear examples of how Radiohead could take a Bond title sequence in different directions.

Industry observers note that olivia Dean was born in North London and honed her craft at the Brit School. The singer-songwriter plays piano and guitar, paring R&B grooves with her warm and sultry voice. She scored two UK number one singles, "Rein Me In," her duet with Sam Fender, and "Man I Need," which reached number two in the US, spending 57 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100 chart.

Dean won the 2026 Grammy for Best New Artist and is up for six awards at the 2027 ceremony, including Record, Song and Album of the Year. "Loud" has the hallmarks of a classic Bond ballad, while "Danger" has a reggae lift with a modern sound. She recorded "It Isn't Perfect But It Might Be" for 2025's Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy, showing how comfortably she can carry a film ballad. Dean's jazz-influenced phrasing and ear for a pop hook would give 007 a theme with the warmth of classic soul.

Harry Styles is a strong candidate to sing the next James Bond theme. His 2017 debut solo single "Sign of the Times" builds from a spare piano to a soaring rock climax, proving he can deliver a Bond-worthy theme. Style's 2026 epic "Coming Up Roses" features a 39-piece orchestra that heightens the tension around his intimate vocals. The combination of his unpredictability, vulnerability and the grandeur of his music would be a fitting cinematic theme for Robert Pattinson's 007.

It has been revealed that styles, who made his acting debut in Christopher Nolan's 2017 movie Dunkirk, was once rumored to be in the running to play James Bond. His representative dismissed reports in 2020 that he was in line to succeed Daniel Craig. As a singer, Styles would be a natural fit for a slow-burning theme in the vein of Adele's "Skyfall," with an arrangement that draws on the orchestral legacy of Shirley Bassey's trio of "Diamonds are Forever," "Moonraker," and "Goldfinger.".

It has been revealed that RAYE was born Rachel Agatha Keen in South London. She attended the BRIT School, as did Olivia Dean, Adele and the late Amy Winehouse. She signed a record deal at 17 and made her name singing dance tracks, while writing for Beyonce and Little Mix. Her second album, 2026's This Music May Contain Hope, features "Where Is My Husband," which topped the UK Singles Chart and peaked at number 11 on the Billboard Hot 100. RAYE leads the 2027 Grammy field with 11 nominations, including Record of the Year, Song of the Year, Album of the Year and Songwriter of the Year, Non-classical.

The singer has already worked with Hans Zimmer, who scored No Time to Die. They collaborated on "Mother Nature" and "Click Clack Symphony" for the 2023 BBC documentary series Planet Earth III. Both songs are exemplary showcases for a sweeping 007 arrangement. "Oscar Winning Tears" brings that same scale to R&B, while "The Thrill is Gone" shows off the bluesy attitude she would bring to the franchise. At the 2025 Oscars, RAYE closed the Bond tribute medley with "Skyfall" after LISA's "Live and Let Die" and Doja Cat's "Diamonds Are Forever." Her soulful voice along with big brass arrangements and a sophisticated orchestra would make Robert Pattinson's 007 entrance feel like a spectacle.

iPhone Duo is getting three new features in iOS 27.3
