💡 Key Takeaways
  • iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s upcoming for Apple’s foldable model.
  • Apple is granting iPhone Duo consumers one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.
  • In a recent development, face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient newly introduced option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 launches next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s upcoming for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo consumers one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

In a recent development, face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient newly introduced option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

In a recent development, use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to swiftly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

Industry observers note that if your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most users, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

In a recent development, on a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

Reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

Industry observers note that you can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great latest option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces fresh iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that users have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a newly introduced setting so users can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

Recent findings suggest that by default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

Industry observers note that it’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and newly introduced keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z.

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how.

Which new iPhone Duo features in iOS 27.3 are you most excited for? Let us know in the comments.

Industry observers note that amazon is running early Black Friday deals on its Fire TV streaming devices, with the Fire TV Stick HD down to $15.99 and the Fire TV Cube at $89.99, $110 off its current list price. The discounts follow an August price increase across the Fire TV lineup. For more editor-vetted tech deals, check out the rest of our Black Friday coverage.

That noted, with the 4K Select costing $2 more and the new Stick 4K $5 more, the HD makes the most sense for TVs that top out at 1080p. This PCMag review has more on its performance.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Game of Thrones was, to put it mildly, a cultural phenomenon.
  • The series was popular for its romantic and political themes, its massive scale, action sequences, and its memorable cast of characters.
  • Legend of the Seeker is a show that was not received well by critics, but was appreciated more by fans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Game of Thrones was, to put it mildly, a cultural phenomenon. It's nearly impossible to describe how huge this show really was in the world of television. Based on the novels by George R. R. Martin, the show ran for eight seasons before concluding, ushering in a newly introduced era of fantasy TV, where the genre has become more popular than ever.

The series was popular for its romantic and political themes, its massive scale, action sequences, and its memorable cast of characters. Since its conclusion in 2019, however, many fans have been left feeling unsatisfied, especially given how many fans were disappointed by its conclusion. If this sounds like you, you may wish to check out these shows like Game of Thrones, which can offer some relief, if not total temporary replacement.

Legend of the Seeker is a show that was not received well by critics, but was appreciated more by fans. Granted, it is not a perfect show; heck, it isn't even a great one. However, it might be just the thing to replace Game of Thrones for those who need a fantasy series to binge. The show is based on the novels by Terry Goodkind, who has always been a controversial figure, which is likely why the show was badly reviewed or barely acknowledged.

Sources indicate that the show follows the life of a young man as he begins seeking revenge following the murder of his father, which unravels conspiracies and reveals secrets. The series was canceled after two seasons, which may have been the right call due to its reception and revenue. Regardless, it's enjoyable enough for some fantasy fans, meaning those who miss Thrones may find some solace in this one.

The Shannara Chronicles is an underrated little gem based on the novels by Terry Brooks. The series of novels is widely considered one of the most defining works of fantasy, though the show never lived up to this reputation. It's not bad whatsoever; it just wasn't super popular upon release. Set in the distant future, after an apocalyptic event has reduced humanity back to the Middle Ages, the story is about a half-human/half-elf on a quest to prevent a magical tree from dying and releasing a horde of demons.

The show stars Austin Butler as the protagonist, Wil, before he became as popular as he is now. As fun as the show is, the fact that it got cut short is a major turnoff for a lot of fantasy fans. However, if you're looking for a series with a complex, layered, and magical world, while also being based on a beloved novel series, The Shannara Chronicles might just be the series for you.

Xena: Warrior Princess is actually a spin-off of another series, yet it became wildly more successful than its predecessor. Today, it is considered a cult series, which is constantly being rediscovered by eager fans. The show is set in Ancient Greece, in the First Century BCE. The principal actor is Lucy Lawless, who plays the eponymous Xena. Xena is a completely original character that does not appear in real Greek mythology, yet the way she is written allows her to seamlessly integrate.

In a recent development, though much of the show is about Xena and her doing battle with various monsters from Greek myth, politics and romance do play a major part in the story. Namely, in the way that Xena attempts to prevent the Roman Republic, under the reign of Julius Caesar, from expanding too far into Greece. It's not as mature or violent as Thrones, but it's still a superb series and a staple of the '90s that is perfect for filling the void that Thrones left behind.

Unlike a lot of the other shows on this list, Outlander is actually a low fantasy. What this means is that it is set on Earth, throughout various points in history, rather than a fabricated, secondary world. It opens in the years following World War II, when a former nurse is magically sent back in time, arriving in the 18th Century. Here, she meets a Scottish Highland warrior whom she falls in love with. Across the show's various seasons, the two star-crossed lovers move through various periods in history.

Recent findings suggest that based on a novel series by Diana Gabaldon, Outlander is, at heart, a romantasy TV show, which can turn a lot of people off. However, it does share a lot of common themes with Game of Thrones. For one, it's actually quite action-packed and features a lot of politics and feuding nobles. And of course, it's chock-full of steamy romance, including sex scenes, which, let's face it, is one of the main reasons Thrones sold so well.

Recent findings suggest that the Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power got off to an admittedly rough start. Based on the enormous legendarium crafted by groundbreaking fantasy author J. R. R. Tolkien, the series is an almost entirely original story using familiar characters. It exists as a separate entity from Peter Jackson's master-crafted film trilogy, and was meant to serve as the flagship fantasy series for Amazon Prime Video.

However, three seasons in, it finally seems to be hitting its stride. Fans and critics alike were much more receptive to this new season, even those who were harsher on the previous two. For those missing Game of Thrones, The Rings of Power provides a similar sprawling, lore-heavy, high fantasy world, political drama, large-scale battles, and a cast of memorable characters.

According to recent reports, the Witcher got off on the right foot, but has been kind of dragging itself down lately. Based on the beloved novels by Andrzej Sapkowski, The Witcher is about a professional monster hunter called a Witcher, who roams around a high fantasy world searching for contracts to make his living. Along the way, he meets numerous enemies and allies, and even establishes himself in some high courts.

This is definitely a dark fantasy show, with all of the cynicism that Game of Thrones bears. Most of the beasts and beings featured in the show are all pulled straight from folklore and mythology from cultures around the world, making for a fascinating mish-mash of magic. This show came out at exactly the right time, just months after Thrones ended, and was the perfect replacement that a lot of people needed. For a time, at least.

The Wheel of Time is based on a series of 15 novels by the late author Robert Jordan. The series is set thousands of years in Earth's future, where a tired age is concluding. As the world prepares for armageddon, the search begins for the Chosen One known as the Dragon Reborn, who is destined to either save the world from its destruction, or to destroy it himself.

The show got off to a rocky start, but each season proved better than the one before it, culminating in the excellent third season. Why Amazon Prime decided to cancel it at this point remains mystifying. Regardless, the show is full of politics, romance, and massive battle sequences. Though it developed its own distinct identity and style from Game of Thrones, the two share a lot of similar tropes.

Netflix's Kingdom is a South Korean fantasy/horror series that's about as close to Thrones as you can get. Set in the historic kingdom of Joseon at the turn of the 17th Century, the story centres on a beleaguered prince who desperately tries to hold onto his throne as a rival clan tries to usurp it from him. In the process, the rival Haewon Cho family uses a mythical resurrection plant to unleash a zombie horde.

Recent findings suggest that based on a webtoon turned graphic novel, Kingdom has all the hallmarks that Thrones did: large-scale battles, an army of the undead, feuding royals, romance, and a cast of colourful characters. It really is one of the most perfect replacements you can find, even if it is low fantasy rather than high fantasy. Sadly, the show was soft-cancelled by Netflix after two seasons and one special episode.

According to recent reports, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms is the second spin-off series from the Game of Thrones universe. It is set 100 years prior to Thrones, though it operates on a much smaller scale. The story is based on the novellas written by George R. R. Martin, colloquially dubbed "Dunk and Egg" by fans. The show follows a hedge knight and his trusty young squire as they travel across the land of Westeros, never quite fitting in wherever they go.

It has been revealed that as mentioned, the scale of this show is substantially smaller. It's not necessarily about politics or huge battles, and is more of a traveller's tale with heavy elements of comedy. It's still action-packed, to be sure, albeit these fights are much more about one-on-one scraps rather than clashes of armies. Regardless, it's a perfect return to form for the universe, and an excellent show in general.

Recent findings suggest that house of the Dragon is the first spin-off of Game of Thrones, which is set centuries prior to the original series. This one is a little more in line with the original, featuring heavy doses of politics, romance, feuding royal clans, and epic battles. Of course, as the title implies, this one also features many more dragons, which are often used as air support during mentioned battles.

In a recent development, specifically, the show is about the Targaryen clan and their rise to power; how they conquered Westeros and united the Seven Kingdoms under one banner, albeit not without their fair share of adversaries. It allows fans of Thrones to examine the inner workings of a nearly extinct family from the original, while also providing the closest experience to Thrones as possible.

#74202. Latest Update: Windows has two settings that bring work back after restart, both off by default

📅 27 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (867 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Makeuseof ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Windows has two settings that bring work back after restart, both off by default

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Makeuseof

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I'd turned off every startup app, yet Windows could still reopen the apps I'd been using before a restart.
  • Together, they let Windows restore much of my interrupted workspace without making me open the same apps every time I start my PC.
  • A PC that's been slowing down forces some, a few low-memory crashes forced others, and updates add their own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I'd turned off every startup app, yet Windows could still reopen the apps I'd been using before a restart. I found this out after enabling a setting that was off by default on my PC. A second setting brought back my File Explorer windows too.

Together, they let Windows restore much of my interrupted workspace without making me open the same apps every time I start my PC.

My restarts are never planned. A PC that's been slowing down forces some, a few low-memory crashes forced others, and updates add their own. Setting active hours only changes when an revision restarts you, not what you come back to. Each time, the apps, tabs, and folder I was using are gone.

The first setting is Automatically save my restartable apps and restart them when I sign back in. It does most of the work. You’ll find it in Settings -> Accounts -> Sign-in options, under Additional settings. It was off on my PC, so I had to toggle it on.

It's different from startup apps in Task Manager. That only opens the same list on every boot, whether you used them or not. This setting reopens what you actually had open before the restart.

Recent findings suggest that I turned it on, opened Notepad with two tabs and some unsaved text, plus Firefox, Word, Settings, and two File Explorer windows, and restarted. Notepad was back before the desktop finished loading, with both tabs and my text exactly where I'd been typing. Firefox, Word, and Settings followed.

According to recent reports, windows doesn’t reopen every app in its exact spot. Settings came back on its home page, not the Sign-in options page I’d been on. That's a small price to pay compared with opening everything manually; even Workspaces doesn't do that much.

This is what sold me. I keep the session restore setting off in Firefox, Chrome, and Brave, on purpose. I use Rewind to restore whatever I’m working on, and I switch between editing and writing a lot. If a browser reopened old tabs on its own, I’d have to clear them out before restoring the session I want, and the tabs would pile up.

I want a clean slate every time I open a browser. None of them is in my startup apps either, and if I open any of them by hand, I get one empty tab.

After the restart, Firefox came back with the tabs restored the way I left them, even before my internet connection was back, with no error page. In my later tests with both settings on, Chrome and Brave did the same. The Windows setting was the only thing I'd changed, and it was the only reason those tabs returned.

To me, that's the right behavior for a restore feature. On a normal day, I get a fresh browser. When Windows restarts and interrupts me, I get my session back.

Industry observers note that file Explorer didn't come back with the first setting, so I turned to the second option: Restore previous folder windows at logon. To find it, open File Explorer, select the three-dot menu -> Options -> View tab. It was off on my PC, too. I switched the restartable apps setting off to test the folder option on its own. Then I opened Downloads, Videos, and Documents in three windows, arranged them with Windows 11 Snap Layouts.

All three came back with the restart, in the same layout, each in the exact folder I’d been in. I didn't have to navigate through any folder paths again, and nothing else reopened. So this setting does one job, and it does it cleanly.

According to recent reports, the two settings are separate on my PC. Microsoft’s release notes for Windows 11 22H2 and 23H2 say turning on the apps setting automatically switches on some File Explorer settings, and they describe a gradual rollout. On my 25H2 build, the folder box stayed unchecked after I turned the apps toggle on, and Explorer stayed closed until I ticked it myself. If you want both, switch on both.

It has been revealed that the fair complaint is that it doesn't bring everything back. With both settings on, I had nine apps open: Chrome with eight or nine tabs, Brave, Firefox, Word, Notepad, Paint, File Explorer, VLC, and CapCut with a file open.

Seven came back where I left them, including the browser tabs. VLC and CapCut never opened. I felt the CapCut exception because I do my edits there, so I still had to relaunch and find my files again.

These settings don’t guarantee that every app will return or resume exactly where it stopped. But I'll still take that every time. Without the settings, a restart leaves me with an empty desktop and nine apps to reopen from memory. With them, I open two apps manually.

If your PC regularly needs a restart, for whatever reason, enable both settings before the next one.

When the next update asks for a restart, let it. Mine brought back the same apps as a routine restart. Whatever stays closed is your list to open by hand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s such a gratifying feeling that comes from finishing a really good book, closing it up, reflecting on its quality and placing it back on your bookshelf.

I spend a good deal of time flipping through autobiographies written by my favorite wrestlers, musicians and media personalities. Visual history books dedicated to the video games, comic books and anime I love also keep me entertained for hours. I’m always searching for the next great book that’ll keep me from staring at my phone and reading rage-baiting tweets in my spare time.

According to recent reports, chatGPT is capable of stepping up to be everyone's personal book curator. It has certainly put me on the right path to finding even more quality reads based on what it knows about the genres I like, the authors I’m a fan of and even the sort of books that I’m not really all that into.

Industry observers note that these prompts have helped expand my collection of books, and I’m sure they’ll do the same for all my fellow bookworms reading this right now. Try any of these out and see where ChatGPT leads you next on your journey for more quality literature.

Inputting any of the following seven prompts into ChatGPT, while also providing it with your literary tastes, favorite authors, preferred styles of writing that compel you the most and current mood, will help it highlight a list of books you may end up adoring next.

The first prompt works quite well in commanding ChatGPT to examine the deeper literary qualities attached to your favorite books. The second prompt works to showcase the type of books that deliver the same type of emotional experiences you derived from your last read. The third prompt is perfect for book hunters who are on the lookout for less celebrated books that you may not have known about beforehand. The fourth prompt is the ultimate mood-book matcher, as it takes note of how you’re presently feeling and shows you the type of books that could get you out of a mental funk or put you in a more relaxing mood.

The fifth prompt puts ChatGPT in the mindset of a book recommendation engine that gives you the sort of books that explore genres you may have overlooked. The sixth prompt goes even further to help ChatGPT suggest what books you should read, as it mentions both your literary likes and dislikes.

As for the seventh and final prompt, it works as a survey that gives ChatGPT everything it could possibly know about you to give you the best book recommendations possible.

Feel free to refer to the seven prompts listed below and try them out for yourself to see where your next book-filled adventures lead you next:.

And as an extra follow-up response, this next prompt can help ChatGPT do another round of evaluation to see which books truly match your tastes and weed out any made-up books it may have suggested:.

It has been revealed that now challenge your own recommendations. Which [number] books on this list are the weakest matches for my tastes, and why? Replace them with better alternatives. Don't invent titles or authors, and tell me where you're uncertain.

Running to ChatGPT to tell it to recommend you a bunch of newly introduced and old books worth reading without being as descriptive as possible about your tastes is a waste of time. The chatbot needs every piece of information about your interests across the literary spectrum to tailor its book recommendations to match everything you enjoy (and don’t enjoy as much).

In a recent development, hopefully, by the end of each ChatGPT session that kicks off with any of these prompts, you’ll leave it with one or a bunch of strong suggestions that could keep you and your book club occupied for months on end. Let me know how you get on in the comments below.

Earlier this week, Apple revealed that Siri AI usage limits will be implemented in iOS 27.3 and explained how iCloud+ increases those limits. Now we have a real-world example of what it looks like when limits are hit, and details on what counts toward those limits.

Siri AI and select other AI features will begin having usage limits in iOS 27.3 for advanced tasks.

This is standard practice with other AI services like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude because these tools rely on server-based models rather than running entirely on-device.

Industry observers note that here’s an example from the iOS 27.3 beta showing what it looks like when you hit your Siri AI daily usage limit. Per Ben in a post on X:.

I hit my Siri AI usage limit, it still works though, including complex questions pic.twitter.com/XYYNPMnSnn.

In a follow-up post, Ben clarifies that complex questions did stop working shortly after posting. As expected though, basic requests continued to work as usual—they don’t have a usage limit.

One question that Apple hasn’t made clear is what qualifies as a complex or “advanced” Siri AI request. The company shares just two examples of something advanced:.

Suppose it gets it wrong like it does most of the time. I wonder if that still counts.

Recent findings suggest that but leaker pdfu has discovered exactly the instructions Siri AI follows to determine whether a request counts as basic or advanced. In a post on X he outlines the parameters for requests deemed “advanced.”.

Siri AI will check the request against this list, and if it involves any of these, it’s deemed “advanced.”.

Industry observers note that it would be helpful if Apple publicly documented these guidelines for users. But perhaps after iOS 27.3 ships and usage limits are fully implemented, we’ll get more detail from the company.

  • Recent findings suggest that but to skeptics of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another tech giant is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

Recent findings suggest that but to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

According to recent reports, love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering latest security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Industry observers note that mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October enhancement. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

Recent findings suggest that it's notable to understand that just about every manufacturer that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

It has been revealed that barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as rapidly as possible.

Industry observers note that the implications aren't specific to any one manufacturer, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that suave looks, premium build, comfortable plush ear cushions, and drool-worthy sound — these make the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset one of the best PS5 headsets around.
  • Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
  • In a recent development, the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset improves on its predecessors in nearly every way to deliver one of the best gaming headsets of 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that suave looks, premium build, comfortable plush ear cushions, and drool-worthy sound — these make the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset one of the best PS5 headsets around. Fitted with custom planar drivers designed in collaboration with Audeze, the Pulse delivers life-like sound across genres. 30 hours of battery life and simultaneous dual-point connectivity are cherries on top of the cake. However, I wish the bass was more powerful and the headset had a mobile companion app.

Bass could have been more powerful.

Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

In a recent development, the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset improves on its predecessors in nearly every way to deliver one of the best gaming headsets of 2026. Sony’s Tempest 3D Audio works in conjunction with the headset’s planar drivers, creating excellent life-like, rich and directional sound. The Pulse is mighty comfortable and looks great. It offers up to 30 hours of battery life, and its mic performance is much better than its pricier sibling.

But it pains me to say that this headset isn’t perfect. While customization is easy through your PS5’s settings, I wish there was a mobile companion app for those using the headset with their computers or phones. And while the overall sound quality is amazing, the bass sounds a little thin.

Recent findings suggest that should you still buy it? I think so. To find out why, read my full Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset review.

PlayStation 5, PlayStation Portal, PC, macOS, Android, iOS.

2.4GHz PlayStation Link, Bluetooth.

From its suave looks and respectable battery life, to its detailed sound and affordable price point, the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset is an excellent headset for PS5 gamers.

As someone who’s been loyal to PlayStation for a decade, I’ve always loved the consoles’ sleek and premium design. While the original Sony PlayStation Pulse 3D Wireless Headset ($99) wasn’t bad-looking per se, I much prefer the minimalist approach Sony has taken towards the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset.

The upcoming headset sports an understated design with round earcups that is still, at its core, quintessentially Sony. Available in either Midnight Black or White, I think the Pulse looks brilliant. It doesn’t draw attention to itself, and its simple design means you can use it as a regular set of cans when you’re traveling.

Sources indicate that in addition to its good looks, the Pulse is mighty comfortable, too. The faux leather ear cushions are soft with a matte texture, and the earcups are spacious enough that they engulf my ears perfectly. Even after seven straight hours of wear, my ears didn’t feel sweaty or too hot. The pads can be twisted off, too, in case they get damaged and need replacing.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

On the Pulse’s headband, you’ll find foam cushioning that helps alleviate pressure you’d otherwise feel on the top of your head. However, this cushioning feels like it’s made up of more air than anything else. I don’t necessarily think this is a massive drawback as the Pulse is a fairly lightweight headset.

The Pulse weighs just 10.58 ounces. That’s similar to the Pulse 3D (10.37 ounces) but lighter than the first-party Pulse Elite ($149, 12.2 ounces) and third-party Cherry XTRFY H3 ($99, 11.46 ounces). Sony hasn’t compromised on the Pulse’s build quality while maintaining its light frame either, as the headset feels solid.

As has become tradition for Sony at this point, it has fitted with PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset with custom planar magnetic drivers (four magnets per driver). These have been developed in collaboration with Audeze, the audio giant of Maxwell 2 ($329) fame, and a brand Sony acquired back in 2023. The drivers are programmed to deliver three-dimensional life-like sound across genres — and the Pulse excels at doing just that.

In a recent development, to take full advantage of the sound quality, I recommend diving into your PS5’s settings and creating your personalized 3D sound profile (it takes around five minutes). PlayStation’s Tempest 3D Audio, in conjunction with the Pulse’s planar drivers, delivers phenomenal spatial and directional audio. I tested it out by playing Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced, and Cyberpunk 2077 on my PS5 Slim.

In a recent development, in AC Black Flag Resynced, I appreciated how immersed the 3D Audio made me feel. At this price, the directional audio is phenomenal. I could tell exactly which direction the sounds were coming from. When surrounded by small and major ships during naval combat, I could pinpoint their locations even when I couldn’t see them. My ship’s creaking was loud and clear, adding to the immersion. When on land, I loved hearing rain falling on the palm trees right overhead, like they were actually falling above me.

Directional audio proved effective in Cyberpunk 2077, too, where I used it to my advantage to listen out for footsteps and determine my enemies’ positions. This made stealthily infiltrating enemy camps a walk in the park. The Pulse also has a wide soundstage with every aspect sounding well-balanced. Bullets sounded sharp as they whizzed past and ricocheted off the walls.

Recent findings suggest that dialogues across all three games sounded detailed and life-like, especially in Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 which has some of the best voice acting known to man (argue with the wall). I could feel the emotions in the characters’ voices, and the wobble in their throats was clear during certain scenes. The Pulse made cutscenes feel dramatic and immersive. My only complaint with the Pulse is the bass… which I’ll discuss in detail shortly.

In a recent development, does the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset have the longest battery life in its price range? Nope, the Cherry XTRFY H3 with its 100-hour rating takes the crown, but the Pulse doesn’t give you much to complain about. Sony says that the headset should last you up to 30 hours between charges — that’s 18 hours longer than the Pulse 3D (12-hour rating) and the same as the pricier Pulse Elite.

Recent findings suggest that given that I have a full-time job, I couldn’t play games for 30 hours to test the Pulse’s battery life (I wish I could…), so instead, I left it running overnight with Cyberpunk 2077 running at 50% volume on my PS5. I was prompted to charge the headset around the 29-hour mark. Your mileage will naturally depend on volume and other settings, but good to see that Sony’s rating is fairly accurate.

Sources indicate that when we reviewed the OG Sony PlayStation Pulse 3D, we found its microphone to be underwhelming. Similarly, the Sony PlayStation Pulse Elite’s mic was simply okay and nothing special. That’s why I am so pleased that the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset’s mic is much, much improved.

Industry observers note that the Pulse features a built-in integrated mic with AI-powered noise rejection, and it makes you sound loud and clear. I tested the mic by calling my friend, Harry, who was also testing the headset for TechRadar (our sister site). I was pleasantly surprised by how warm he sounded — and he said the same about my voice. There was plenty of nuance in his voice and his words didn’t bleed into one another. When I was hovering over the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 icon, his voice still came through clearly without being overpowered by the background music.

Even though it doesn’t feature a detachable boom mic, the Pulse’s mic’s performance feels on par with that of the Cherry XTRFY H3, and it even upstages the Turtle Beach Stealth 500 ($99).

The Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset is compatible with the PlayStation 5, PlayStation Portal, Windows and macOS machines, and iOS and Android smartphones. There are two ways of connecting the Pulse to your device. Simply plug in the included PlayStation Link USB-C dongle into your console or laptop for lag-free audio, and you’re good to go. There’s also Bluetooth connectivity for connecting to the Portal (which has PlayStation Link built into it).

It has been revealed that what’s even better is that the Pulse features audio mixing and dual-point connectivity. What this basically means is that if you’ve got the Pulse connected to your phone via Bluetooth and to your PS5 using the dongle, you’ll be able to listen to both at the same time. No need to swap sources manually or pause one to listen to the other. Want to watch/listen to a YouTube tutorial while playing GTA 6? Easily done.

Audio mixing isn’t a brand new feature as we’ve seen it on headsets like the Razer Barracuda V2 Pro ($199)... but it’s also missing from headsets that cost more than the Pulse, like the Logitech G Pro X3 Lightspeed ($249) and the Fractal Design Scape ($199). That’s a win for Sony in my book.

One of the best things about the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset is that it doesn’t break the bank. It has a retail price of $99 at Amazon U.S. / £89 at Currys U.K. and given the trend with other Pulse models, I expect the Pulse to receive major price cuts during sales events next year.

The Pulse is priced similarly to the OG Pulse 3D ($99), the Cherry XTRFY H3 ($99), and it’s cheaper than the Pulse Elite ($149). I also think it offers more bang for your buck compared to the latter. The Pulse is also $100 cheaper than the Pulse Explore earbuds ($199). If you’re willing to wait until early 2027, the Pulse Edge will be launching with even more features, but naturally, I expect it to be pricier than the Pulse.

There isn’t a lot wrong with the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset, but it’s vital to note that there’s no smartphone app, and the bass sounds slightly thin.

While I love the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset’s wide soundstage and life-like sound (as I waxed lyrical about earlier), I really wish the bass was more powerful. In Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, I found that my magic attacks didn’t land with much oomph. Luna’s Elemental Trick and Elemental Genesis are meant to rumble and shake the ground, but that wasn’t the case through the Pulse.

In a recent development, similarly, in Control, the Hiss’ low-end drone felt more like a buzz, which meant that the alien-like enemies didn’t feel as unnerving as they do through a high-end headset, like the Razer BlackShark V3 Pro ($249). You’ll need to spend a lot more to get full-bodied sound.

As I mentioned earlier, the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset’s settings can be adjusted via the PS5’s settings — and there’s no other way to do it. Yes, even though the headset is compatible with computers and smartphones, you won’t be able to change its equalizer and other settings unless you have access to a PS5.

According to recent reports, I wouldn’t say this is a dealbreaker per se as the Pulse is a PlayStation-first headset. But I would caution against getting it if you play across multiple platforms. A headset like the Logitech G325 Lightspeed ($79) or the Turtle Beach Stealth 500 might be better suited to your needs if that’s the case.

Industry observers note that the Sony PlayStation Pulse Wireless Headset might not be perfect but it’s still a darn good set of cans. Sporting plush ear cushions that feel like hugs for your ears, the Pulse is supremely comfortable for long gaming sessions. 30 hours of battery life, dual-point connectivity, and strong mic performance are great, but it's the headset’s 3D audio that will swiftly win you over.

Sources indicate that while its soundstage is commendable, the Pulse struggles to reproduce ground-shaking bass (which is to be expected at this price). Customizing the headset is easy through your PS5’s settings but if you proposal on using it with your smartphone or computer, you won’t find any companion apps on those platforms.

According to recent reports, at the end of the day, if you’re after detailed, life-like sound that feels immersive, and a comfortable fit that doesn’t hurt your ears after a few hours, I can’t recommend the Pulse enough. It punches way above its weight.

#74182. Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1500 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple, TTP respond]

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow consumers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow consumers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of Latest Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Enhancement, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:.

Industry observers note that “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for owners. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

In a recent development, just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the company said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Recent findings suggest that apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company mentioned that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Update, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

Apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps crucial problems and leaves out key context. The company says it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

There are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The company defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also says it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

In a recent development, as for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out fresh child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

It has been revealed that every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an update that addresses one of its people’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let users edit a Story after publishing.

This means users will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that customers will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”.

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

Today’s upgrade is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting consumers manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a newly introduced interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month.
  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.
  • In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue mentioned Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a newly introduced interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue mentioned Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

Recent findings suggest that when we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a significant way on latest and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are upcoming or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a upcoming logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe remarked he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a firm and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

How to nail your lawn’s final cut — without inviting winter moss and frost damage

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That last cut before winter is the trickiest mow of the year, and most lawn damage blamed on harsh winter weather actually starts with a badly timed final pass.
  • In a recent development, because shifting fall weather rarely follows a neat schedule, watching the calendar will only steer you wrong.
  • It has been revealed that the surest signal it's time to pack the mower away is when your grass noticeably stops growing between cuts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

That last cut before winter is the trickiest mow of the year, and most lawn damage blamed on harsh winter weather actually starts with a badly timed final pass. Leave your grass too long and damp fall air turns it into a breeding ground for moss and snow mold, scalp it too short or mow over waterlogged turf, and the first hard freeze will weaken the roots until spring.

In a recent development, because shifting fall weather rarely follows a neat schedule, watching the calendar will only steer you wrong. Instead, your lawn gives away one clear visual sign when it is ready for winter, and knowing how to spot it, alongside a few simple mower adjustments, makes all the difference before the first freeze arrives.

It has been revealed that the surest signal it's time to pack the mower away is when your grass noticeably stops growing between cuts. Once the blades stay roughly the same height a week or two after a trim, your lawn has entered winter dormancy and no longer needs cutting.

Grass responds directly to soil and air temperatures, so most cool-season lawns continue putting on slow growth until daytime temperatures dip consistently below 50°F (and around 60°F for warm-season grasses).

As long as your turf is still actively growing, it benefits from occasional maintenance — but once temperatures drop and growth stalls, continuing to mow only stresses dormant blades that cannot repair themselves until spring.

In a recent development, when your grass is still putting on a little growth in late fall, a careful, well-timed trim sets it up to bounce back thicker and greener next year. Follow these four rules before storing your mower for the season:.

Industry observers note that never scalp the lawn for its final pass of the year. Set your mower to one of its highest settings, leaving the grass around 2 to 2.5 inches tall, so the blades have enough surface area to absorb winter sunlight while shielding the roots from freezing air.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It has been revealed that before making your final pass, rake or blow away thick layers of fallen leaves. Wet leaves block sunlight and smother the grass underneath, and running a mower straight over a heavy blanket of them clogs your deck and leaves soggy clumps behind.

Industry observers note that clear stubborn, matted pine needles in seconds with the EGO Power+ 56V Cordless Blower. Blasting up to 880 CFM and 200 MPH, its lightweight carbon-fiber frame, digital status display, and brushless motor deliver gas-rivaling muscle without the fumes or hassle.

Fall rain can leave lawns saturated for days at a time. Never mow wet grass or soggy soil, as heavy mower wheels compact the ground, tear out weakened roots, and leave muddy ruts that linger until spring. Wait for a dry, mild afternoon when the turf feels firm underfoot.

Even if your lawn looks a little shaggy, keep the mower in the shed whenever frost is on the ground or a hard freeze is in the forecast. Walking on or cutting frozen grass snaps the brittle blades, leaving brown, scorched patches that take months to recover.
